This paper proves that all graded Zinbiel algebras possess a significant lie property - they are solvable. To achieve this result, a new idea is introduced - the algebra's solvability can be determined by examining the solvability of its associated lower central series of distributions. This concept is demonstrated to lead to a straightforward verification method for an algebra's solvable nature. Specifically in the case of Zinbien algebras, it is shown that their derived distribution and its subsequent distributions generated from repeated commutator products are sequentially solvable. Consequently, these yield a sequence of distributive structures, ultimately allowing for the conclusion that Zinbiel algebras are solvable. Notably, this property can be visibly exhibited through the algebras' related identities. Moreover, a notable connection is established between the solvable property of an algebra and the solvable property of its associated Biharam group of automorphisms. This specifically takes the form of a solvability criterion for the Biharam group, which in turn serves as a necessary condition for the algebra's solvable nature. This particular condition is shown to be both required and sufficient for a particular class of algebras, thereby demonstrating its utility. All aforementioned results and their implications are made evident through a selection of Zinbiel algebras presented as examples. These results and their implications also extend to a more general class of algebras known as G-algebras. All original research presented within this paper has been previously unpublished. It is worth noting that the results and their derivations can be achieved using a more general concept that is applicable beyond the specifically examined Zinbiel algebras. This broader principle can be applied to any algebra that satisfies the condition of being defined by a specific set of identities related to its own automorphisms. This particular set of identities specifically related to the Biharam group of an algebra $A$, denoted as $B\Im (A)$, is given by the system of coefficients $c_{abc}^{def}$ that satisfy the condition $\phi_{abc} (c_{abc}^{def}) =0$ for all possible $a,b,c,d,e,f$. This principle can be utilized to establish the solvable property of a particular class of Malcev algebras. All the aforementioned results and their proofs will be presented and discussed in the subsequent chapters. Our novel framework, Neural Description Fields, overcomes the challenge of creating object representations that account for different possible orientations and positions within three-dimensional space when comparing descriptions to objects. This issue with orientation and scale ambiguity has long been a limitation in computer vision, ever since the introduction of the Markov Random Field in 2009 by Houghton and Fraser. We have demonstrated that our Neural Description Fields can effectively capture the symmetry of three-dimensional objects, ensuring that object representations made at various orientations and positions are considered equivalent. This is achieved without requiring a vast number of samples to train our model, nor does it involve complicated inference procedures. Our approach takes advantage of a compact and differentiable representation of the symmetry of three-dimensional objects, derived from their 3D mesh models. This representation serves as the foundation for an innovative orientation-aware L2 loss that further enhances the uniqueness of object representations when comparing descriptions to objects. We have tested the efficacy of Neural Description Fields on six diverse datasets, encompassing both simulated and real-world data, with results showing significant improvements in accuracy compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ivma-se3/neural-description-fields.

Recently, machine learning based pose estimation methods from a single image have seen significant advancements but are still prone to pose estimation with large orientation angles exceeding 90 degrees being challenging. In response, a new framework called DeepHMap++ has been proposed to estimate full 6D poses directly from just one color or monochrome image. Within this framework, the orientation estimation component uses clustering in projected images to break down the pose search space, splitting it into a series of smaller class-specific problems that are more manageable, allowing our algorithm to focus on better local minimum capture. In addition, we present an innovative method called the Strongest Correspondence, based on the analysis of multiple feature points across different clusters, designed to enhance the robustness of our framework by combining the benefits of both local and global correspondences. The inclusion of a quality assurance metric helps filter out any potentially unreliable orientation estimates. The DeepHMap++ framework has been put to the test on a subset of the ITA dataset that is particularly difficult, showing a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods. With its robustness demonstrated, this framework also shows potential for real-world applications. All code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuanghua/DeepHMap++. Moreover, an optimized version of our framework has been utilized to create the DeepHMap++ dataset, consisting of a large set of images with challenging orientation angles exceeding 90 degrees, along with their corresponding 6D poses. This new dataset can be used as a rigorous test for any machine learning based pose estimation algorithm seeking to demonstrate its capability in determining full 6D poses from just one image. It is available for download at https://kuanghua.github.io/DeepHMap++.htm. The DeepHMap++ framework has also been shown to outperform the current state-of-the-art methods on a widely used benchmark called the BOP Benchmark. With its strong performance, this framework has the potential to contribute to the advancement of various real world applications including but not limited to 3D object manipulation, autonomous driving, and robotic assembly. We present GGLasso, a Python package designed to calculate the Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGLasso) and related metrics for compounds and partial correlations in multivariate linear regression models. This library can also determine node and compound sparsity thresholds, facilitating the selection of hyperparameters that balance model complexity and prediction accuracy. GGLasso is tailored for large datasets and employs optimized Cython implementations of key functions, leveraging the scipy.optimize.minimize function with default solvers, including SLSQP, COBYLA, and BFGS. The package comprises example use cases, including synthetic data and real-world applications such as the NIPS 2009 simulated data, Alzheimer's disease, and a colon cancer microarray experiment. Numerous methods for molecular simulation configure molecules into initial positions, but determining the optimal set of configurations remains a significant challenge. I propose the "Minimum Mean Square Distance" (MMSD) objective to guide Monte Carlo samples of configurational ensembles through gentle, random movements using Langevin Dynamics. This proposal leverages the principles of ergodicity and stationarity to ensure that the most reliable configurational ensembles are generated, fully utilizing the available computational resources. A hybrid algorithm is introduced to balance between multiple degrees of freedom, allowing for an adaptive time step that prevents wasting steps in the flat regions of the potential energy surface. The results show significant improvements in precision and speed in achieving converged configurational ensembles for a Lennard-Jones cluster and polyethylene chains. The proposed MMSD objective and the associated Langevin Dynamics framework can be applied to a broad range of molecular models, offering a powerful tool for addressing various molecular simulation tasks, from biomolecular simulations to material design and chemistry, facilitated by the open-source code available for this method.

Our novel method, Eigenvector Prominence, adapts the traditional eigenvector centrality approach to effectively identify notable nodes at the intersection of multiple interconnected networks or within a single multilayer network. Unlike conventional eigenvector centrality, which places equal significance on the values of connected nodes, our approach incorporates a flexible parameter to differentiate between the importance of each node within a given layer. This allows us to account for instances where the significance of connected nodes varies substantially. We have specifically found that this approach can successfully capture the distinct properties of multilayer networks by comparing it to the individual layer eigenvector centrality values. To demonstrate the practical utility of Eigenvector Prominence, we conducted a series of experiments, including identifying influential spreaders within multilayer networks, detecting prominent nodes across networks with varying node significance, and analyzing the results of a simulation where a rumor spreads across a multilayer network. This has implications for a wide range of applications, including sociology, biology, finance, and transportation, among others. Our work also offers a numerical formulation that can be efficiently solved using a quasi-Newton method, making it a practical and readily deployable option for various real-world multilayer network analysis problems. This approach, along with the associated code and data, is available for use and modification upon access to a suitable repository. This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being dropped into flowing water from various heights. When dropped from lower heights, the spheres bounce back, but when dropped from higher heights, they become sealed and stick to the bottom of the water channel. If dropped from an extremely high height, they can also create a cavity and become sealed. The way the water responds to the dropped spheres was studied using a high-speed camera, and from the recorded images, several key points were determined, including when the water and sphere make contact, when the water enters the sphere, and when the sphere becomes sealed. In 1977, Partridge and Ressler-levin developed a method for deciphering text in unknown languages by analyzing linear combinations of their character frequencies. We build upon their technique by applying it to decipher polymers with unknown structures. Specifically, we utilize a linear regression-based approach in conjunction with whole-program analysis to determine the syntax of these polymers. By combining type inference and linear regression, our method is able to provide meaningful estimates for (1) the frequencies of combined productions in context, (2) the probabilities of individual productions, and (2) the probabilities of combined productions in context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique on a range of benchmarks, showing that it is capable of accurately predicting both lexical and syntactic properties given numerical characteristics of individual monomers. Furthermore, our technique for deducing syntactic properties with a linear regression-based approach is applicable to a broader range of contexts, not limited to language development. We also explore and analyze various parameters that influence the accuracy of our technique and present a novel extension called linear type inference, where we use linear regression to guide type inference by estimating the probabilities of types being valid in a program. This extension enables the numerical representation of program properties that capture the statistics of a program's behavior, offering a novel solution to the problem of deductively proving the correctness of random program samples. This achievement is particularly significant because it turns an NP decision problem into a polynomial-time problem. A novel medical image segmentation technique called DDAUnet has been developed to accurately identify neoplastic regions within the esophagus on CT scans. This model incorporates a unique Dense Focus Unet architecture, which combines both dense and focus Unet methods to effectively process images and enhance representation learning. To further improve data processing, the DDAUnet model incorporates residual connections and dilated convolutional layers. To train the model, a customized loss function and data augmentation techniques were employed. Evaluation of the model showed a 75.80% accuracy in predicting neoplastic regions, a 0.85 dice coefficient, and a 0.82 IOU score, outperforming several baseline models, including U-Net, UNet++, and Dense Unet. Code for DDAUnet is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrasoul/DAUnet. With over 12 hours of computation required to train the model, a designed pipeline was developed to train and test the model, as well as generate prediction results. This pipeline facilitates easy replication of the results achieved with the model. A discussion on potential issues with the model, such as slow computation and limited validation set size, is presented. This research was conducted in collaboration with King Fahd Specialist Hospital in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. A simple application of the model known as FocusUnet was also developed, which combines both dense and focus Unet methods to facilitate rapid computation and accurate neoplasm segmentation on CT scans, as demonstrated in the accompanying video. This model was designed to be user-friendly, with a straightforward GUI that allows healthcare professionals to easily input CT scans and generate colored maps indicating neoplastic regions. This model is suitable for use on workstations with limited memory, requiring only 3.5 GB of memory to run, and can handle real-time computation of image segmentation. A downloadable executable program for Windows is available at https://drive.google.com/drive/downloads. This model has the potential for application in various medical imaging analysis tasks, as evidenced by its successful validation on publicly available image segmentation datasets, including CAMRA, DOG, and SHIV. This model has a modular design, with modular code for both the FocusUnet and DDAUnet models, facilitating easy modification and integration of new features. This research was funded by the Deanship of Scientific Research at King Khalid University in Abha, Saudi Arabia. Tantalum oxide compounds, with their varying valencies of five and four, enable the creation of electronic interfaces between different types of charge, a feature shared with other transition metal oxides that can display intriguing phenomena when their interfaces are controlled. Studies on these materials mainly rely on empirical methods due to the complexity of their structures, lacking a clear and certain understanding of their basic, non-defective crystal state. Our ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations aim to establish a comprehensive and precise description of the Ta$_{2}$O$_{5}$ layer structure, and help clarify the earlier reported results of $n$-doping and interface engineering. Our findings show that the Ta$_{2}$O$_{5}$ layer structure consists of two TaO$_{2}$ layers, with one being more oxidized than the other, and this particular arrangement is essential for maintaining the stability of the material. Additionally, our research pinpoints the likely sources of previous discrepancies and outlines possible paths for $n$-doping and interface engineering. These breakthroughs not only provide a deeper understanding of Ta$_{2}$O$_{5}$ but also offer valuable insights that can be applied to other complex oxide layers. Suggested future studies on $n$$-$doping and interface engineering to control the valency of another transition metal oxide, TaNiO$_{3}$, are also presented.

This research investigates the premise that a geographic explanation for language patterns can also be linked to the spread of misinformation. To achieve this aim, the study examines the Big Geographic Arrangement (BGA) proposed by Williams et al. (2019), which posits that internet users in the United States can be grouped into four regions with distinct cultural connections. Utilizing Reddit data from 2009 to 2018, the BGA was confirmed through multiple analysis methods. In further exploration, the research finds that: memes diffuse faster on the periphery than in the interior of the BGA; a notable period in 2010 saw an accelerated spread of new memes across the BGA; and analyzing meme diffusion across the BGA reveals varying regional speeds of adoption. These findings are consistent with theories of infrastructure and network optimization that prioritize diverse regional development over localized consolidation. In conclusion, the BGA provides an actionable framework for studying the dissemination of misinformation on a large scale. As such, it offers potential value in various applications, including the detection of emerging false information. The research highlights the significance of considering both online and offline factors in areas like vaccine distribution and public health communication. In response to criticisms of the BGA's limitations, the study also explores alternative analytical methods, including a non-geographic, community-based approach using Reddit's discussion groups. The results obtained from this analysis reveal similar outcomes, indicating that the BGA's findings are robust and applicable to a broader context. In total, this research contributes to a better comprehension of the complex interplay between geography, culture, and the spread of information, presenting a versatile tool, the BGA, that can be applied in a variety of analyses. This work focuses on analyzing the speech used by humans to label robotic actions through a pointing gesture while providing verbal descriptions. This study's findings can be used to design more precise speech-based robot instruction systems, enabling robots to learn from human demonstrations more efficiently. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the growing number of users with varied online profiles. Existing studies primarily concentrate on intra-domain problems, whereas a plethora of real-world scenarios involve multiple sparse domains in need of joint analysis. Presently, a novel multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation framework, called MS-DOMCA, is introduced to enhance the performance of recommendations across multiple sparse domains. Unlike current methods that overemphasize item popularity, MS-DOMCA employs an improved thorough aspect preference learning strategy, incorporating separate preference and artificial attention mechanisms for deriving a user's true preferences from abundant data. Furthermore, MS-DOMCA optimizes the recruitment of items and the calculation of user and item embeddings through a dynamic process. Experimentally, our findings demonstrate substantial enhancements in recommendation accuracy for various real-world sparse domains, including book, movie, and music recommendations. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chengshin/MS-DOMCA.

Conic programming is an efficient and effective method for optimizing organically-concave functions, which have a specific U-shaped or negative curvature. However, defining these functions can be challenging, especially with non-separable problems that require a global minimum. In response, researchers have developed alternative forms of the Nesterov function and global negative concave functions that can be used in place of their original, non-convex counterparts. These substitutes enable the use of conic programming, a more efficient optimization method, for solving a broader range of problems. This paper introduces Hypatia, a Julia package designed to facilitate the creation of these alternative, conic formulations for an expansive range of organically-concave functions that can be defined by a single, universally applicable parameter. With Hypatia, users can generate these formulations and apply them to various optimization tasks. The package also includes a range of pre-determined formulations that can be used directly, in addition to user-created custom solutions. The code is then used to demonstrate the creation of a formulation for the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno algorithm. The Hypatia package is designed to be user-friendly and extensible, allowing for the creation of custom formulations and interfaces with other optimization tools. The code is available under the MIT license and can be downloaded from GitHub. The package is intended to facilitate the use of conic programming for solving optimization problems that involve a wide range of organically-concave functions. The code is also used to demonstrate the application of Hypatia to the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno algorithm and the Newton Conjugate Gradient method. The package includes a range of user-created custom solutions, in addition to the pre-defined formulations and definitions of the Nesterov function and global negative concave functions. Traditionally, this has been achieved through repeated tests on standardized brain images. A new approach presented here uses machine learning to ensure image quality, based on a broad range of features including both low-frequency data typical of specific image types and high-frequency anomalies indicative of particular defects or artifacts. By recognizing patterns in these features the model is able to make predictions about image quality and type. It has been tested and shown to accurately predict the quality and type of new, unseen images both with the same scanner as well as on a different MRI machine. To analyze the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power grid resilience during distribution network disturbances such as terrorist attacks or natural disasters, a new decision-making model is proposed that prioritizes infrastructure targets for private electric vehicle owners in an attempt to enhance grid stability and minimize damages. A multi-agent optimization framework is introduced to accommodate different electric vehicle owner characteristics and preferences. A dual projection subgradient algorithm is developed to solve the complex multi-agent optimization problem efficiently. A real-world case study from Belgium is used to demonstrate and test the proposed model successfully. The results show that allowing private electric vehicle owners to charge during peak hours when the grid is under stress or when the grid is unstable may compromise the effectiveness of resilience measures. On the other hand, studies have found that encouraging electric vehicle owners to charge before peak hours when the grid is stable or delaying charges until the grid becomes unstable could all contribute to better grid stability. The proposed framework provides utility companies with valuable insights to create targeted policies to manage private electric vehicles effectively and enhance power grid resilience. The research highlights the significance of considering electric vehicle charging patterns in infrastructure target setting and the potential benefits of tailored policies that take into account various electric vehicle owner characteristics and preferences. In our research, we delved into an intriguing aspect where multiple autonomous agents convene in a linear timeline to discuss and agree on a mutual goal. Previously studied models typically feature stationary agents with fixed positions, making it a non-cooperative game where each agent pursues its own distinct objectives. In contrast, our focus is on a more dynamic and challenging problem, incorporating elements of control theory within a multi-agent setting. Each agent maintains its own internal state and strives for a unique target, all while attempting to collaborate with others to reach a collective central objective by a predetermined deadline. Our proposed solution leverages a hybrid strategy, combining both optimistic and pessimistic approaches as the agents move towards their central goal. This leads to a two-layer game where a cooperative component ensures the collective goal is met, and a competitive layer guarantees each agent achieves its individual target. Through numerous simulations, our model has shown significant improvements over existing solutions, adapting to intricate problems with multiple agents and a linear timeline. With the capability to apply incentive systems, our model can also handle problematic scenarios where some agents act maliciously. Our research introduces several new metrics to evaluate meetings effectively, enabling the quantitative analysis of complex multi-agent discussions. Our findings are validated across diverse scenarios, incorporating both natural and artificially designed problems, as well as various sizes of conferences. Our model's adaptability to different conference sizes is also demonstrated, showcasing its ability to handle large meetings with multiple participants. Our research is open-source, available for public use and modification. Our proposed evaluation tools, capable of assessing meetings based on various objectives, can be applied to a wide range of discussions beyond the Recurrent Meeting problem. Our model's ability to incorporate systems of rewards and penalties enables it to handle complex discussions with multiple objectives and constraints, further expanding its purposes to other domains. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of the novel right-handed helical materials GdSn3 and CmSn3, as well as a proposed alloy GdxCm1-xSn3. These calculations, based on density functional theory within the generalized gradient approximation, were analyzed to determine the ground state magnetic configurations of these compounds. Evaluating the lattice parameters, band structures, and density of states enables us to classify GdSn3 and CmSn3 as half-metallic ferromagnets and a potential helical magnet, respectively. Notably, CmSn3 exhibits a unique 5f orbital occupation in its alloy with GdSn3, suggesting it may display an anisotropic 5d-5f double shell electronic structure. Doping CmSn3 with Gd also leads to fascinating consequences, such as the formation of a 5f electron pocket near the fermi level and potential non-collinear magnetic moments. These predictions open the door for further experimental verification and potential use in spintronics and magnetic helical materials. Moreover, we propose that these compounds may exhibit unusual anisotropic magnetic properties, along with an inherent tendency to non-collinearity in Cm-based alloys. These novel characteristics arise from the complex interplay between their helical structure, 5d and 5f electron fillings. These predicted properties make the XSn3 (X = Gd, Cm) and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds an exciting area of research with a wide range of potential applications. This study also highlights the value of computational modeling in guiding both ongoing and future experiments, as well as providing a framework for developing novel materials with tailored electronic and magnetic properties. This research has been theory-based, and future work will focus on experimental verification, including magnetic and electronic transport measurements, as well as X-ray absorption near edge structure. These experiments will enable a deeper understanding of these compounds' electronic structures and validate the predicted helical magnetic ground states, further solidifying the position of these materials at the forefront of novel helical magnetism and spintronics research. This design enables the T hubs to operate as a one-way street for light and quantum information. A novel feature of the T hubs is their ability to create a non-trivial, long-lived entanglement between two distinct points in a silicon-on-diamond material. The proposed design can be further modified to incorporate quantum diamonds as the substrate, which allows for the efficient integration of the T hubs into a silicon-on-diamond platform. The non-reciprocal and quantuminformation properties of the T hubs make them an ideal choice for constructing complex, distributed quantum systems, such as large-scale, multi-qubit networks and quantum simulators that can operate in multiple dimensions. The proposed design offers a high degree of flexibility, enabling the non-reciprocal and quantuminformation properties of the T hubs to be tailored to suit a wide range of applications, from fundamental quantum research to the development of large-scale, practical quantum technologies, including secure communication and optimized material synthesis. The underlying structure of objects within images can be represented by a hierarchical model, consisting of a core and a surrounding context. While context is widely acknowledged as beneficial for object recognition, there is no universally accepted method to evaluate the context effectively. We propose a novel framework that leverages a generated synthetic mask to analyze the relationship between an object and its surrounding context at three different hierarchical levels. By comparing a trained model's responses to both the original image and a processed mask image, our approach enables clear interpretation of these interactions. Specifically, we demonstrate how this framework can be used to assess the influence of context on a model's predictions, as well as provide insights into the presence of artifacts or overfitting. To illustrate the utility of our context assessment framework, we also perform a range of additional analyses to gauge its capabilities. These evaluations can be accessed in the supplementary materials provided. Our approach, intended for general application to any object detection model, is not tied to a particular dataset and can be employed across various scenarios. Our code is available online at https://github.com/AndreaHafner/AssessingContext.

Given a closed symplectic manifold (M,ω) and another non-negative symplectic form ω' on the same manifold M, we can define a new symplectic manifold to be the quotient of M by the flow generated by a Hamiltonian vector field. This results in a new manifold being the time-one map of this flow, which is then equipped with the pushforward symplectic form. We are interested in examining which of these modifications yield rotations. This encompasses a broad category of invariants that can be applied to symplectic reductions, including an alternate proof of the fact that certain transformations, such as negative Darboux, are not realized through symplectic reductions. This also provides a starting point for analyzing and classifying these reductions, which includes an examination of locally symplectically flat reductions and their relation to harmonic functions and Higgs bundles. This is based on the work of several mathematicians, including Harvey, McDuff, Polterovich, Ritter, Sziklai, and Viros, as well as Murphy, Ritter, and Sziklai, and Caglione, Murphy, and Ritter. This is in addition to the contributions of many other mathematicians. This paper also discusses some open problems related to these reductions. This includes a conjecture regarding which negative definite matrices can be realized as the Hessian of a Hamiltonian whose flow generates a rotation, and the relation of these reductions to the symplectic bundle reductions and the monodromy of singular symplectic connections. This in turn is related to the non-overlapping version of Gromov's Weyl law, which states that the number of simple closed trajectories on a symplectic surface (S^2,ω) is determined by the eigenvalues of the moment of inertia tensor, which is equivalent to the sum of the squares of the eigenvalues of the Laplacian of ω. This also encompasses the relation of these reductions to the Schottky group and Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates, as well as the open problem of determining which of these reductions can be realized through symplectic reductions of hyperbolic surfaces. This in addition to the open problem of realizing the Eiermann matrix, which is a negative definite matrix with a specific pattern, as well as the open problem of determining which of these reductions can be realized through bundle reductions and the monodromy of singular connections. This further includes the open problem of establishing an analog of the Hodge theorem for connections in bundles

A significant obstacle in transplanting kidneys arises from the imperfect information available to medical professionals, making it difficult to determine whether a donated kidney is suitable for a particular patient. This issue is particularly pronounced in liver-kidney transplant programs, where patients with end-stage liver disease are often offered kidneys donated by individuals with the same hepatitis C virus genotype. Presently, guidelines recommend transplanting a hepatitis C-positive kidney into a hepatitis C-positive patient, yet this policy lacks a solid scientific basis. Our study examines this practice by analyzing over 1,000 transplants of this nature, where the patients received kidneys from donors with the same hepatitis C genotype. Our findings support the current recommendations, indicating that accepting incompatible kidneys from genetically matched donors with the same hepatitis C genotype does not significantly decrease the one-year survival rate of patients. This study provides valuable insights for healthcare professionals, patients, and organ donation programs, offering a foundation for further research aimed at establishing ideal criteria for accepting incompatible kidneys. Ultimately, our goal is to increase the availability of donated kidneys, given the critical shortage of transplants worldwide. This study focuses on hepatitis C genotype C, which affects a significant population in Asia, particularly in China, India, and Korea. Further studies are necessary to evaluate the suitability of kidneys for other viral genotypes, such as those associated with hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, and human immunodeficiency virus. Our work has important implications for organ donation programs, offering a framework for evaluating the suitability of kidneys for patients with specific viral genotypes and increasing the efficiency of transplants. This, in turn, can help address the critical shortage of available kidneys for transplant surgery. This study was conducted in collaboration with the International Pancreas and Islet Transplant Association, the International Liver Transplant Society, and the American Society of Transplantation. This research can serve as a foundation for further studies aimed at establishing ideal criteria for accepting incompatible kidneys in various transplant programs. This may involve analyzing other viral genotypes, reviewing the suitability of kidneys for patients with specific medical conditions, and examining the effectiveness of transplants in various organ donation programs. This study found no significant difference in one-year survival rates among patients who received kidneys from genetically matched donors with the same hepatitis C genotype. This is consistent with the current medical guidelines. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through multiple neural network language models including GloVe, BERT, RoBERTa, SPACE, and TechGraphLex. In analyzing these representations, a novel multivariate distance metric is introduced to provide a numerical assessment of the word representations' ability to capture the emotional nuances of words as identified in the Loughran-McDonald corpus. Empirical data shows that the majority of words with similar negative and media-oriented sentiment scores share substantially similar representation vectors despite initial intuition suggesting they would vary greatly. Furthermore, a finding that 99.5% of words with opposing orientations are clustered close to each other in the vector space: if two words with a high degree of semantic similarity also exhibit significantly different orientations, they are likely to exhibit contrasting negative orientations towards either the field of finance or the media. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the BERT-based representations used in the analysis. Notably, a subset of words exhibiting this phenomenon appears in prior research, such as tech-related jargon like "emoji" and "skype". This study's results also reveal a interesting pattern of oriented word vectors that lies outside the scope of prior research. This pattern is described as the "anti-orientation" phenomenon, where many words that exhibit a particular orientation towards a particular domain end up having the opposite orientation towards a different domain. This phenomenon is demonstrated through an example in the paper, where the word "virtual" is negatively oriented towards finance but positively oriented towards technology. This study's findings suggest a new direction for the development of word representation models that account for the complex and diverse nuances of the word orientations. This development could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the word orientations and their variability across different domains. This could also provide a more effective way of capturing the semantics of words that exhibit a complex mix of positive and negative orientations. In multiagent competitions, an ideal equilibrium would have all players following optimal strategies that prioritize honesty over deception. However, this vision is compromised when faced with manipulative agents that exploit weaknesses in the game's design or the learning processes of their opponents. We identify a specific category of games where an undesirable equilibrium, characterized by excessive dishonesty, dominates all others. These games, which we call "honesty-free" games, lack a rationalizable Nash equilibrium that prioritizes honesty, making it challenging to develop a general learning-based approach that yields this desirable equilibrium. We demonstrate that by employing a specific reinforcement learning-based method in conjunction with a memory-based representation, we can obtain an approximate, rationalizable Nash equilibrium that favors honesty, thus addressing the difficulty presented by these honesty-free games. We test and validate our approach across a diverse set of games that include both cooperation-based and auction-style games, and include comparison learning-based methods in our evaluations. Our research offers insights on how to design effective learning processes that prioritize the development of a rationalizable equilibrium that values honesty, even in games where such an equilibrium does not exist. We also provide open-source code to facilitate further replication and extension of our results. Our work builds upon several existing research papers that we explicitly identify. We find that our approach is particularly effective in responding to aggressive opponents that exploit weaknesses in the games' designs or the learning processes of their opponents. We discuss several potential weaknesses of our approach, as well as several promising directions for its further development. We conclude by highlighting the challenge presented by games that lack a rationalizable equilibrium that prioritizes honesty, and we propose a new classification of these honesty-free games that includes both cooperation-based and auction-style games. We also discuss the broader implications of these results for various research areas, and we provide a numerical characterization of the games that we tested. We end by outlining several promising research directions, including methods that prioritize fairness over honesty, as well as methods that address the validity of our results for games that we did not test. We acknowledge the financial support that we received, and we thank the numerous research participants whose contributions we gratefully acknowledge. We conclude by emphasizing the challenges that we encountered, as well as the opportunities that we identified, and we express our confidence that our results and our code will benefit both the broader research community and the various applications that rely on the learning-based approaches that we tested. We note that our results provide an explicit numerical characterization of the games that we tested, and we believe that these results will facilitate further replication and extension of our findings

This paper introduces a comprehensive theoretical framework for adjusting partonic distribution functions (PDFs) in a way that is consistent with the principles of perturbative QCD. A crucial aspect of this framework is identifying the optimal targets for adjusting PDFs, which are determined by the partonic processes underlying specific processes. We illustrate the applicability of this framework by analyzing deep inelastic scattering processes. Furthermore, we establish equations that partonic distribution functions must satisfy in order to maintain consistency with each other. These conditions are particularly important for adjusting PDFs. Additionally, we outline the steps and guidelines for implementing this framework. This framework is intended to underpin the development of methods for adjusting PDFs. As an example, we discuss the relationship between this framework and methods that use embedded partons. As processes are typically studied at a single rapidity, we simplify the adjustment process by removing evolution effects except for those necessary to maintain consistency. As a result, we find that the adjusted distribution functions can be determined using a set of coefficients that depend solely on the partonic processes and the PDFs themselves. As such, we propose a way to display these coefficients graphically. As an alternative, we discuss an approach to adjusting PDFs that is based on the embedded parton structure. To accelerate policy improvement in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, we propose a revised experience replay method that adapts the sampling strategy to optimize the variance of the policy's value function, leveraging either the first or second moment to guide policy enhancement, and prioritizing rarer, rationally-chosen episodes for greater impact. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of challenging scenarios, including multi-agent reinforcement learning, by showing it outperforms both standard experience replay and several state-of-the-art methods, such as proximal policy optimization and distributed reinforcement learning, often significantly so. Code for our proposed method is available at https://github.com/ghulghulav/vdER.

In our analysis of Google's DialogFlow data, we observed many instances where straightforward sequence generation failed, particularly when multiple relevant subtopics emerged. To address this, we developed a dialogue framework called MultiTalk, in which multiple branches of consecutive messages can diverge from a central point. To facilitate this, we introduced several innovations, including a method for creating distinct message branches and a style of response known as a "brancher", which steers the conversation off course. Our results show that combining these features with a simple sequence generation approach yields significant improvements over traditional methods. When applying this approach across all branches, we see a more modest gain. Our code is available at https://github.com/nytimes/MultiTalk. With extensive evaluation details, this paper provides a blueprint for modifying the MultiTalk design and adapting it for various purposes. This work is relevant to a broad range of conversational applications like customer support, where responses often branch out based on specific issues raised by users. Our data and models are suitable for public use, offering an opportunity for further analysis and improvement. With over 300 distinct branches observed in our DialogFlow dataset, we analyze the categories these branches represent and explore strategies for efficiently guiding the dialogue in this way. Ultimately, our solution delivers responses that not only comprehend user input but also guide the conversation through various branches and subtopics, making it an valuable addition to the field of conversational generation. This work is distinct from more complex approaches like graph-based methods, yet it shares commonalities with them. Furthermore, our evaluation encompasses a dataset composed of narrative recollections, demonstrating that this model is capable of producing engaging, multi-branch dialogue even in the absence of user input. This paper presents several suggestions for modifying the model, along with an exploration of the themes the branches represent. This research began as a part of the 2021 Text Generation Conference's Hidden Test Track, specifically the MultiTalk challenge. With 5 branches of consecutive messages, our initial model achieved a score of 0.1545 on the MultiTalk evaluation metric. We've developed an approach for executing comprehensive N-body simulations in altered gravity theories with Einstein gravity as the reference, utilizing a conformally related gravity framework. This method applies to a broad category of $f(R)$ gravity models and encompasses all N-body interactions, not just those involving gravitating objects. Our technique involves modifying the metric instead of introducing extra degrees of freedom through scalar fields, which allows for fast and efficient simulations. In a test case involving a single non-relativistic galaxy, we discovered that our model replicates the desired altered gravity effects while maintaining computational speed, and demonstrated how it can be applied to altered gravity simulations involving interacting galaxies. Our approach provides a means for exploring altered gravity theories through simulations and offers a way to analyze observations that involve multiple gravitating objects. Our code, written in C and utilizing SIMD instructions, is capable of executing N-body simulations for $f(R)$ gravity in a conformally related form, and is distinct from other codes used for similar purposes. Our simulations are designed to be easily extendable and we provide a basic implementation of our method as a starting point for further development. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a Gaussian free field coupled with stochastic local times from discrete lattice walks. Specifically, for a planar domain $D$, they considered the imaginary surface $\mathcal{N}_D$ as a free field coupled with radial SLE$_{2}$ boundary flows driven by a continuous version of the discrete log-gas model. Our work builds upon this idea by developing continuous versions of multiple SLE$_{2}$ boundary flows driven by discrete log-gas models on an interval, and we demonstrate that these models converge to a coupled discrete field that can be smoothly extended to a continuous field, specifically $\mathcal{N}_D$ for $D$ being the unit disk. As a result, we establish that the discrete versions of $2$-$\kappa$ SLE$_2$ flows driven by the discrete log-gas models converge to $\mathcal{N}_D$ for $D$ being the unit disk, allowing for specific cases of $2$-$\kappa$ SLE$_2$ driven by Dyson's discrete log-gas models. These findings extend the initial imaginary surface properties introduced by Miller and Sheffield. Additionally, we derive specific chordal $2$-$\kappa$ SLE$_2$ flow properties driven by a continuous version of the discrete log-gas model on an interval, along with tight upper bounds for the growth of certain discrete imaginary height functions driven by Dyson's discrete log-gas models. These latter estimates resemble, although they exceed, the well-known Kardos-Rényi (1966) and Aizenberg-Lolich-Lybera (2005) discrete log-gas perimeter squared estimates. These results also yield a special case of the latter estimate. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between $2$-$\kappa$ SLE$_2$ driven by a continuous version of the discrete log-gas model and a specific variant of the continuous Riemann-Hilbert problem, providing further context with related works by other authors. MediaWiki platforms, as seen in Wikipedia, utilize an inverted pyramid publishing model, where research is built upon existing knowledge, often neglected in its own right. This model can lead to difficulties in pinpointing reliable sources, accurately assessing content, and identifying areas for collaboration. In contrast, the WorkingWiki model emulates a traditional pyramid approach to knowledge, where verified information serves as the foundation for new discoveries. This structure is designed to facilitate a more linear assessment of content and make it easier to identify potential areas of collaboration, even with complete strangers. The launch of WorkingWiki is accompanied by an open-source plugin for MediaWiki that enables the reordering of pages along a linear thread, facilitating a more structured and cooperative research experience among its users. This development caters specifically to the needs of scientists working together, though its applications extend to any collaborative project seeking a linear progression of ideas. As open-source software, this plugin is accessible for use on any MediaWiki platform. The underlying principles and code of WorkingWiki are detailed in the appendix, available at https://github.com/robmyles/WorkingWiki. The potential of WorkingWiki is far-reaching, with the comments and ratings features offering a novel approach to peer review, and the private project settings providing a secure platform for industrial-scale collaborations, among other uses. The core of WorkingWiki remains highly adaptable, capable of being applied to a diverse array of uses, from academic collaborations to corporate knowledge management systems. The code for WorkingWiki is licensed under the GNU General Public License Version 2. Only a few short months after its launch, WorkingWiki has already given rise to an notable instance of industrial-scale academic collaboration, as detailed in the case study presented in the appendix at https://www.overleaf.com/project/5e0d3c5a5c5c10593845451f. This collaboration resulted in the development of a notable open-source project, further exemplifying the productive outcomes facilitated by WorkingWiki. The underlying structure of WorkingWiki remains an effective and versatile platform for any form of collaborative research, as demonstrated by the numerous small-scale projects thriving on the platform. With its open nature, this platform also presents opportunities for academic research into the dynamics of these collaborations, offering a unique 'inside-out' perspective on the workings of individual minds through the many public project notes. The WorkingWiki platform is poised to continue supporting a diverse array of projects and collaborations, given its adaptable design and open access to its code and data. This research investigates how a turbulent jet fire interacts with an acoustic chamber and affects the combustion process. To study this phenomenon, an experimental setup was used which consisted of a closed loop system including a combustion chamber, an acoustic chamber, a fuel injection system and a method for generating hydrodynamic instabilities in the combustion process. The experimental setup also had the capability to operate in both passive and active flame modes. In the passive mode, the interaction between the combustion process and the acoustic system was examined, while in the active mode, a signal was generated that could influence the combustion process and the acoustic interaction. The results from both modes of operation were then used to validate the linearized equations of mass, momentum and energy by considering only the mean values of the combustion process and acoustic interaction. This validation enabled the reduction of the experimental setup to a simpler model which consisted of a closed loop system including a mass of flames, a chamber representing the acoustic space, and a linear feedback loop influenced by a signal that could be generated in the active mode. To examine the stability of the combustion process in more detail, the distribution of the temperature in the acoustic chamber was also measured. The experimental findings from both the active and passive modes of operation were then used to validate a numerical model which was then used to examine the combustion process in more complex scenarios. The numerical model was a closed loop system which included a submodel of the combustion process, a submodel of the acoustic interaction, and a submodel of the feedback loop influenced by a signal that could be generated in the active mode. The results from the numerical model showed that it could accurately represent the experimental findings and was then used to examine the combustion process in more complex scenarios which included the influence of a vibrating wall on the combustion process and the reaction of the combustion process to acoustic excitation in a linearized structure. The numerical model also enabled the examination of the distribution of the temperature in the acoustic chamber which provided valuable information for the analysis of the combustion process. The numerical model also enabled the examination of the distribution of the temperature in the acoustic chamber which provided valuable information for the analysis of the combustion process. This paper introduces a nonlocal gravitational theory where gravitons constitute a distinct class from geometric connections, building on the framework of nonAbelian monopoles and the Einstein field equations. We show that general relativity can be recovered when the nonlocal effects of gravitons are negligible, without the need for singular connections. This version of the theory offers new physical interpretations and mathematical representations, such as the use of tetrads that are invariant in number and type, providing a more conservative application of the Einstein equivalence principle. We then derive the nonlocal nonAbelian monopole equations and demonstrate that they are consistent with the Einstein field equations when the nonlocal effects of gravitons are taken into account using a variation of the Born approximation. This version of the theory can be extended to describe the nonlocal effects of massless nonAbelian vector fields and may have implications for the understanding of hadron structure and the properties of atomic nuclei. Despite its predictive power, this version of the theory cannot be tested using available data, which limits its value to a descriptive science. On the other hand, a modified version of this theory that includes a direct interaction between the nonAbelian vector fields and the hadrons that make up atomic nuclei does provide new physical predictions that can be tested, such as the nonlocal effects of delta mesons on the properties of atomic nuclei which cannot be described using the traditional quark models. This version of the theory also offers a new perspective on the properties of reggeons and effective field theories that include them. This version of the theory can be applied to a wide range of hadronic processes and reactions that involve the exchange of the delta meson, from the nonperturbative properties of atomic nuclei to the high energy processes that occur in high energy collisions. This version of the theory can be applied at both the classical and quantum levels. We've developed an open-source tool to integrate results from functional genomics and genome-wide associations studies, and have applied it to examine 18 different human characteristics, finding that certain features such as expression levels, DNA accessibility, and repeats that generate copy numbers, vary significantly among individuals who do or don't exhibit a particular trait. The LHC will enter its second period of operation with upgraded experiments, 
characterized by an increased collision rate and a broader detection range 
for lighter particles. This development creates opportunities for searching 
for new, weakly interacting sub-GeV particles, either with the Standard Model 
or beyond it. To take advantage of these capabilities, this work presents a 
set of detectors tailored for discovering particles with masses and widths 
ranging from 10 MeV to 10 GeV, with cross-sections as low as 10^-12 db 
and interactions that could be either with the Standard Model or beyond it. 
Each detector is designed to excel in a specific area and can be grouped 
into three categories: (1) 2-3 GeV range detectors with high resolution 
for rare decay processes, (2) 10 MeV-5 GeV range detectors optimized 
for missing energy or metastable particles, and (3) 5-10 GeV range detectors 
for heavy dark matter. To facilitate collaboration, these designs can 
be used as building blocks for individual research groups or as a starting 
point for new collective efforts. With the LHC's expanded capabilities, 
it's an ideal time to reconsider or new proposals for sub-GeV experiments 
that can complement the existing experiments at the B-factories and neutrino 
experiments. To this end, we outline a set of possibilities, from upgraded 
versions of existing designs to novel, cutting-edge detectors. If approved, 
these experiments can be constructed and ready to operate in time for 
the 2027 data collection. We also discuss potential physics outputs, 
including the discovery of sub-GeV heavy neutrinos, new light scalar particles 
that could link to dark sectors, and mechanisms for the LSP, and list 
some of the existing proposals that could be developed into functioning 
experiments. We conclude by highlighting the scope of sub-GeV research, 
the opportunities it presents, and the diverse set of detectors that 
could contribute to it, and the need for a coordinated effort to 
prioritize and support these efforts. We provide a list of the discussed 
detectors, with links to more in-depth information, and outline some 
of the open questions in the field that these experiments can help answer. We end by emphasizing that the time is right for initiating a program of sub-GeV experiments at the LHC, and we propose a set of experiments that can be constructed and ready to operate in time for the 2027 data collection

Observations of some variable X-ray sources among the Galactic Centre suggest that these sources, which have remained inactive for an extended period, may have undergone a significant wait time since their last outburst. A potential explanation for this observed pattern is related to the characteristics of repetition intervals found in variable neutron star binary systems. This study examines repetition patterns in neutron star binaries that have been observed over an extensive period, spanning many years to decades. Analyzing 83 known neutron star low-mass binary systems globally, researchers found that the distribution of repetition intervals in these systems is generally uniform when expressed as a fraction of their orbital period. When applied to the 10 previously unclassified dormant X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre, this model predicts that the repetition intervals of these sources could fall within a certain range, allowing for accurate predictions of when these sources may become active again. This study offers insights into the nature of these dormant X-ray binaries, including four that may exhibit long delay times since their last outburst, potentially associated with compact binary mergers and large black holes. The intricate bond between diverse semantic elements within a discourse is a subject that has been broadly explored in the fields of pragmatics, semantics, and inference. It's well established that diverse elements can contribute to a discourse's cumulative meaning, yet the specific ways in which a discourse's semantics and inference are affected by varied elements are not well understood. This study endeavors to delve into these unknowns by introducing a novel task, called Semantic Variety Inference, which aims to determine whether a diverse set of elements in a discourse justifies accepting a particular statement as true. To accomplish this, we created a substantial dataset consisting of 20,000 sentence pairs, drawn from the Commonsense Reasoning section of the CommonsenseQA. Our key finding is that diverse elements in a discourse are often tenacious in their individual meanings, rather than combining in complex ways that could contribute to their combined significance. As a result, justifying the acceptance of a statement as true generally entails a straightforward integration of these individual meanings. To achieve this, we developed a set of hand-crafted rules that yield a simple and effective approach to addressing the Semantic Variety Inference challenge. Nevertheless, this study remains largely exploratory in nature, and there are numerous avenues left unexamined that offer potential for future research. Nevertheless, the straightforward character of the diversity discourse is made manifest through the rules developed here, offering a tangible understanding of the relationship between diverse elements and their combined significance that can serve as a foundation for more intricate analyses. For the benefit of the broader AI community, all-data sets, models, and code have been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/salestock/variety.

By sharing these visualizations, we aim to promote the effective depiction of experimental uncertainties in the results of amplitude-based analyses. This, in turn, will help researchers interpret both amplitude and phase information, facilitating a more precise and unbiased determination of signals from noise. This approach is particularly valuable for evaluating and comparing different models and interpreting their phase information. We establish that BVP in this variant can be solved using a framework that constrains individual vertices rather than a two-way division, effectively demonstrating a significant improvement over existing two-way division methods and offering a more efficient parameterized time solution for this specific problem type. Additionally, our approach provides a precise expression for the desired solution that can be factored, and this expression serves as the foundation for a subsequent algorithm that, for a given instance of size n and parameter k, determines whether a subgraph of size k exists within each edge connection of a graph consisting of n vertices. This paper will present our design approach and preliminary findings for a biologically-inspired walking system that includes a powered lower leg. Differing from traditional approaches that focus on upper body actuation, our design aims to enhance lower leg actuation to match the body's dynamic movements during gait. This movement synchrony is critical for preventing resonance that can lead to instability and fall, and for increasing energy efficiency and durability. Our approach utilizes a compact, high-power hip joint that includes a passive ankle with controlled freedom of movement. This design allows for natural foot rollover, reducing the risk of resonance and facilitating smoother, more energy-conserving gait. Our initial prototype demonstrates improved energy return characteristics and shows a 30% increase in gait speed and 30% higher step height with the same energy input. These benefits suggest that our design may be adaptable for various applications, from humanoid robots to prosthetic legs for individuals with below-knee amputations. The current prototype has several limitations and there are many areas where it can be improved, including the addition of proper foot structure, more advanced actuation and power transmission systems, and more sophisticated control algorithms. Nevertheless, our design and the associated test results provide a foundation for future enhancements and innovations in powered lower legs. This approach is also an integral part of our broader research focused on creating a highly efficient, resilient, and dynamic bipedal locomotion system that can be used in a variety of environments. The escalating demand for real-time, low-latency video processing fuels the
development of new, high-performance CPU architectures. Prior research has
focused on enabling 4K video processing at multiple GHz rates. In contrast, we
pursue a previously unaddressed goal of constructing an efficient CPU that can
effectively process 4K video at rates below 1 GHz. To support this, we present
a new, 4K video processing CPU architecture called HyperDegrade. When implemented
on a 5 GHz capable CPU, HyperDegrade achieves an energy efficiency improvement
of over 10x, reducing the operating frequency to just 100 MHz while still enabling
4K video processing. We also present a customizable, post-fabrication design
optimization framework for our architecture, which in turn enables a further
5x reduction in operating energy, facilitating efficient use of future, power
efficient CPU technologies. Notably, our research demonstrates an applicable, 4x
video processing degradation technique, alongside a design framework that can
be utilized for various CPU-based workload energy efficiency enhancements. Our
results are validated through a combination of simulation studies and a real-world
implementation on an Intel NGL-based FPGA. Overall, HyperDegrade presents a
novel, 4K video processing degrader architecture and a design optimization
framework, both capable of enhancing the energy efficiency of various CPU-based
workloads. Our research and findings are applicable to a wide range of CPU-based
workloads, not just video processing. Our code is available at https://github.com/abhinavp1/hyperdegrade.

We demonstrate that the 2-component Fox-Hatcher wobble loop complies with the Vassiliev invariant criterion, thereby confirming that it constitutes a 2-component Vassiliev invariant of order three. This expansion into 2-component Vassiliev invariants supersedes its previous representation as a single Vassiliev invariant and facilitates the identification of a distinct, universally-renamed 1-component Vassiliev invariant of order three, which we term the little null-link invariant. A direct demonstration of the 3-order Nakanishi-Ohtawa invariance for the little null-link invariant is provided. Moreover, we establish that this 1-component Vassiliev invariant can be viewed as a derivative of the order-three Kauffman polynomial under specific monomial differentiation applications. Lastly, we establish its relationship to the second-order Arf-Kauffman invariant and the little self-linking number. This work builds upon and expands the findings of a prior, unpublished study by one of the authors. The previously-unpublished results from that study are presented here in their modified form as the second and third main theorems. The first main theorem, however, is an independent contribution. The study of the little null-link invariant suggests that single-component 3-order Vassiliev invariants may be exceptionally rare, implying that most 3-order Vassiliev invariants are likely composite, constructed from the combination of two 2-component 3-order Vassiliev invariants. This conjecture is supported by an analysis of the diverse range of 3-order Vassiliev invariants generated via direct and indirect means from the little null-link invariant. The study of the little null-link invariant also yields valuable, related outcomes, including an originally-unknown 1-component Vassiliev derivative of the order-three Kauffman polynomial and a previously-unknown 2-component 3-order Vassiliev invariant constructed from the little self-linking number. The proofs of both of these outcomes are provided. This paper investigates functions defined on a compact hypersurface within the (n+1)-dimensional sphere that are conformally determined and satisfy specific mean curvature properties. We prove the uniqueness of such functions that are parallel to the M\"obius operator, providing them in a form that can be applied to a broad class of surfaces. We also establish and counterexample to the conjecture that only constant functions satisfy the curvature condition for a specific mean curvature measure when defined on the unit $4$-sphere. Additionally, we offer a lower bound for the M\"obius energy of hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature and provide a solution to a related problem of Ge and Wang. Our research extends and builds upon previous uniqueness results and provides a foundation for potential generalization to higher dimensions. It also introduces a new approach for analyzing and comparing the M\"obius operator and the conformal Laplacian. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the presence of laser noise in Michelson-type gravitational wave detectors. To enhance the sensitivity of these devices, a variant of the Sagnac interferometer called the sloshing Sagnac has been proposed as an alternative configuration. This new design involves dividing the end mirror of a traditional Sagnag interferometer into two separate mirrors, positioned at opposite ends of the interferometer, which allows for the implementation of a signal recycling scheme while counteracting backscattering effects that intensify laser noise. Through numerical analysis, it becomes apparent that the sloshing Sagnac design can either significantly or modestly improve the signal-to-noise ratio of certain gravitational wave signals, with the advantage of this design being its simplicity over more intricate configurations that achieve similar results, such as recycled Michelson interferometers. Nevertheless, the sloshing Sagnac design may have a drawback in its reduced common mode signal rejection, which could be a concern for certain analyses. To assess the effectiveness of this design, a parameter called the "effective signal rejection" has been introduced, which provides a quantitative comparison of the sloshing Sagnac and traditional Michelson configurations over a range of parameters. This analysis paves the way for further exploration and optimization of the sloshing Sagnac design in response to varying geophysical targets. Additionally, this research offers insights into a broader design category known as multi-loop configurations, which could be of interest to researchers working on other projects. Sagnac geometries and their variants are generally distinguished by their signal rejection properties, with the average signal rejection of the sloshing Sagnac design falling within the 100 to 1000:1 range, offering a more explicit and open interpretation of this property that could be useful to extended research on this topic. A numerical tool has been developed to simulate the dynamics of the sloshing Sagnac design and its response to laser backscattering, which could also be applied to the analysis of other Sagnac geometries. A design with a specific parameter set is presented as a final example, which could potentially be optimized for improved signal-to-noise ratios in response to a wide range of geophysical targets. This target range includes gravitational waves produced by supernovae, binary neutron star mergers, rotating neutron stars, pulsar glitches, magnetic field changes in solar analog stars, and oscillations in rotating stars, among others. A call to action is made for further research on the sloshing Sagnac design

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that several young stars with protracted accretion disks also feature a second, distinct population exhibiting a "double ring" structure. Prior research attributed such a double-ring pattern to either an external gravitational influence or a disk with a significant misalignment. This paper's companion work simulated these patterns and found them linked to the development of the vertical shear instability (VSI), which causes substructures in the disk. This study's companion work also discovered the VSI's influence on the disk can result in patterns even in the presence of turbulent mixing. Given these findings, we can expect the VSI's effect on the disk to become more prominent over time as it takes centuries to a few millennia to develop its characteristic features. The predicted changes in the $870\mu m$ continuum emission from the T Tauri star TW Hya's disk offer a specific and observable example - a double-ring structure with a gap in the inner ring and a prominent outer ring with a width of approximately $20 AU$. This prediction can be tested through the use of sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelength observations on similar stars with protracted accretion disks. If such patterns are found on a timescale that's consistent with the VSI's development, it would provide evidence for the VSI's occurrence and, by extension, the presence of a long-lasting, unstable disk. This would also open up avenues for researching a population of young stars with similar ages and properties. If the VSI's effect on the TW Hae disk is found to be in its early stages, it would require a reevaluation of the VSI's development and the factors influencing it. This paper introduces the "Big Apple parameter", a new saturation property requiring specific behavior from nuclear matter as it approaches infinite density, characterized by a constant incompressibility of approximately 620~MeV. We determine the resonance patterns of mesons with various isospin properties in infinite nuclear matter and derive a crucial "Big Apple ratio" of approximately 5.37 for mesons to effectively contribute to quark-antiquark pairs in thermal distributions of finite nuclei. We calculate thermal distributions for mesons in infinite nuclear matter and finite nuclei, both with and without the Big Apple parameter. Notably, the Big Apple ratio remains generally stable even when the Big Apple parameter is varied significantly. To further explore its implications, we apply the Big Apple parameter to neutron stars, finding that it helps explain the upper limit of their temperature, particularly evident in the case of PSR J0346+0241. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios also influence the properties of finite nuclei, most noticeably in their isospin distributions and oxidation patterns. We observe that it generally aligns with existing data but could potentially explain odd patterns in certain isotopes that defy periodic trends. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios have the potential to be tested through upcoming experiments that will provide more detailed isospin distribution data for various isotopes. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios can also be applied to quark-gluon plasma, which shares similarities with infinite nuclear matter, and may help clarify the deconfinement phase transition in heavy-ion collisions. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios have a broad scope of applicability, from finite nuclei to astronomical objects, and could provide a fundamental explanation for the behavior of matter in various conditions. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios await verification through experimental data on finite nuclei, neutron stars, and quark-gluon plasma, which will confirm their status as established physical principles or guide their ongoing development as speculative hypotheses. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios can be applied to study the behavior of strange hadronic matter in neutron stars formed in distant galaxies, which may reside in the outer reaches of the universe but are within the reach of next-generation telescopes that can provide detailed spectral analysis of these objects. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios can also be used to study the properties of infinite nuclear matter at finite temperatures, which may help clarify the results of heavy-ion collisions and provide a better understanding of the phase transition from hadronic to quark-gluon matter. The Big Apple parameter and associated ratios await further verification through experimental data

Our investigation focuses on a crucial building block for quantum systems: the Mølmer-Sørensen gate. Unlike traditional implementations that rely on a single motional mode with an explicitly specified frequency, we've successfully generalized the gate to be operable using balanced input on multiple motional modes, regardless of their individual frequencies. Key findings demonstrate that the gate's minimal operating frequencies can be both efficiently determined and a condition identified that ensures the gate's accuracy, even when dealing with a wide range of frequency disparities between the modes. To illustrate the feasibility of these findings, we propose an experimental design that successfully implements a frequency-resilient Mølmer-Sørensen gate for both two- and three-mode scenarios, using a trapped ion system. Notably, one of the proposed designs surpasses the 99% two-mode or 98% three-mode state preparation accuracy at a 10 dB signal-to-quantum-noise ratio. Our frequency-resilient gate design offers a promising solution for implementing the Mølmer-Sørensen gate in systems where controlling individual mode frequencies is challenging, such as with certain trapped anti-atom configurations, where coupling geometry hinders direct access to some of the motional modes. Our design also provides a valuable model that can be used in other systems with multiple motional modes and offers a valuable tool for analyzing the frequency disparities' impact on the gate's performance. Our investigation further explores two additional gate variants: one that allows for a wider frequency range and another that can be used with modes that have significantly different frequencies. Our proposed design can be used in a variety of experimental setups, including those with optical cavities, where the modes' frequencies are determined by the cavity's geometry, providing a promising solution for implementing the Mølmer-Sørensen gate in systems where controlling individual mode frequencies is challenging. Our theoretical analysis indicates that a certain type of transition metal dichalcogenide, specifically trilayer PMo3S7, possesses unique electronic properties. At the point (0.3eV binding energy, 0.5eV above the Fermi level) we are focusing on, the material exhibits three pairs of highly dispersive Dirac bands. These bands arise from interactions between neighboring moiré lobes and distinguishing features of this point are the "three-gaps" and "three-peak" structures in the spectral function. These characteristics are preserved when accounting for correlations between electrons. In fact, even under strong interaction, the peapod-like dispersion of the three pairs of Dirac bands continues unabated. This remarkable resilience is a result of the wide distance between electron coupling points, allowing for the formation of a strong, interlinked Dirac metal phase. This phase can be realized through chemical doping of the PMo3S7 compound or using silicene/graphene layers deposited onto its surface. Notably, the 3d orbital-based point normal to the moiré superstructure at 0.9eV above the Fermi level is distinguishable from 2d orbital-based points found in other materials, making it an exclusive feature of this material.
