Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial data. This research addresses an important issue, namely how facial occlusions impact the accuracy and robustness of 3D face reconstruction techniques. A novel framework called SADRNet is introduced to enhance the resistance of 3D face reconstruction to partial occlusions. It employs a self-aligning technique that brings the left and right 2D face images into a unified coordinate system, facilitating the training of two dual facial regression networks that work together to recover an unoccluded 2D face mesh from a single image with partial face coverage. This recovered mesh serves as input to two separate 3D face reconstruction networks, each recovering a 3D face mesh in the coordinate system defined by a specific 2D face mesh. Finally, the two 3D face meshes are registered to a single 3D face mesh based on their respective corresponding 2D face meshes. A rigorous evaluation of SADRNet involves assessing its performance on both the CMU Panoptic dataset, known for its complex real-world 3D face reconstructions and the Adience Age Database, which presents an age-based modification of the CMU Panoptic dataset. Experimental results indicate a notable enhancement in both the robustness and accuracy of 3D face reconstruction techniques in the presence of facial occlusions. A labeled ordered tree of height h is a tree with distinct labels for its nodes, sorted in ascending order from left to right, and having no leftmost recurring label. The number of labeled ordered trees of a specific height h is known to be determined by a sequence called the Schröder number. We have derived an explicit formula for the number of labeled ordered trees of height h that do not contain the largest label, which we call "rooted deepest trees". This number has a significant relationship with the Schröder number, enabling us to convey essential information about the structure of these trees. Specifically, we have discovered that there are multiple nodes at the deepest level of these trees, and our formula allows us to determine the exact number of these nodes for any given height h. This finding can be expressed as a product of integers representing the number of these nodes, which forms a sequence that may have implications for other mathematical domains beyond its immediate application to labeled ordered trees. This product sequence is exceptional in that it allows us to define a natural, non-decreasing function, known as the "Ferrers map", that acts on the set of integers representing the number of nodes at the deepest level, which in turn has a significant impact on the overall structure of these trees. This domain of study also shares commonalities with the field of non-commutative logic, as identified by the mathematician Stanley, and our work may have a relevant contribution to make in this area. In recent years, over-parametrized linear models have gained significant attention, and their ability to tolerate large mismatches between training and operational data has been found to be tolerable. However, the extent to which this mismatch's impact can be considered minor has not been thoroughly established, especially in regards to distorting the structure of time series data. The current study seeks to explore this issue and provide a rigorous analysis of how data destruction affects the performance of over-parametrized linear regression when working with time series data under certain conditions. Our findings reveal that even when the destruction is substantial and affects the autoregressive external context, it will not lead to a significant decrease in a model's ability to forecast that context. More specifically, we find that the performance of the model in forecasting the context will decrease at a rate that is logarithmically dependent on the number of parameters. This outcome can be compared with existing performance decay analyses in the literature, which have found linear rates of performance decline. This current study's approach to analyzing over-parametrized linear regression and time series data also offers a unique and previously unpublished result that provides a more general and model-agnostic statement about the minimal impact of data destruction. This more general statement is not bound to any specific linear model but rather any model that can be accurately described using a linear time series framework. This latter finding is made possible by the study's use of a linear time series framework as its analytical tool, allowing it to uncover and analyze the fundamental underlying reasons for the destruction's destructive effects. This enables a more in-depth examination of the relationship between the destruction, the model, and the data, and provides a better comprehension of the dynamics at play, and potentially a more comprehensive and generalisable understanding of the destruction's impact, and hence potentially a more generalisable result. A growing number of electricity end-users are equipping their homes with smart storage systems, which allow them to balance supply and demand of electricity and earn additional income through peer-to-peer trading. As a result, storage owners are increasingly considering whether to invest in a personal storage system, taking into account various factors including purchase and maintenance costs, expected returns from energy balancing and local trading, and the potential risks and uncertainties associated with market fluctuations and grid operations. In this research, we develop a robust decision-making model for individual storage owners, aiming to determine whether to purchase and use a storage system, and if so, how to set its parameters in a way that maximizes their expected returns while minimizing potential losses. We utilize robust optimization and multi-objective programming techniques to create a comprehensive and versatile model that accounts for multiple possible future scenarios and prioritizes optimal self-scheduling and trading strategies. By applying our model to real-world data and scenarios, we demonstrate its practical effectiveness and valuable insights into the trade-offs between cautious and generous storage management policies. Ultimately, our research provides a reliable and customizable tool for guiding individual storage owners, as well as operators of community microgrids, in their storage planning and management decisions.

Although these models are not mutually exclusive and often blend both balance types, they are useful in categorizing circulation patterns on other worlds. This study uses a simplified computer model to recreate and contrast atmospheric circulation on three types of planetary bodies: those with strong rotation rates and significant temperature gradients between their day and night sides that exhibit super-rotation; those with slow rotation rates and moderate day-night temperature gradients that demonstrate cyclostrophic turbulence; and those with the slowest rotation rates and the greatest day-night temperature gradients that exhibit multiple-vortex storm patterns. In this work, we explore the potential for a specific type of neural network, named Hamiltonian Neural Networks, which is derived from Hamiltonian mechanics, to acquire gradient information as its output. We demonstrate that this is indeed feasible and illustrate two uses for this property. Firstly, we show that it is possible to train a Hamiltonian Neural Network as a proxy optimizer for another system, without directly providing the optimizer with the original system's parameters. Secondly, we demonstrate that it is possible to integrate a Hamiltonian Neural Network into another system as a module that acquires the gradient of the integrated system, without the need to directly provide the parameters of the integrated system. Notably, we find that training such a module is significantly easier than training the integrated system directly. We propose the term Hamiltonian Neural Networks, and our work is the first to explore this concept. We hope that our results will pave the way for a wider range of applications of Hamiltonian Neural Networks. We have made our code available at https://github.com/ghul5/Hamiltonian-Gradient-Explorer. To address this issue, a collaborative multi-agent approach has been proposed that works in real time and involves humans in the loop. It rates the trustworthiness of trained machine learning models and selects them for use in specific cases. If a model produces an inaccurate result, it suggests a possible cause, and human input is used to validate or correct it. If the result is found to be incorrect, the model is penalized to reduce its future use. The system also learns from its mistakes and uses them to update the model automatically. If a model produces an ambiguous result, human input is used to classify it, and the classification is used to update the model's confidence levels. The system's output is then presented to a decision-making agent that chooses the model to use based on its predicted performance. If a model's performance is inadequate, it suggests human intervention to correct any errors. Human input is used to validate the model's confidence levels and its output, and to classify its results as certain or uncertain. The system then updates the model's confidence levels and performance prediction for use in similar cases in the future. To accurately determine the meaning of words with multiple definitions in a given context, known as Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), relying solely on dictionaries can be insufficient. This limitation can be addressed by incorporating a companion resource called Glosses, which provides definitions for each interpretation of a given word. Unfortunately, most current WSD approaches overlook utilizing these definitions. In this research, we enhance the performance of a state-of-the-art word representation model by integrating context and gloss information through a multi-task model. Our model successfully leverages word definitions to inform the context. We evaluate this approach on a WSD dataset and a related task called Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), achieving superior results compared to the current standards. To validate our approach, we conduct multiple experiments, including modifying the model to incorporate an alternative gloss resource, selecting optimal hyperparameters, and comparing it with a strong baseline using a simple concatenation method. Our findings demonstrate consistent improvements in both WSD and SRL tasks, under a range of conditions. We make our code publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/ContextGloss-ENHANCE.

We've developed a quantum hydrodynamic approach that applies to interacting Bose systems and is based on random wave functions. This method represents a significant improvement over previous mean-field theories, offering a more accurate description of Bose fluids, especially in their far-from-equilibrium behavior. By combining this with a Bogoliubov approach, we've created a comprehensive framework that incorporates both a mean-field description of interacting Bose fluids and a coherent state representation of their quantum fluctuations. This new model serves as a starting point for multiple perturbative expansions, including a $c$-number representation of hydrodynamic operators and a $q$-number representation of Schrödinger operators. Notably, it yields a linearized quantum hydrodynamic model that closely resembles the original version, while also allowing us to introduce a one-parameter family of non-linearized versions. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of a semi-infinite Bose fluid that is in contact with a thermal reservoir, and have identified key model parameters that influence its behavior. We establish that for both types of sequences, a vast array of functions that measure text complexity will asymptotically exhibit unusual behavior when examined across a broad range of texts that adhere to these statistical rules. The asymptotic behavior of these functions is determined by their lowest-order term and a precise constant, which can be calculated using a new large-deviation principle. This principle is applicable to functions that satisfy a specific smoothness condition and provides an asymptotic estimate for the asymptotic behavior of these functions. Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for the asymptotic behavior of functions that capture the statistical properties of these Markovian sequences, including frequency-based and correlation-based measures. These formulas arise from integrating the row-wise Jacobi matrix associated with the transition probability matrix that defines these sequences. Our results are verified through multiple numerical examples, covering a range of texts, from brief paragraphs to extensive literary works, including famous novels and a vast collection of Wikipedia articles. When fine-tuning pre-existing NLP models, a common issue arises from the conflict between two types of noise. Firstly, there is the inherent variability of the validation data set due to the random selection of instances for training and testing in the K-fold method. This is compounded by the existing linguistic abnormalities in our training and validation data sets. This research explores how different validation techniques can be used to reduce the impact of this inherent variability, enabling a more precise adjustment of model parameters. Our study involves comparing K-fold, leave-one-out, and stratified five-fold cross-validation methods to determine their effect on both the validation error and the adjusted parameter estimates. We also establish some important consequences of using the K-fold method. Notably, we find that the reduced variance associated with the leave-one-out method misrepresents the underlying issue, suggesting that it's not a suitable approach for problems high in noise. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the K-fold method yields a variance that is directly proportional to the square of the instance ratio, providing valuable statistical insight that can be used to our advantage. One such advantage is mentioned in this paper, along with several potential applications including but not limited to, leveraging the variance to our advantage in order to enhance the effectiveness of our model adjustments, selecting an optimal instance ratio that minimizes variance while keeping it in balance with the existing noise, generating a new set of test instances that can be used to further validate our findings, and investigating the implications of this bias for the strata that contain disproportionately small groups of data instances. We demonstrate the practical utility of this approach in a part titled ``Some Practical Applications'' where we discuss the implications of this bias on model adjustments and the resulting balanced instance ratios. We also explore the connection between this approach and the left-out (hold-out) method, alternative techniques for reducing the variance, as well as several empirical studies that validate our findings. With the aim of keeping the research focused, we have limited the scope to a straightforward adjustment of NLP models through regularization methods, describing a general framework for reducing the variance associated with the K-fold method, obtaining the optimal instance ratios, as well as discussing the appropriate techniques for generating new test sets from this framework. We conclude the paper by outlining some promising future research directions along with some code that can be used to replicate our results. We hope this work will pave the way for a controlled and systematic noise in the validation data sets that can be used to our advantage in a wide range of machine learning tasks, not just limited to NLP model adjustments.

The study of shear-driven crystalline-to-liquid transitions in granular media has revealed distinct patterns of failure at various scales. Our research involves creating large-scale models of granular materials, specifically composed of polydispersed grains, and subjecting them to shear stress. We observe a wide range of shear-induced crystalline-to-liquid transitions in these models, ranging from abrupt to gradual transitions, and identify three prominent patterns of failure at the grain level. Our analysis focuses on a small subset of models where the grain-scale transitions primarily take an abrupt form. By examining the distribution of shear stresses that lead to non-crystalline states, our findings reveal a narrow, consistently scaled structure that remains remarkably stable across all our models, regardless of whether the transitions are sharp or gradual. This scaled distribution serves as a fundamental component in our comprehensive model of shear-induced transitions. We also introduce a nonlinear height function that connects the scaled distribution to the overall dynamics of the system during shear stress augmentation. Our results highlight the intricate interplay between the external shear stress and the resulting non-crystalline state, revealing a distinctive, scalably nonlinear height profile that helps define the transitions from global crystalline states to localized shear bands. Our research demonstrates that a specific, universally observed distribution serves as a guiding principle for the external shear stress required to induce a range of non-crystalline states, from localized shear bands to global liquefaction. We identify a critical shear stress augmentation that marks the transition from localized shear bands to global crystalline-to-liquid transitions, and demonstrate how it scales with the individual grain sizes in our models. This research on polydispersed grain models complements our previous findings on monodispersed grain assemblies, and together they provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex patterns of shear-driven transitions in granular materials. Our models and analysis tools also offer a framework for investigating other systems that exhibit discrete shear-induced transitions in scaled and global contexts. We envision a broad range of potential applications for our research, extending to the analysis of various natural phenomena, such as rock failures and avalanches, as well as human-made systems, including emulsions, foams, and crowds, that are affected by shear stress and discrete transitions. We conclude by outlining a pathway for further development and refinement of our models and analysis tools, and highlight a promising area of research that involves the integration of our models with a non-local height function and a related pattern formation mechanism, known as Amplitude Death, which we discovered in our previous studies on monodispersed grain assemblies.

This phenomenon is particularly evident among younger adults and those with lower educational levels. Our findings have implications for how online knowledge and reality are shaped, suggesting that customized searches may contribute to the fragmentation of shared cultural knowledge and highlighting potential difficulties in assessing the effectiveness of search engines in this context. A novel approach is proposed for creating four-dimensional (4D) T2-weighted images with adjustable compensation for abdominal respiration and bodily movement. By utilizing a combination of motion sensing, real-time data processing, and targeted data reordering, the technique delivers smooth continuous data throughout the scan duration. Unlike conventional methods, this proposed technique does not rely on a fixed sampling schedule and can produce 4D images with adjustable motion correction. A designed sequence and algorithm are presented along with results from motion-tested and clinically obtained data. High-quality 4D images are obtained and comparable to conventional methods in terms of image quality, as assessed using PSNR and SSIM metrics. This technique offers enhanced clinical utility for 4D T2-weighted imaging in various bodily imaging applications. The fabric flow equation is a second-order nonlinear diffusion surface growth model, initially developed by Adler and Feldman in 2005. This equation serves as a representation of a specific conformal field theory, possessing a vast collection of primary state operators. The fabric flow equation possesses unique characteristics, such as the existence of a curve of states marked by a singular point, which the conformal field theory cannot tolerate. To address this issue, we introduce the fabric space $M$ by equating the set of states accessible via smooth paths from the initial state. The fabric space $M$ is observed to evolve in a way that's topologically identical to how random geometries evolve in 2D quantum gravity. This connection is shown to extend to the point where Weyl weights become locally defined, resulting in a hierarchy of the Ashtekar-Hansen barrier, and ultimately guiding us through an analytical computation of a specific fabric space component. This study provides visual evidence for a particular state, which displays a fractal pattern that's accessible via an iterative procedure beginning from an initial random geometry. We perform a set of transformations that convert any given second-order Lagrangian describing gravity in any dimension, with no cosmological term, into an equivalent form consisting of first-order Lagrangian parameters. This conversion allows us to identify specific combinations of the Riemann tensor's contractions that contribute to the total degree of freedom count. A recent study disputed the claim that these combinations can be generated using a certain spinor-based method known as the Schouten-Nijenhuis algebra. We demonstrate that this assertion is incorrect by both directly utilizing the spinor-based method and through explicit degree of freedom counting. A key observation from our conversion process also yields an alternative expression that can combine the two first-order Lagrangian parameters into a single scalar when the dimension is even. This expression can be further manipulated to reveal a hidden Bianchi identity associated with the conformal gravity sector. A brief discussion on the implications and relationships with other equivalent formulations of gravity completes this study. A set of appendices is included to address supplementary details on the spinor-based method, an algebraic expansion procedure, an analysis of the degree of freedom counting, an examination of the even-dimensional, first-order Lagrangian parameter combination, and a comparison with other formulations of gravity.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, a common approach involves matching pre-operatively obtained magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to the surgical site. Our research focuses on advancing self-supervised scene flow analysis with a 2D stereo camera setup. After training a flow estimator using a limited set of labeled images, the model can be fine-tuned for unsupervised scene flow estimation. However, existing self-supervised approaches rely heavily on neighboring points to establish a dense correspondence between images, which can lead to overfitting and limit the model's ability to generalize. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Adversarial Metric Training framework that encourages the model to avoid relying on neighboring points by introducing a discriminator that evaluates the spatial distance between corresponding points. This leads to a better generalization to unseen areas and reduces overfitting. To further enhance the model's performance and address the issue of positive class imbalance in foreground regions, we incorporate an classification-based loss and a foreground-downsampling strategy, respectively. Experimental evaluations conducted on datasets EF-BD and SIFT Flow demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework, with a 9.3% and 11.3% improvement in 3D flow estimation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods DLPF and CRAFT-DF. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangweng/AdMTRC-SF.

An abstract for the paper titled: Ideal pairings, Hamiltonian circuits and edge-tinting in a cubic graph
An (X,Y)-pairing in a graph consists of two perfect matchings, whose union is a Hamiltonian circuit, and a one-to-one correspondence between the vertices of the two matchings, respecting the direction of the circuit. A cubic graph contains an (X,Y)-pairing if and only if it contains an (X,Y)-double covering, which can be thought of as a set of edge-disjoint copies of K3,2. Two of these copies in a cubic graph are compatible if their combined edges form a Hamiltonian circuit. The problem of determining the pairings in a cubic graph is then shown to be equivalent to identifying the subsets of edge pairs that can be part of an (X,Y)-pairing, and determining the edge set of an (X,Y)-double covering in a cubic graph is shown to be equivalent to finding a set of edge pairs that can be part of an (X,Y)-pairing, as well as finding the edges that are not part of any pair, and a more general statement known as Conjecture 1.3 from "Bipartite Graphs and Hypercubes" by Albin and Győri. A Hamiltonian circuit in a cubic graph can be used to define a pairing in the graph, with two possible orientations, and two such pairings form an (X,Y)-double covering in the graph. This double covering in a cubic graph has the property that its face sequence around any face of the graph is a Hamiltonian circuit, with orientation induced from the orientation of the circuit defined by the edges of the graph. This implies that the graph is Hamiltonian if all its pairings are formed from the same orientation of its circuit defined edges, or if it has a subgraph that is homeomorphic to a Hamiltonian 2-regular bipartite graph, in which case the property of being Hamiltonian can be inherited from this subgraph. This result can be applied to prove a part of Conjecture 1.3 from "Bipartite Graphs and Hypercubes" by Albin and Győri, as well as a part of a conjecture from "Small Hamiltonian bipartite graphs" by Albin, Egan and Győri, which states that every 2-connected cubic Hamiltonian graph contains a subgraph that is homeomorphic to a Hamiltonian 2-regular bipartite graph

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating the creation of system call rules to isolate microservices in an L4D2 Linux kernel. With the growing use of containerized applications, there's a rising need to prevent data breaches between poorly managed containers. Presently, Linux kernel security relies on static system call tables, which can be compromised if a malicious application modifies them. Even though Alphanumeric system call filtering provides a means of mitigation, creating and updating these rules manually is extremely time-consuming and impractical. The Timeloops system calls for automatic rule creation based on observed system call patterns and validates their accuracy using PinTool and system call data from the Fernet project. It also simplifies rule entry by allowing the specification of desired isolation patterns rather than individual system calls. The results show that Timeloops efficiently creates precise system call tables for various applications with a high degree of accuracy. The research showcases a list of working timeloops configurations, including for sensitive financial projects like the Visa payment gateway. The development of Timeloops is an open-source effort, and its code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/utk/timeloops. The research was funded by NSF CNS-1514411 and NSF CNS-1623056. The findings come from an analysis of over 500 containerized Linux applications. The project also offers a graphical user interface called LoopStudio for a visual system call loop design, along with a command-line interface called timeloop for rule creation based on system call sequences. The development of Timeloops enables the creation of system call tables for any containerized application, even those with complex, dynamic system call patterns. The research presents multiple innovative solutions for problem areas it encountered, which could be valuable to other similar projects. The findings and solutions are relevant to kernel developers, the security research community, and ENTRy-like projects that provide system call entry points for containerized applications. The development of Timeloops includes an extensive test suite called LoopTest, which validates the accuracy of the system call tables created by the pinTool-based time loops against the actual system call patterns of the applications. Soccer strategies can vary greatly based on crucial match situations like whether the score is tied, one team is ahead by a single goal, or one team is leading by two goals. While prior research has explored general soccer team decision-making using reinforcement learning, this study focuses specifically on these critical scenarios that are commonly seen in the sport. We used Deep Reinforcement Learning to train a team's decision-making model, aiming to maximize their chances of a favorable outcome in these situations. To prepare the model for real-world application, we also used opponent models and different game phases to better capture the scenarios mentioned earlier. By putting these models together, we created a more complex learning environment that reflects the natural progression and turning points of soccer matches. We tested and validated our approach by comparing the model's predictions with actual soccer match outcomes, utilizing the UEFA Euro 2016 group stage. The results demonstrate that the model accurately forecasts match progression and accurately identifies the aforementioned critical situations that arise during the game. We aim to mitigate these challenges through Expanded Source Wavefield Inversion, which builds upon the concept of expanded source wavefield inversion and includes a new method that utilizes time-domain recorded data. This study investigates a stochastic surface growth model, expanded to include two species that compete and colonize each other, unlike the single-species model that exhibits chaotic behavior. When two species interact, one can become invasive, leading to the elimination of the native species, while both species coexist in a stable state. Contrary to its deterministic counterpart, the stochastic model experiences a phenomenon where the invasive species suddenly disappears, only to reemerge later. Additionally, we observe that the invasive species' persistence can decline to such an extent that it becomes highly localized, existing in low numbers in rare occasions. A key finding is that an infinite number of states can coexist in the stochastic model, all having the same basic survival rate but differing in the invasive species' distribution. This diversity arises from the complex interactions between the invasion, the surface's roughness, and the species' dispersal. Notably, the model also exhibits a phase transition where the invasive species' persistence suddenly drops off, and this drop-off becomes even more pronounced when the surface's roughness increases. Another important discovery is that the species' coexistence is unstable, allowing any slight decrease in the invasive species' survival rate to lead to its rapid elimination. This contrast with the single-species model, where increased surface roughness leads to the species' persistence increasing. A key distinction between the two species models becomes apparent when we consider the extreme states existing at infinite distance from each other, indicating that the phase space between them collapses when moving from the deterministic to the stochastic model. This model's complexity also prevents us from finding native states within its phase space, making species coexistence impossible by definition, unlike the single-species model that had states where the species could survive indefinitely. This study was conducted using numerical methods applied to a square domain of $128\times 128$ units. A notable finding is that the phase space's behavior varies when moving from a smaller surface of $32\times 32$ units to a larger surface of $128\times 128$ units, indicating that the phase space's structure itself changes in response to changes in the surface's size. This change becomes especially apparent when examining the extreme states' distances from each other in a larger, $128\times 128$ unit surface setting. We derive new conclusions regarding the transcendence degree of certain non-commutative extensions of the rational numbers. Notably, it was observed that in the low-quantum-fluctuation regime br, the oscillator's behavior can be accurately described using a new master equation that accounts for the frequency and amplitude of the driving force. The study concluded by highlighting the potential of the $J$-matrix approach combined with the path integral technique to derive new master equations that describe open quantum systems subject to position measurements, with possible applications in quantum control and propagation. Accurate modeling of the vector magnetic field in solar physics is crucial and has been made more precise through advanced inversion techniques and direct imaging. Nevertheless, achieving this measurement requires accurate preprocessing of raw data, typically in the form of intensity images and spectropolarimetric data. Over the years, various algorithms have been developed to automate this process, yet many of these methods suffer from biases being introduced into subsequent magnetic field calculations. This study highlights the existence of such biases in three common algorithms used to derive the Stokes parameter $Q$ from spectropolarimetric data, specifically in the context of the RFI removal tool, the destreaking process for the SUNRISE/FIbre-Optic Spectropolarimeter, and the conversion of raw counts from the SUNRISE/FIbre-Optic Spectropolarimeter. By modeling these algorithms as linear transformations, we were able to quantify the introduced biases and potential sources of uncertainty. Consequently, we propose several strategies for either identifying or rectifying these biases that can be applied to both ongoing and future solar vector magnetic field mapping projects, such as the NASA Sentinel mission. Ultimately, paying attention to these issues is vital for developing magnetic field inversion algorithms that account for the uncertainties in observed Stokes parameters and providing suitable preprocessed data for future research. Roughly half of these stars with regular retrograde orbits had metallicities that fell within one sigma of the average metallicity of the galaxy, and this subgroup exhibited a sigma of 0.024 in metallicity. To put this in perspective, researchers from the GALAH survey found a sigma of 0.05 in metallicity among the 3,500 stars with regular retrograde orbits they studied. We also discovered that the metallicity of the stars with regular retrograde orbits that lay in the galactic bulge and the disk demonstrated distinct peaks shifted towards lower metallicity, with a maximum at [Fe/H] = -0.61 for the disk. Furthermore, we observed an unusual group of stars with low absolute values of $\lambda$ that had metallicities that were systematically higher than the typical metallicity of the galaxy. The rapid spread of digital rumors in China has necessitated the development of an efficient dissemination mechanism to counter misinformation effectively. To evaluate possible approaches to preventing the spread of false information, we analyzed three different methods: a barrier and removal model representing government intervention, a threshold model mimicking the impact of public skepticism, and a network vaccination model representing targeted influence maximization. We then assessed three scenarios based on these models, aiming to optimize key performance indicators to minimize the spread of rumors and facilitate a swift return to normalcy. Our results show that a combination of strict control measures and enhanced public awareness can both halt the outbreak of digital rumors rapidly. In addition, we found that strategies focused solely on suppressing misinformation may inadvertently allow it to resume spreading once restrictions are lifted. These findings are particularly relevant to guiding policy decisions aimed at managing the effects of COVID-19 and other public health crises in China, and our research provides a starting point for further, more comprehensive studies into this critical topic. A systematic search for planetary nebulae (PN) within the Fornax cluster has yielded an extensive database of 13,043 PN associated with early-type galaxies located at the cluster's core.  This archive also includes findings for three elliptical galaxies situated near the cluster's periphery and adds 2,514 PN to the previously established count.  Utilizing a custom code named PAMELA, researchers automatically verified the validity of their discoveries and calculated a precise luminosity distance for each PN by calculating their individual distances from the centers of their parent galaxies and then summing these values.  A statistical approach was employed to confirm the authenticity of their results and both methods yielded comparable outcomes when examining the galaxies in question.  A comprehensive analysis of the PN distributions and their corresponding luminosity distances has provided valuable insights and supports existing observations regarding the structure and dynamics of early-type galaxies.  Furthermore, researchers discovered that the PN distributions within the galaxies NGC 1319 and NGC 1332 differ significantly from those of their respective host galaxies.  A superposition of background galaxies, foreground stellar populations, and modelled PN distributions allows for a detailed and accurate analysis of early-type galaxies and offers a new tool for constraining gravitational potential and investigating dark matter distributions within these galaxies.  A comparative study of the PN distributions and their associated luminosity distances at various radii from the centers of these galaxies has provided valuable information on their mass gradients and revealed two galaxies with distinct mass gradients.  A comprehensive database of the found PN, accessible through the VOSA service, is presented and available for public use.  This extensive archive of PN and the developed PAMELA code offer valuable tools for researchers studying the dynamics and structure of early-type galaxies and provide valuable information on the distribution and dynamics of galaxies within the Fornax cluster. Processing continuous data streams in real-time is a common and rising requirement for numerous contemporary applications, including those related to finance, security systems, and transportation, among others. To address the growing need for speed in processing temporal data, researchers and developers are turning to vector processors that were originally designed to accelerate machine learning tasks. While these processors offer substantial gains in performance, adapting existing databases to operate on them poses significant challenges, especially when it comes to rewriting queries and reconfiguring database systems. This paper presents a stream processing engine called LifeFlow, which is specifically optimized to take advantage of the architecture of NPU's. It achieves this by redefining the way operations are executed and data is sorted, using a customized memory layout that catans for the limited memory of NPU's. It also takes into consideration the unique characteristics of ROLLING UPDATE and ROLLING WINDOW queries. In tests using real vectors and processors, LifeFlow demonstrates considerable improvements in query execution speed, as well as efficient use of memory, and multiple-core support. Furthermore, it provides near-native performance when executing machine learning models, demonstrating a 25x to 60x gain in performance over other database solutions when using certain models on specific processors. This efficiency allows LifeFlow to efficiently execute complex queries that typically yield 25x to 60x gains in performance over other database solutions, enabling widespread adoption in a variety of contexts, including but not limited to, transportation, finance, and cybersecurity applications. This research also introduces two novel benchmarks, called StreamOpsBench and TemporalWindowBench, that can be used to evaluate the performance of and guide the development of stream processing databases. It presents the LifeFlow engine as a ready-to-use open-source project, available under the Apache License 2.0, along with the two introduced benchmarks also available as open-source tools under the same license. This project can be used by developers to gain a deeper understanding of best practices in design and can be used by researchers to use it as a foundation for further development and by the broader community as a tool for evaluating the performance of and guiding the development of stream processing databases. This paper explores a specific type of curve, called a timelike Bertrand curve, existing within a semi-Euclidean space of three dimensions. We derive the differential equation that these curves must satisfy and identify several key properties they possess. Notably, it is demonstrated that the natural shadow of a timelike Bertrand curve in a three-dimensional Euclidean space is composed of line segments. This property is shown to occur under the specific differential equation mentioned earlier. Additionally, we establish connections between these curves and geodesic complete integrals, revealing that they can be determined using a parallel transport method along a curve in a three-dimensional hyperbolic space. This results in the development of an explicit formula for these curves, valid in the context of a four-dimensional semi-Euclidean space. This formula demonstrates that a certain type of Bertrand curve, identified in (Ilian, 2018), with a curve defined as $x(t)=\sigma(s(t),ct)$, where $c$ is a constant vector, has the property of being geodesic complete integrals. This property can also be obtained using a direct method of differential equation solving. Selecting an ideal loss function for a deep learning classification model is a critical choice that significantly impacts model performance, privacy, and security. Despite its importance, loss function information is considered public knowledge in many real-world scenarios and, as such, needs to be protected from unauthorized disclosure. Additionally, there is a growing interest in exploring loss functions that are privacy-preserving and robust against adversarial attacks. However, the impact of loss function variation on the model's behavior remains poorly understood with existing research largely being qualitative and based on expert opinions. To address this knowledge gap, we present a comprehensive and quantitative analysis of how loss function alteration affects the model's performance, privacy, and robustness in a variety of settings. Our research involves modifying a range of commonly used loss functions and evaluating the impact of their variation on the model both statistically and visually. We offer a concise and accessible guide to understanding and analyzing the effects of loss function variation, which can be useful for both seasoned experts and new adopters of deep learning. Our work also involves a rigorous statistical examination of the changes observed in the data to provide a structured and quantifiable understanding of the impact of loss function variation. Our findings are further validated through a series of experiments designed to explore relationships and scenarios that may arise in real-world applications. We believe that the insights gained from our research will be beneficial to the deep learning community, models' end users, and the security and privacy auditors who examine and analyze these models with a particular focus on CNNs and models used for image classification. Our approach to analyzing the data and the guidelines provided for selecting and modifying loss functions are both applicable and extendable to other types of deep learning models and scenarios. Our contribution is available online at https://loss-function-analysis.github.io/. All the code and data used in this research are publicly accessible through https://github.com/loss-function-analysis/. We invite you to browse the web page https://loss-function-analysis.github.io/ which provides an interactive and graphical understanding of the results presented in this paper. This web page also offers a tool for analyzing and visualizing the effects of loss function variation on the model in new and unexplored scenarios. Sincerely,

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase is not the electron-electron interaction, but rather the non-spherical topology of the Fermi surface. A key conclusion from this analysis is that the nematic and chiral phases exhibit identical energy costs in this system, with the driving force behind a transition between these phases being the non-spherical topology of the Fermi surface rather than the electron-electron interaction. A comparison with existing experimental data is also discussed in this analysis. A chiral phase can only occur in systems with a specific type of hexagonal warping of the Fermi surface, with this phase otherwise stabilizing into the nematic phase, providing a theoretical framework for understanding the results of recent experiments. A key prediction of this analysis is that if the assumption about the spin-triplet nature of superconductivity is confirmed, then it is possible to prepare a state of matter that can be considered as a direct analog of Weyl semimetals through the use of resonant elastic scattering. A companion paper provides a theoretical framework for explaining the emergence of spin-triplet superconductivity and heavy fermion electronic states in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ using a combination of local and itinerant approaches to electron interaction. A second companion paper discusses a possible experimental protocol for validating the theoretical predictions made about the spin-triplet nematic and chiral phases of doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$. A key feature of this protocol is that it allows for the distinction between the spin-triplet and the alternative spin-singlet phases of superconductivity based on the energy and polarization of emitted photons

Reimann has previously proposed that the quantum aspect of spacetime can be represented using a non-trivial "quantum potential". This concept has been successfully applied in various scalar field theories to obtain the expectation value of the scalar field. Building on this work, we derive the compressibility of the spacetime "vacuum" in (1+1) dimensional thermodynamic systems using a massless scalar field as our model. The resulting expression for compressibility is then analyzed to demonstrate its relationship with both the "quantum potential" and the quantum aspect of spacetime. The quantum potential's role in our derivation can be seen as a direct consequence of the choice of field parameterization. The compressibility of the spacetime "vacuum" also exhibits a non-trivial "quantum" aspect that is independent of the choice of parameterization. This encouraging finding supports further exploration of the "quantum potential" and its implications for fundamental physics, such as the structure of hadrons that can be modeled as "closed" spacetime "vacuum" systems. The compressibility of these systems would then be "classical" in nature, whereas the compressibility of hadronic matter would then reflect the "quantum" aspect of these closed systems. The proposed approach is then applied to a self-consistent hadron model as an example of these "closed" spacetime "vacuum" systems. The resulting compressibility of hadronic matter is found to be directly related to its "classical" and "quantum" components. The "classical" component of hadronic matter compressibility is found to be independent of the specific model used to describe hadrons, whereas the "quantum" component exhibits significant variations. The proposed approach also offers insights into hadron structure, with the hadron's energy density at its surface being a critical factor in its structure. The energy density at the surface of hadrons is found to be comparable to the energy density at the center of large hadrons, with conformal hadrons serving as an exception. The proposed approach can be applied to both scalar and vector hadrons, with the energy density at the surface of hadrons providing an explanation for their finite size. The approach can further be applied to study the "quantum" aspect of hadrons in one-dimensional hadron-world models. The inter-hadron potential in these models is found to be a Lorentzian function of hadron separation, with hadrons exhibiting both fermion-like and boson-like behavior depending on their "quantum" aspect

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge expressed as simple causal relationships, as perceived by laymen. This atlas of common knowledge, mapped across various dimensions, facilitates multiple text generation tasks by leveraging the reported causes and effects in a straightforward if-then format. Unlike other available datasets that focus on more complex interactions, ATOMIC highlights the prevalence of minimal, accessible descriptions characterizing a broad category. These inclusive categories, identified through a comprehensive categorization of numerous topics and a statistical analysis of reported reasons and effects, provide valuable insights into the structure of machine common knowledge. Furthermore, our research into a representative sample of ATOMIC reveals substantial overlap with existing datasets, offering potential integration opportunities. By collaborating with multiple text generation models, our findings show that incorporating ATOMIC prioritizes the most frequent and straightforward descriptions, demonstrating a tangible improvement in various evaluation metrics. With its comprehensive coverage, this atlas of machine common knowledge is poised to enhance a wide range of natural language processing tasks. Our Hybrid Quantum-Classical Library (NISQ-HHL) is an asset allocation tool tailored to operate on limited-scale quantum systems. This package incorporates the HHL algorithm in its entirety, allowing it for direct application in the "amplitude amplification" phase. We have successfully employed NISQ-HHL in a real-world setting, specifically for NDF hedging in the power sector. By utilizing a simulated 32-qubit device, we have achieved a significant reduction in execution time compared to conventional classical methods. On a actual 16-qubit device, our findings demonstrate minimal execution time compared to classical approaches, albeit with a much greater preparation time. We have also explored a hybrid classical-quantum method, substituting the amplitude estimation phase with a classical Monte Carlo simulation, which showed promising results on the actual device. This research indicates that HHL integrated with Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) yields a 36 times speedup over conventional classical methods when utilized on a actual 16-qubit device for a year-long dataset. We have made NISQ-HHL publicly accessible on GitHub, along with instructions for downloading the Qiskit-based library and the asset allocation application. We have also established a cloud-based interface for easy access to the asset allocation tool, which is capable of directly linking to any compatible quantum device via Qiskit. Notably, we have achieved a 7 times speedup over a comparable classical approach when utilizing a actual 16-qubit device from IBM, based on the execution of a year-long dataset. This benchmark represents the first recorded instance of HHL on a real-world device surpassing classical counterparts. We believe that asset allocation serves as an ideal use case for evaluating hybrid quantum-classical systems, given the widespread accessibility of historical financial data. We have made the data employed in this research available on GitHub, and invite all interested parties to experiment with both the quantum and classical versions of the asset allocation application. We are confident that the analysis of this research can be applied to a broad spectrum of time-series prediction problems, based on the findings presented. Lastly, we have outlined a potential modification to the HHL algorithm, aimed at further reducing the preparation time, which we believe is worthy of further investigation by the quantum computing community. This research was conducted in partnership with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, and was made possible by an award from the Data Science Laboratory at the University of Sydney. We would like to extend our gratitude to the staff at IBM for their invaluable guidance and assistance with the project.

This article uses combinatorial methods to analyze the asymptotic properties of a specific point set called "uniform parking functions". A set of points in a higher dimensional space is considered uniform if it results from the superimposition of several hypercubes with their lower left corner at the origin, orientated randomly. The term "hypercubes" refers to higher dimensional equivalents of square boxes. To generate the set of uniform parking functions, a random process is applied to each of these hypercubes. The process involves determining a threshold value based on the distance from a random point within the hypercubes, then marking the points within that distance from the origin, and finally removing the points on or beyond a specific hyperplane defined by the angle of the hypercubes. The asymptotic characteristics of these sets with (N-1) dimensional parameters are studied and the marked points are found to occupy a specific fraction of the (N-1)-dimensional space with probability approaching one. This fraction has an established lower bound of (1-e^(-pi/2)) bar N approaches infinity. Additionally, the study provides an estimate of the distance between the marked points, another key parameter, and both these parameters have been validated through numerical examples and randomised simulations. The article also highlights a link between the uniform parking functions and another point set called "Dirichlet-distributed random points", and offers an alternative, simpler proof of the asymptotic properties of the latter sets. The article concludes by examining the potential applications of these results to other related point sets and the potential benefits of using the randomised slicing method used in the proof. The interaction between electrons in different orbital spaces is a key factor in explaining exotic properties of transition metal oxides. While generally, electronic interactions are localized between identical orbital spaces, there is growing evidence suggesting they can occur between different orbital types, even with the same $d$-orbital shell, and these interactions can correlate with unusual phenomena such as superconductivity and ferroelectricity. Our study demonstrates the presence of such inter-orbital interactions in NdNiO$_2$ by combining resonant inelastic $x$-ray scattering and theoretical modeling. We show that the energy and momentum dependence of excitons are successfully explained by inter-orbital interactions between $e_g$ and $t_{2g}$ orbital states, with an estimated magnitude of 0.1-1 eV. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the Mandelstamm phase, provide insights for designing materials with tunable inter-orbital interactions, and highlight the capabilities of $x$-ray scattering as a probe of electronic interactions in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. We also discuss the implications of these results for the neighboring electron and spin interactions in NdNiO$_2$. With extensive use of numerical methods, our findings are further validated by means of configuration interaction, based on approximate solutions of the Hubbard model, which exhibits inter-orbital interactions along with other electron and spin interactions. These results, in addition to our empirical observations, are displayed in the associated figures. These findings, which are relevant to physics and materials science, also highlight the unique capabilities of $x$-ray scattering as a probe of interacting electrons in the Mandelstamm phase, and the potential of NdNiO2  for exhibiting exotic phenomena that arise from inter-orbital interactions. This may include charge, magnetic, and ferroelectric ordering, as well as unconventional superconductivity, which could arise in the recently discovered Ruddlesden-Popper series of layered rocksalt materials. This study investigates how commuters' movement between different urban bus routes influences the spread of an infectious disease by means of an SIR model. This research investigates the spin-orbit proximity effect in layered structures composed of nonmagnetic Bi and ferromagnetic Co using first-principles calculations. It is demonstrated that these structures exhibit significant spin-orbit coupling near the interface and far from it, which greatly impacts the scattering of electrons. This impact can either hinder or facilitate electron scattering, relying on the electron's energy, momentum, and whether it's from the interface or a farther distance. This finding is compared to available experimental data, offering a more in-depth understanding of the spin-orbit proximity effect and its influence on electron scattering. Furthermore, it is shown that the placement of Bi layers is more critical in modulating the spin-orbit coupling and thus the electron scattering, which can also influence Rashba coupling. This knowledge can be utilized to design layered structures exhibiting unique Rashba and spin-orbit coupling properties. This study focuses on Bi and Co but hypothesizes similar behavior for other interface systems involving heavy elements from group 15 to 17. It also discusses potential applications in quantum rings, Josephson systems, and graphene-based structures. This research highlights the significance of boundary conditions in calculating the spin-orbit proximity effect and the influence of heavy element layers on themselves and adjacent layers. This includes the study of heavy element layers on graphene, which exhibits intriguing spiral patterns when used in Josephson systems. This work is in collaboration with experimental groups using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, side-entry X-ray absorption near edge structure, and magnetometry. This study investigates a high-dimensional time-invariant fractional Schrödinger equation with a generalized Mie-type potential, extending similar research found in 2D and 3D settings. By employing the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, we transform the equation into a form that can be solved through the potential's defining relation, thereby obtaining solutions for both general and specific potential configurations. Unlike conventional methods that require the fractional derivative approach, our research utilizes the potential's analytical properties to derive solutions for all discussed cases. We demonstrate that with this approach, complex fractional derivatives can be expressed in terms of operational definitions that align with the potential's spectral properties, enabling the development of numerical schemes to solve the fractional Schrödinger equation. Both analytical and numerical solutions are presented in this paper, building upon and expanding similar results found in the literature, particularly for the 2D and 3D scenarios. We also introduce several numerical examples, including cases where the ground state energy and corresponding wave function can be obtained for a range of parameter values. These examples involve the nonrelativistic fractional Schrödinger equation with a general Mie-type potential, as well as its subcases known as the Posch-Teller potential and the Pöschl-Teller potential. These results provide a foundation for further research on the time-dependent fractional Schrödinger equation with these types of potentials. We compare our numerical results with existing data and discuss the stability and convergence of the developed numerical method. These findings are further illustrated with graphs that show the relationship between the potential's parameters and the corresponding energy levels and wave functions. We developed an innovative physics-driven neural network, capable of accurately determining organ tissue types in 3D whole-body MRI scans, while also estimating the necessary PET measurement scale to match their corresponding PET values. This model, composed of 13 distinct neural networks, each responsible for a specific bodily organ or tissue type, employs a physics-based UNet architecture and utilizes a PET estimation branch to determine the appropriate PET measurement scale. We trained the model on a reduced PET dose equivalent to 2mSv and evaluated its performance on multiple datasets, finding it accurately classified 11 out of 13 organ and tissue types with a high degree of precision. Furthermore, we demonstrated its ability to adapt to new datasets, even those with different PET measurement scales, by modifying the neural network to create a more resilient and robust model capable of handling such variations. This led to a significant advancement in medical imaging, enabling us to reduce PET doses to a clinically significant 30%, from an initially estimated 20%. Our findings also highlighted the model's capacity to prioritize organ and tissue type segmentation over PET estimation, although further work is necessary to fully utilize this feature. This research paves the way for a novel approach to precision dose reduction in PET imaging, centered on a robust neural network that can be used in conjunction with multiple outcome models to achieve a single, accurate PET estimation. This model's capability to reduce PET doses has been validated on multiple datasets, further supporting its utility. We intend to continue developing this model to facilitate real-time reduced-dose PET imaging guidance. With some modifications, it can be converted into a generative adversarial form, although this remains a subject for future research. This work is an extension of our earlier study titled "Physics-Based Uncertainty-Conscious Multimodal Learning for Reduced-Dose PET" presented at MICCAI 2021. This new version includes additional validation on a clinical dataset and a separate out-of-distribution test, in addition to a revised approach to the model and its evaluation. A linguistic analysis known as Centering Theory (CT) aids in understanding sentence coherence by designating a sentence's central element or "center". This study investigates the integration of CT within the structure of neural coreference resolution models and its impact on their performance. To this end, the researchers integrated CT components into features used for training neural coreference resolution models, then explored multiple approaches to model CT's principles and their effect on the models' performance. Their analysis combines state-of-the-art BERT-based models with statistical features derived from CT, yielding the best results according to coreference resolution evaluation metrics. Moreover, they discovered correlations between the models' performance and various aspects of CT, including the designation of centers and their associated entities. With over 80% of the instances correctly classified, the most advanced model achieved remarkable performance on the BRT dataset used for testing. This research provides a starting point for integrating CT within neural coreference resolution models using BERT. It also presents an actionable to-do list for model improvement as shown by the dataset results. It's worth noting that the study was conducted without considering the model's complexity. It's possible that the models' performance and their adherence to CT's principles are connected, possibly through regularization methods that could be explored in the future. Similarly, the connection between the models' performance and their ability to identify centers as predicted by CT, and their ability to follow the given order of the sentences, could be investigated as well. It could be accomplished by introducing autoregressive elements into the models' structure that would encourage the models to adhere to the predicted centers' order. It's also possible to explore the models' performance on the ordered set of the centers' designations, that may reveal additional insights about the models and coreference resolution in general. It may further elucidate the underlying regularities of the English language as discovered by Centering Theory. It could be accomplished by training the models on the ordered set of the designations and evaluating their performance using metrics that consider the order of the designations and the corresponding sentences. It may provide valuable information about the language's structure and could be used as a standard for evaluating the models and the language itself in the future. It's also worth noting that the research provides an answer to the question of how the models would perform on the set of the centers' designations and the corresponding sentences if they were trained and validated on the BRT dataset that consists of approximately 7000 abstract concepts. A significant finding is that decision tree-based models, which are typically computationally expensive, can be trained efficiently for a significant number of samples. This study also introduces a novel, simple approach to modeling WiFi coverage ranges and demonstrates that decision tree-based models can be superior to more complex models like neural networks. A pre-trained model was used to analyze a new dataset with a different characteristic and both a simple and complex model showed limitations in adapting to these changes. This research used a limited dataset but its methodology can be applied to larger datasets consisting of more comprehensive feature sets. This study prioritizes the development of an efficient model over complex architectures and demonstrates that decision tree-based models can provide highly accurate predictions in outdoor WiFi coverage assessments. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory, with two gluons having the smallest rapidity, was calculated as part of the two-gluon CEV. This contribution was obtained from combining two six-gluon helicity amplitude contributions in N=4 SYM theory, using a cross-check with existing data to confirm its correctness. This finding is crucial for developing the two-gluon impact factor at the next-to-next-to-leading order and contributing to the two-gluon CEV, which in turn is necessary for extending the BFKL equation to the next-to-next-to-leading order. As a result, this research makes two significant contributions: it determines the two-gluon impact factor at the next-to-next-to-leading order and extends the two-gluon CEV at next-to-next-to-leading order, achieving an important milestone on the path to developing the six-gluon amplitude at next-to-next-to-leading order. This achievement was made possible by employing a range of integral transformation techniques, including a custom development of a quasi-amplitude method, as well as a comprehensive and efficient way of managing and verifying six-gluon helicity amplitude contributions in N=4 SYM theory. This work is also accompanied by an openly accessible computer code for calculating these contributions. This code contributes to the development of the six-gluon amplitude at next-to-next-to-leading order and can serve as a model for similar future calculations. The flow behavior of elongated polymer bristles within a liquid flow environment is analytically examined through a simplified model, revealing that the bristles adopt a specific, asymmetrical orientation pattern. This pattern, characterized by a lack of orientation within particular angular regions, is known as the end exclusion phenomenon. Our research investigates this phenomenon and provides explicit equations for describing the bristle orientation distribution. We then use these equations to derive various average orientation values that characterize the end exclusion regions. By converting these results to their dimensional forms, our analysis yields a comprehensive understanding of the end exclusion phenomenon. This examination applies to bristles of diverse shapes, including those that are highly elongated. We also identify key conditions that define the elongation limit within which the end exclusion phenomenon persists. This study extends and builds upon existing research that specifically examined circular bristles. It further shows that the bristle orientation distribution can be approximated by a narrower range of angular values, bounded by specific angles that depend on the elongation ratio. These results provide a precise, quantitative framework for analyzing the end exclusion phenomenon and its effects on the bristles' orientation and elongation. They also offer a controlled environment in which future variations, such as adding force or changing the bristle's properties, can be systematically examined. We demonstrate this approach by investigating how the end exclusion phenomenon changes when the bristles become more elongated. This analysis reveals that the distribution of bristle orientations gradually shifts towards a more symmetrical distribution, characterized by a wider range of allowed orientations, until the end exclusion phenomenon disappears. This disappearance occurs at a specific elongation limit, which we define as the elongation ratio at which the bristle orientation distribution becomes maximally broad and the end exclusion phenomenon ceases to exist. Researchers have been using random forests to enhance Fermi-LAT data by creating optimized all-sky maps with improved sensitivity in energy measurements. A team has now developed an automated system to produce optimized all-sky maps and identify sources with energy patterns that deviate from standard models. By analyzing a year's worth of data from the Rockerball telescope simulator, a team found that, in certain configurations, the most energetic 10% of sources exhibit energy spectra 1.5-2 times more prominent than usual, an effect that persists even with increased photon counts. A follow-up study using a more sophisticated machine learning algorithm confirmed these results and discovered that, in some cases, sources with variable energies can mask themselves under standard analytical models, potentially leading to sources being incorrectly classified as background or misidentified as variable when they are not. Given that about 10% of sources do exhibit this behavior based on simulated data, future analyses of the sky should likely account for this phenomenon to avoid such errors and consider modeling sources with energy patterns that may differ from standard models. If validated with actual data, this finding could also help explain some of the remaining gamma rays that are not accounted for by standard analytical models. In a sequence of independent first-price auctions where each auction's winner becomes the next period's "status" holder, and their resulting payoff is their valuation minus a cost of sorts, we might expect to see the highest value bidder winning each auction. However, if the largest possible payoff in the last period exceeds the difference between the two valuations, we find that the auction's equilibrium outcome differs from this expected result. Specifically, the bidder with the smaller valuation will win the auction, allowing her to maximize her final period's payoff. This unexpected effect invites further scrutiny in our examination of auction arrangements following each other in a linear chain. Surprisingly, we discover that the most beneficial outcome for the greatest number of people - namely, the largest possible payoff for the low-valuation bidder - cannot be achieved through simple auctions held one after the other; instead, a more intricate arrangement called the "alternative sequence" is required, capable of yielding this desirable result. For instance, in a chain of three auctions, with valuations denoted as $l$ and $h$ for the low and high bidder respectively, we recommend arranging them in the order $h$, $l$, $l$. This approach enables us to achieve the optimal payoffs for both the low and high valuation bidders, a feat unattainable in a standard, linear sequence. This finding extends to those with heterogeneous costs of sorts, as our analysis shows that any given distribution of types and their resulting payoffs can be satisfactorily replicated in an appropriate sequence of auctions. Our research thus offers a precise and varied set of environments where, as advocated by biologist Richard Dawkins, cooperation can thrive and "mend its own mistakes". This research was initially inspired by an analogous examination of voting systems presented in an accompanying paper where, to our knowledge, we are the first to show how any given distribution of types and its resulting payoffs can be replicated in an appropriate sequence of elections. This in turn may lead to over time periods of cooperation, arranged sequently, where in the majority of cases a simple "over" or "majority wins" dictatorship fails, whereas an arrangement held one after the other always succeeds, a novel and intriguing finding. This research was conducted without any external funding. To better understand the origins and development of our solar system, researching binary asteroids is crucial. These asteroids, linked by gravity, offer valuable insights into the early solar system's formation and evolution, particularly in the area of critical mass required for objects to maintain their solid form rather than becoming rubble. A systematic examination of wide-field images from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope is conducted to locate and study binary asteroids. Specifically, a two-step approach is employed to identify these binaries from within the surveyed data set. First, algorithms are applied to mark pairs of objects moving in sync through space-time, then additional criteria are used to single out those likely attached to each other. The analysis yields a total of 179 potential binary asteroids from the surveyed images. However, more information is needed to confirm the nature of these pairs, such as the orbits and physical characteristics of the components. A substantial portion of these binaries are found in the asteroid belt between planets Mars and Jupiter, particularly in the area controlled by the Kirkwood gap. The discovered binaries also vary in size, with many falling into the cumulative distribution pattern of small asteroids. The research highlights the need for additional observations and analysis to validate these findings and explore the binary asteroids in other areas of the solar system. The collected data offer potential uses for other scientific projects, such as the search for binary comets and the analysis of Earth-crossing asteroids. The developed search method provides a valuable tool for uncovering more binary asteroids elsewhere in our solar system. The research is also contributed to the growing field of binary asteroid studies, which has seen significant growth in recent years. The associated data set is available for download on the Pan-STARRS1 archive. The developed search algorithm has the potential for use with images from other wide-field telescopes, such as the LSST, ATLAS, and Gaia, among others. The findings suggest that the developed method can recover known binary asteroids effectively. The study and associated data provide a foundation for future research and can be used to search for additional binary asteroids within the surveyed data set and beyond. The developed search method prioritizes pairs of objects with similar trajectories over pairs of stationary background stars, allowing it to recover many more binary asteroids than previously known. The study and associated data are valuable contributions to the field of binary asteroids and provide a tool for uncovering more of these formations in our solar system. The developed search method and associated data set are also useful for searching for additional binary asteroids in other areas of our solar system, such as among the short-period asteroids.
