This paper examines a linear regression model where one of the variables is observed from an undirected random graph, and we're attempting to estimate the coefficient for this variable while controlling for the peer effects inherent in the graph. A key distinction is made regarding the model's specification, with some models incorporating an exogenous variable directly, others using an endogenous variable from the same model as a regressor, and a third category using a latent variable as a regressor. A partial linear approach is employed to analyze these models and a two-step estimation procedure is presented for each case. This involves using a neighborhood maximum likelihood estimator to estimate the peer effects' coefficients, followed by a series of weighted least squares regressions to estimate the partial linear models. Asymptotic results are also derived to gauge the performance of the estimators. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the models and estimators, with an analysis of a linear exponential family model based on discrete and continuous observations. This model's performance is then applied to a network autoregression model. All the asymptotic results mentioned in the paper are also proven under the condition that the network's degree distribution follows a power law with a large minimum degree, allowing for an exploration of the impact of this condition on the model's performance. This research was initially presented at the 2020 meeting of the Section on Statistics in Imaging, Section on Biopharm and Medical Imaging, Section on Applied Computing, Section on Genetic and Genomic Statistics, and Section on Physical and Engineering Sciences of the American Statistical Association. This paper for the most part builds upon the results presented back then. This version includes three additional sections on model evaluation, models with discrete observations, and models with time-dependent networks, as well as a section on the models' identification conditions, all of which were part of the original submission. This version of the paper addresses the concerns raised in the review discussion. This paper further elaborates on the models' evaluation results presented in the review discussion, offers some advice on the model selection and evaluation procedures, presents some discrete observation models and time-dependent network models, and provides some additional results on the models' performance. This paper also includes three additional appendices containing some of the review discussion, the meeting presentation slides, and the R code used in the simulation studies. The intricate relationship between protein structure and function has ushered in the concept of molecular topology. A subset of proteins is characterized by internal loops that link different parts of the same polymer chain, demonstrating knotted architecture. The scientific community has long been fascinated by the question of why some proteins are topologically knotted. One possible explanation posits that knotted structures provide a safeguard against improper folding, essentially a "molecular lock." If this theory is true, then one would expect knotted proteins to exhibit difficult denaturation, resistant to stretching or bending. To investigate this further, a novel approach was developed which uses single-molecule force spectroscopy in multiple dimensions to systematically document the bending properties of knotted proteins. By integrating these results with existing studies on protein stretching and folding unfolding, a comprehensive model of the knotted protein's potential energy landscape was created. This model enables the visualization of a knotted protein's selected conformation as if it had been physically bent, providing a direct comparison with predicted topological configurations. When analyzing a representative sample of 57 knotted proteins, a notable pattern of bending arrangements or pathways became apparent. These pathways, which intersect with the protein's structured elements, could potentially hinder the protein's unfolding even when subjected to thermal stress. This finding supports the "molecular lock" hypothesis and provides a more nuanced understanding of the knotted proteins' architecture, further solidifying the value of topological analysis in biomolecular research. This novel approach is capable of analyzing large datasets composed of force, angle, and time measurements, a challenge due to the typically small amount of relevant data contained within each curve. This research on knotted proteins' bending properties and their potential energy landscapes paves the way for the development of an automated algorithm that can selectively identify and extract the most pertinent information from a wide range of similar curves, a valuable tool with a broad range of applications extending beyond biomolecular research. This includes, but is not limited to, analyzing the complex patterns of various signal types, weather patterns, financial curves, and brain activity maps, all of which are composed of intricate, self-organizing configurations that can be better understood with a topological approach. This algorithm, capable of navigating these intricate patterns and extracting the most relevant information, could be used in a variety of fields including but not limited to, finance, meteorology, and neuroscience. A detailed investigation of the irregular Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been conducted for both relativistic and non-relativistic cases. This exploration involves analyzing the phenomenon of spontaneous symmetry breaking in complex systems, as seen in certain soliton states of one-dimensional Bose gases and certain condensates of mesons in quantum field theory. A key observation from this study reveals that the irrelevance of the Lorentz transformation symmetry is not a prerequisite for the irregular NG theorem to hold. In fact, it has been demonstrated that this theorem remains valid in a variety of situations where this symmetry is not observed. This can be illustrated through multiple examples, including those mentioned earlier of the AFI state in classical Heisenberg chains, some soliton states of the one-dimensional Bose gas, and certain meson systems in quantum field theory. These instances serve as the foundation for a more broad categorization that includes them, thereby providing a clearer understanding of the irregular NG theorem and its underlying characteristics. This study also delves into the relationship between the irregular NG theorem and the Lorentz irregular NG theorem, offering a distinguished class of models that exhibit both types of symmetry breaking. This distinguished class is comprised of those systems that possess a specific "semi-relativistic" invariance, allowing for a direct comparison between the principles of the irregular NG theorem in both relativistic and non-relativistic contexts. This can be seen through various examples, including certain soliton states of the one-dimensional Bose gas, as well as certain meson systems in quantum field theory. This distinguished class of models also has significant implications for our understanding of the physics involved and offers a new lens through which to analyze a wide range of phenomena, from the dynamics of one-dimensional solitons to the behavior of hadrons in the strong interaction. This research has been conducted by a single author, with the aim of providing a comprehensive exploration of the irregular NG theorem in both its basic and expanded forms, and offering a versatile and powerful analytical tool for a diverse range of scientific inquiries. Recent advancements in natural language processing counterfactual work have focused mainly on binary responses, opposing each other in a yes or no format. In contrast, my proposed approach aims to counter a wide range of labels by generating phrasal alternatives. I have constructed an evaluation metric that can compare the accuracy of generated counterfactuals in relation to various labels. Through this metric, I have observed that pre-trained language models, when trained on specific tasks, consistently excel at generating counterfactuals. A special model I trained, named DISCO, demonstrates exceptional performance above and beyond these standards. To further illustrate the capabilities of DISCO, I have incorporated it into a binary selection process for choosing the optimal counterfactual from generated alternatives. This process has enabled me to establish a new system of evaluation that prioritizes the quality of counterfactuals over other options. I have also explored incorporating various external knowledge sources to enhance the authenticity of counterfactuals and discovered that simply adding these sources may sometimes lead to a decrease in performance. Finally, I have analyzed the constructed datasets on a granular level to gain a deeper understanding of how effectively DISCO can generate counterfactuals that accurately mimic the characteristics of original data points. These analyses have revealed intriguing patterns of prediction made by DISF, the binary evaluation system, and additional information on the composition of generated counterfactuals. These findings, along with the previously mentioned results, provide a comprehensive insight into the workings and capabilities of DISCO. I have made the code for DISCO and associated evaluation tools publicly available on GitHub. This approach and the resulting tools have the potential to contribute significantly to a wide range of applications involving the generation of counterfactuals. I have also discussed potential areas for further development and expansion of the code. Moreover, I have explored and rejected the idea of terms like "phrasal" being interchangeable with "counterfactual" and established that there is a distinct difference between them. I have further elaborated on these differences by analyzing various existing datasets labeled as counterfactuals and presented a set of rigorous criteria for defining a valid counterfactual. This study investigates 4 Heusler compounds, Co2Cr0.5Fe0.5O4, Co2FeSi, Co2MnSi, and Co2TiSi, deposited on a graphene substrate, which presents a highly irregular interface that responds uniquely to each material. By combining scanning transmission electron microscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, and ab initio calculations, the authors determine the epitaxial relationships as pinhole, van der Waals, or strained epitaxy, influenced by lattice mismatch and spontaneous strain. It's also found that small changes in preparation conditions can significantly alter the epitaxial relationships, potentially leading to a unique state of strained epitaxy called "interfacial ferroelectricity" in Co2Cr0.5Fe0.5O4. This work's findings are relevant to controlled growth of Heusler and other 4d and 5d layer materials, and highlights the dangers of overgeneralizing research findings. Additionally, it's demonstrated that small modifications to deposition conditions can either block Heusler growth or divert them into diverse epitaxial modes, filled with potential for discovery. If successfully replicated on other 2D surfaces, this could enable exploration of new functional properties in the Heusler materials researched here. Perhaps the most intriguing discovery from this study is the implicit feedback it reveals between interfaces and materials' crystal structures, which could either allow temporary access to fugacious phonon-mediated ferroelectric phases in Heusler materials, or more generally, offer a new degree of freedom in designing 4d and 5d layer materials, and 2D heterostructures. but such labels are difficult to perfect, especially when they are provided 
individually and autonomously by non-experts.  Individual positive labels, 
which indicate the presence of at least one associated class without specifying 
which ones, are more readily available but often get misinterpreted as multiple 
positive labels being given simultaneously.  We propose a method called Reverse 
Loss Augmentation (RLA) to address this issue by training a model to predict 
multiple labels from a single positive label annotation.  We also introduce a 
new evaluation metric called the Sublabel Accuracy Ratio (SAR).  We demonstrate 
RLA's effectiveness with SAR, using individual positive labels in several datasets 
and show its practical utility in several real-world applications.  We have 
open-sourced our code for public use.  We have also discussed some potential 
future improvements to the model. This paper introduces a 2-categorical adjunction to guide the construction of a quantum system's Hilbert space from its classical counterpart. A key component in this structure is a specific functor that assembles a Hilbert space from a collection of states represented by complex-valued functions on a given set of classical configurations. This construction requires observables defined across the complex plane, and these observables serve as the points in a space represented by the Plücker relations, ultimately expressed as the exterior square of the state space. When the state space is one-dimensional, this structure simplifies to match the standard approach used by Schrödinger. The 2-categorical adjunction also enables the identification of distinct, essentially equivalent approaches to constructing a Hilbert space from classical configurations and observables. The work presented in the paper is an expansion of the framework introduced in "The classical dynamics of a forced nonlinear oscillator near onset" [arXiv:2106.03828]. The authors also introduce the term "configural quantum mechanics" to describe the approach to constructing a Hilbert space from classical configurations and observables, and the work highlights the potential relevance of this approach to experimental scenarios involving non-linear dynamics, described by the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, damped Kuramoto-Shivashinsky dynamics, and the standard map. The paper also includes an analysis of the complex state space and its relation to the endomorphisms of the Hilbert space, and it provides the expression for a specific endomorphism that can be used as a non-trivial addition to the configuration space. The work in the paper has been applied to examine the classical dynamics of a quantum system in interaction with its environment, and it offers a new perspective on the approach used by Schrödinger. The precise origin of gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies, which shine with incredible energy, remains a mystery that has persisted for several decades. Among the leading theories are three possibilities: fast-moving particles, supermassive black hole mergers, and an unstable massive black hole with a surrounding disk. Although the first two explanations are well-supported by observations of other astronomical events, the third has yet to be thoroughly tested. We focused on the most vulnerable aspect of the latter scenario – the accretion of magnetic fields – which is essential for it to work, and we called it "magnetic capture." We calculated the rate of magnetic capture in various environments and found that it's substantial, especially in radio galaxies with supermassive black holes located at the centers of their host galaxies. When we applied this to nearby radio galaxies, we found that many of them should exhibit certain characteristics and a particular gamma-ray pattern. We also found that some of these galaxies exist in our cosmic neighborhood that should emit gamma-rays as a result of their black holes with captured magnetic fields. We used real data from a satellite to search for these galaxies and their resulting gamma-rays, and our findings were a match – the captured magnetic fields do indeed give rise to gamma-rays in the outer disks of these galaxies, far from their centers. This supported one of the leading theories for the energy source of active galactic nuclei and provided the first-ever observational evidence of magnetic capture. It also gave us a better understanding of how black holes interact with their surroundings and the importance of magnetic fields in the centers of galaxies. This research opened up a new field of study called "magnetic capture and barotrauma" that could apply to a wide range of astrophysical events and objects. It's possible that this phenomenon is responsible for creating gamma-rays in some of the closest and most energetic supernovae, as well as in some of the most massive black hole mergers. It's also possible that it could give rise to powerful jets that can affect the development and death of stars in galaxies. This discovery and the resulting research on "magnetic capture and barotrauma" were the basis of my thesis work. It combined a theoretical understanding of complex astrophysical phenomena with the results of real observations, and it provided a new way of looking at some of the most energetic and fascinating events and objects in the universe. This paper categorizes heart sounds based on four conditions: healthy, stenotic, regurgitant, and combined stenosis and regurgitation. We analyzed 318 recordings from 87 patients suffering from valvular disease and 47 healthy individuals. Each recording was 10 seconds long and included a heart sound sequence from both the left and right heart chambers. We used two features: one spectral and one temporal, to describe the sounds. We tested three machine learning approaches – k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, and support vector machines – using 10-fold cross-validation. The results showed that all three methods accurately distinguished between normal and abnormal recordings but struggled with the four specific condition classifications. This challenge was compounded by the varied degrees to which the recordings were affected by background noise and the position of the listening device, which altered the sound patterns. To address these issues, we employed two feature enhancement techniques: one that removed background noise and another that corrected the device position effects. We found that these techniques improved the classification results. Notably, one of the patient recordings with severe stenosis and regurgitation in both chambers was misclassified as healthy in the initial analysis. This result is significant because such a severe case would typically present with both stenotic and regurgitant sounds, and clinical professionals would likely consider it a borderline case requiring further diagnosis. This finding highlights the difficulty in distinguishing between stenotic and regurgitant valvular disease based solely on heart sound recordings and underscores the necessity for a comprehensive medical evaluation that includes both audio recordings and visual imaging results. Furthermore, it emphasizes the value of machine learning models in identifying unusual cases that may have been overlooked in a simplistic analysis. This study analyzed recordings from both the left and right heart chambers but found that the data from the two chambers were highly correlated and could be analyzed separately without losing much predictive information. This discovery is relevant for reducing data dimensionality in similar heart sound analysis problems. Lastly, this research used two simple machine learning features but found that more advanced spectral and temporal analysis techniques may yield even better results. This challenge can be modeled as a problem of pattern recognition in signals that have been altered by both additive and convolutional noise. This research provides an example of a solution to this problem but notes that there are many possible approaches to it. This study was conducted without the assistance of a big data platform. Our main goal is to determine whether there exists an optimal control that minimizes the supremum of $Y$ over all time periods $t$, or to establish that such a minimal control does not exist. We analyze a new, relatively small selection of 39 galaxies with measured far-infrared colors, 21-cm radiation widths, and neutral hydrogen contents, focusing on how external, intergalactic radiation influences their gas. We consider the effect of subthermal stimulation on line emission from two key atomic species, primarily filling in absorption lines, which is noticeable especially in galaxies with low hydrogen gas densities. By accounting for this line emission, our analysis indicates that external radiation may be more intense than previously estimated, primarily through the filling of the $^3P_1 \rightarrow ^3P_0$ fine-structure line at 973 GHz. This, in turn, could make it more difficult to detect certain line transitions, offering a potential utility for observing the interstellar medium. Our work also cautions against overestimating the gas temperature in some galaxies based on observations of atomic lines. This study is primarily based on data from the IRAM 30 m telescope, supported by additional information from other surveys, and our results are generally consistent with similar previous analyses of larger galaxy samples. If confirmed, external radiation's impact on line emission may be observable through interferometric observations of galaxies with sensitive line receivers. This study is a part of a broader project that has been ongoing for over a decade, focused on comprehensively understanding the interstellar medium, from the subparsec to the megaparsec length scales, primarily based on observations of the [C I], [O I], and [C II] lines. In this challenge, a series is created from a set of observations, and the objective is to decipher the original structure that generated the series. This structure is represented by a permutation, and the series is constructed using the Hamming scan, a well-established numerical method. To succeed, any proposed solution must accurately determine the original permutation that produced the observed series, using only a limited number of the available spectral coefficients. The SRCPH is examined to assess the performance of three different approaches: artificial neural networks, genetic algorithms, and classical optimization methods. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) observations will permit the detection of numerous binary black hole mergers similar to GW150914, although most are expected to have highly elliptical orbits. By directly integrating general relativistic effects into the PTA signal model, we generate numerical data that mimics inspiraling binary systems with eccentricity. Our results show that PTA signals resulting from mergers with high eccentricities can be accurately replicated through a combination of logarithmic terms, modulated oscillations, and phase corrections. By parallax effects, close binaries with moderate eccentricities will need to be searched for within wide solid angles, necessitating more computationally intensive methods for signal analysis. In contrast, wide-separated binaries with high eccentricities require less sophisticated analysis tools due to their predictable timing patterns. For these binaries, we propose a more efficient detection algorithm that significantly reduces the computational expense of signal detection while retaining high precision. The proposed method yields a precision of at least one part in ten billion for individual pulsars over a decade of observations, and can handle a vast dataset that comprises thousands of pulsars and multiple binary merger signals. The algorithm's effectiveness is validated through numerical testing. The development of this research is crucial for enhancing the capabilities of PTA searches for merging binary black holes with high-eccentricity orbits. The associated code is publicly accessible on GitHub. The optimal parameter range for the efficient algorithm is given, along with an estimate of the detectable merger rate for high-eccentricity binaries with total mass of fifty solar masses, primordial eccentricity of one part in ten thousand, and an orbital period of several years, which lies within the capabilities of current PTA observations. The algorithm's efficiency enables the detectability of these binaries through observations spanning several decades, with hundreds of millions of seconds of data available from individual pulsars like EROS B182 Clark, PSR J0347+0241, and NST, among others. The proposed method paves the way for the analysis of similar binary mergers with moderate eccentricities, with the potential to increase the predicted merger rate for PTA detectors like the Square Kilometre Array by several orders of magnitude once it becomes fully operational. The proposed algorithm's precision for one part in ten billion over several decades of observations, coupled with its reduced computational expense, allows it to efficiently detect the gravitational waves emitted by massive binary mergers with high-eccentricity orbits, with the potential to significantly increase the predicted merger rate for PTA detectors once they have greater sensitivity

This article illustrates how ASEP's velocity process on single-layer regular lattices can be realized through a simple algorithm that maintains detailed balance. To achieve this, we first review ASEP and examine the velocity process in detail. Next, we outline the algorithm and analyze it in both its basic and modified forms. These analyses enable us to derive various hydrodynamic expressions that characterize linearly stable states when initial conditions are smoothly varied. We also investigate how the algorithm's behavior changes when it is applied to a two-layer lattice. In this context, we observe the occurrence of nonlinear shocks and confirm that they align with the results obtained using other methods. Additionally, we discuss and review relevant previous work. This research was presented at the 2019 Probability and Statistics Seminar held in Paris.

Current methods write data in a linear sequence without considering a hierarchical arrangement, which can lead to prolonged rewrite times and make it difficult to update specific chunks of data. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel approach that utilizes a hierarchical structure consisting of multiple layers to store and manage data more efficiently. By allocating specific layers to different types of data, we're able to update only the desired layer without affecting the others, thus significantly reducing the amount of rewriting required. Our approach also enables the data to be written in a non-linear sequence, enabling a 10-fold decrease in rewrite time compared to the conventional method. To further enhance the data's durability, we introduce a method of transcribing repeated regions of the (6,8) dNTP sequence, which can be achieved through a 2-fold reduction in sequencing coverage and a 5-fold decrease in the number of base pairs affected by a single error. We've validated our approach with an extensive set of tests, utilizing both real and simulated data, and our findings are 10 times faster in rewriting, 5 times faster in data retrieval, and capable of updating just 1 out of 1024 chunks of data in just 3 hours. Our research paves the way for an efficient and scalable DNA storage system, which we believe is crucial for meeting the growing demands of hierarchical data and efficient update capabilities. High-dynamic-range photography is a well-established technique in the photography field, and a wide-ranging variety of apps and platforms that work on computers have been developed to capture HDR images. Nevertheless, making use of mobile devices, particularly those with limited processing power, presents certain challenges. This study aims to tackle this issue by introducing an innovative method for choosing and combining exposure settings automatically in mobile devices. A key aspect of this approach is the presence of a simple yet effective algorithm that determines optimal exposure levels, while a more complex machine learning method is utilized to establish a optimal range for merging the selected images. This research was put to the test using a smartphone and a popular outdoor scene with extensive lighting contrasts. Recently published research offers a distinct perspective on a 2004 solar event. This approach takes into account the unique way particles interact with the Earth, specifically through its magnetic field strength at different latitudes. By using this method, a re-examination of neutron and proton levels was conducted during a specific solar flare event from November 7, 2004. The analysis revealed a contrasting pattern of particle accumulation in the Earth's magnetic fields compared to historical records of the same kind of solar flares. The findings suggest that neutrons play a greater role in high-energy solar flares than previously believed, affecting cosmic particle research and potential satellite protection. The observed behavior in some rapidly spinning young stars, characterized by broad hazy patterns and temperature fluctuations across their surfaces, is found to also exhibit patterns that may indicate the presence of disk systems surrounding these stars. A detailed analysis is conducted of the rapidly spinning star EPISCOPUS, with a 0.78 day rotational period, to understand the causes behind its temperature and luminosity variations over its surface. Multiple possible explanations are considered for this phenomenon, including the presence of exoplanetary bodies, as well as alternative scenarios such as an uneven distribution of angular momentum or magnetic activity. A newly developed code is utilized to simulate the effects of heat transfer and light absorption from a surrounding disk system, revealing that multiple stars with similar characteristics, including a slowly spinning star called VV Crucis, exhibit similar temperature patterns. These findings suggest that the primary cause behind these patterns may be the absorption of light and heat by surrounding disks rather than the uneven distribution of angular momentum. This research highlights the importance of considering the presence of disk systems in young stars with rapid rotational periods and provides a potential method for detecting exoplanetary bodies even when they are too distant to be seen. This study also underpins the value of monitoring the surfaces of these stars over time, as it can reveal the complex and dynamic behavior of these systems. This work is part of a broader project focused on developing code that simulates the interactions between stars and their surrounding planets and disks, as well as the ways in which these systems change over time. This code is being made available for use by the scientific community. This research was supported by an appointment to the California Space Grant Consortium. This paper is based on a presentation delivered at the annual meeting of the American Astronomical Society held in San Diego, California, where it was awarded the prize for the best student presentation. This research was funded by a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship and a stipend from the University of California, Berkeley. This research was also supported by a grant from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to the University of California, Berkeley. This research was conducted in partnership with the research group led by Dr. John Stauffer at the California Institute of Technology. This research was conducted using data and resources provided by various astronomical observatories around the world, including the Kepler space telescope, the Spitzer space telescope, the Two-Micron All-Sky Survey, the Infrared Astronomical Satellite, and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. This research has been accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series.

We propose a novel approach, called MECCO-Net, which utilizes the meta neural process framework to generate counterfeits and train a neural network to recognize them. This approach can be applied to both emerging counterfeit and normal news articles. In order to enhance the quality of generated counterfeits and guide the neural network to focus on relevant features, we introduced a counterfit similarity metric and a neural network decoder. Additionally, we incorporated a decoder that enables the network to generate text based on the encoded information. Our results show that MECCO-Net surpasses existing baselines for both text-based and multimodal counterfeit news detection methods. This approach was tested using a new dataset called MultiNews-Counterfeit, which comprises both normal and intentionally created false reports from various sources, along with corresponding image and text features. We establish a recursive formula for calculating the entries in a specific table related to Thom spaces in stable homotopy theory. This formula connects each entry to a sum of previous entries, reminiscent of combinatorial principles such as Fibonacci numbers or partition-generated recursions. By identifying the underlying recursion as (n+1)th-partition-related, we link it to a fundamental characteristic of the J sequence, which arises from the join operation in combinatorial mathematics. This connection wasn't anticipated and yields a new, distinctive formula for the (n+1)th-partition number. This result expands upon a earlier, more specific finding for odd partitions. As a result, it unifies and generalizes several known numerical expressions, including those derived from a specific principle of inclusion-exclusion used in homotopy theory. This research was initially presented at the 2018 International Conference on Mathematics and Statistics. The (n+1)th-partition number can be expressed as $\frac{1}{n+1} \binom{2n+2}{n+1}$, which may be further simplified to $\frac{n+1}{n+2} \binom{2n+2}{n+2}$. This last expression arises from expanding the binomial $(1-x)^{n+2}$ raised to the power $n$. This relation to the binomial also allows for the efficient computation of these numbers using established algorithms. This finding expands upon a previous result for the odd partition number, providing a parameterized approach that enables the derivation of not only even partitions, but also odd, total, and Laguerre partitions, among others. A significant issue with traditional medical imaging is the presence of lesions that can distort and make it difficult to analyze, especially in tasks like reconstructing detailed brain images. To tackle this challenge, a new framework for generating detailed cerebral lesions is proposed, drawing inspiration from the Adversarial Autoencoder architecture. This proposed method consists of multiple VAE components working together, each responsible for creating less intricate lesions through a progressive construction process. To evaluate this proposed framework, a comprehensive set of experiments was conducted for both cerebral lesion generation and brain reconstruction, pitting it against existing state-of-the-art approaches. The results show that the proposed method excels in generating detailed lesions and, as a side benefit, also yields high-quality reconstructed brain images. Code for this work is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr96/Progressive-VAE.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation systems to their fullest potential. However, efficiently developing correct and verified programs using GP 2 can be challenging due to the complexity of its syntax and extensive need for rewrite rules in program analysis and verification tasks. We introduced a type of partial rewrite rule in GP 2 to enhance program analysis and verification capabilities while simplifying the syntax. To further simplify the syntax, we introduced type of embedded rules in GP 2. Now, we have refined these embedded rules to permit a more flexible and expressive syntax, allowing the inclusion of attribute types in production rules. This extension enables us to develop efficient and correct program analysis and verification tools using verified program transformations and validation functions. To illustrate the benefits of GP 2, we present a case study involving a compiler for a simple functional programming language, demonstrating the capabilities of the Enhanced GP 2 specification language. To achieve this, we generated a sequential executor from the specifications, and through performance analysis, discovered optimization opportunities to enhance the compiler's efficiency. We also discuss the implications of our experience for the design of GP 2. To facilitate further investigation, we made the GP 2 compiler and tools, as well as the case study, publicly available. To build upon our work, we propose several directions for future research in GP 2. To conclude, we review the key features of GP 2 and the results obtained from our case study, encompassing the generated code and performance improvement suggestions. To summarize, we believe that the Enhanced GP 2 language provides a superior foundation for developing efficient and correct program analysis and verification tools, offering a verifiable and correct implementation of program transformations and validation functions with attributes, and proven program correctness through type and value-based validation functions. A type of attribute extraction model is discussed that leverages descriptive language to convey attributes such as emotions, sentiments, and personalities. These models aim to identify pre-defined attributes from input descriptions. We propose a structured approach that consists of multiple attribute-specific encoders working in tandem. Each encoder is trained to compare a set of descriptive samples that exhibit a particular attribute. These encoders are further integrated using attribute-specific weights. We also explore the use of a weighted sum to integrate the encoders. Experimental results show that our structured approach yields superior performance over flat designs, where encoders operate independently. We further examine the effect of weighted integration and find it is essential for optimal results. Code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Unified-Attribute-Structure. We also present a detailed analysis of a failed experiment where we attempted to employ a latent space instead of weighted integration. This failed approach is notable because it is a common strategy in clustering and dimensionality reduction. We conclude by discussing potential areas for improvement and providing an example of how the model can be used for intuitive sentiment analysis visualizations. A related issue is also explored where we discuss the challenge of determining attribute weights. This challenge is a broader problem that can be addressed through the use of task-specific sets of descriptive samples. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach through additional experiments. This structure and set-based learning strategy can be applied to a broader category of problems known as few-shot attribute extraction. These problems involve training models on minimal data that includes a range of attributes. We propose a simple yet effective protocol for training and evaluating these models called the Set-Based Attribute Extraction Protocol. This protocol consists of multiple rounds of random sampling from pre-defined sets of descriptive samples. We provide the code for this protocol at https://github.com/ghrua/Unified-Attribute-Structure. We also explore the relationship between attribute extraction and few-shot classification. This relationship can be leveraged by using the descriptive samples as the first set in classification tasks. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach through additional experiments. This current work builds upon the earlier work by exploring a structured design and presenting a type of problem known as few-shot attribute extraction. A finite simple graph is considered to have a twisted wreath structure if it contains three distinct subgroups of 3 vertices each, where each subgroup is fully connected within itself but not connected to the other two subgroups, and these subgroups are pairwise isosceles. Our research reveals the existence of an infinite number of star non-equivalent local twisted wreath structures that can be realized in a graph's neighborhood stability under the star quotient transformation. In fact, we demonstrate that there is an infinite set of graphs that resist 3-star closure but can form a 3-twisted wreath structure when a specific number of 3-stars is added. This achievement becomes apparent once we establish certain criteria for determining the stability of a graph that features a 3-twisted wreath structure. This achievement provides a distinct contrast to the notion that only finite star non-equivalent local structures exist. This work was originally presented at the 12th Greek Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Intelligent Systems, held in 2021. A more expansive version of this work can be found in reference [1]. A related open problem is also discussed in this paper. Working with categorical data for modeling and regression tasks can be made more efficient by representing them as binary one-hot encodings. However, as the number of categories increases, using this expansion becomes impractical due to the extensive memory it requires and the computational speed it compromises. A common strategy for managing this challenge involves using the Group Lasso, also known as sparse group selection, to eliminate the irrelevant categories. Yet, this approach has a significant limitation in its own right by requiring all categories within a particular feature to be either included or excluded en masse. This restriction can be circumvented when using the Group Lasso by employing a more sophisticated algorithm known as the Group Lasso with Overlap, which permits a more flexible and nuanced selection of features by allowing a subset of the categories within a feature to be retained while others are dropped. Yet, this more advanced algorithm has a major drawback for large datasets; it no longer guarantees the same level of computational efficiency as the standard Group Lasso. A new and alternative algorithm, the Iterative Shrinkage and Selection Optimisation, is proposed as a more desirable solution for dealing with categorical data. This novel algorithm not only offers a level of flexibility that surpasses the Group Lasso but also does so while maintaining the same high degree of computational efficiency. In evaluating this new algorithm, we adopted Group Lasso with Overlap as a point of comparison and conducted a range of trials with both real and generated data to assess its performance and functionality. In every case, this new algorithm demonstrated not only the capacity for feature selection but also a level of efficiency that was comparable, if not significantly better, than that achieved with the Group Lasso with Overlap. In addition to this, we applied this new algorithm to a real-world regression task that involved categorical information at a dataset of a million rows and showed that it was capable of handling large-scale datasets of this type with a high degree of success. This novel algorithm presents a valuable tool for any data analyst or scientist working with categorical data for regression tasks, be they machine learning based or Bayesian in nature. This new algorithm is particularly valuable for modelling electric appliance load data which often consists of a wide range of categorical information. This new algorithm is capable of selecting and modelling only the truly relevant information from such large datasets, thus enhancing the quality of the resulting model. This new algorithm is also capable of handling positively correlated features which adds to its utility and value. This new algorithm presents a valuable solution to the common challenge of data analyst's struggling to decide between the use of one-hot encodings

Recent large language models have demonstrated significant advancements in various tasks, surpassing the performance of specially designed models in several instances. This research seeks to explore the potential of integrated knowledge structures within neural language models by designing a new approach, dubbed Structured Insight Infusion for LLMs, which deliberately crafts a model that can effectively make use of pre-existing knowledge bases without being tied to a particular dataset. By leveraging a novel attention mechanism and a rich knowledge representation, our approach enables the model to effectively tap into its integrated knowledge structures. We have tested this approach using both YAGO2 and Freebase knowledge bases and consistently obtained superior results compared to a base transformer model, as well as other comparison models, including those that utilize external memory. Furthermore, our approach has shown an interesting ability to extract relevant knowledge when compared to these models. This research is accompanied by a publicly available code and guidelines for utilizing YAGO2. With over 99% of the entity mentions accurately identified, our approach has the potential to facilitate a wide range of tasks that involve the incorporation of extensive knowledge bases. High-resolution vector maps are gaining popularity in various applications such as driving and flight navigation, gaming, and graphic design. However, when these maps are displayed on devices with limited graphics processing power, they often suffer from poor anti-aliasing, particularly along lines and their connections, which significantly detract from the overall visual experience. To address this issue, a novel anti-aliasing technique is presented that efficiently handles line connections and joining lines, rivers, and borders on vector maps. This technique leverages a simplified screen-space algorithm that produces high-quality, physically representative lines with rounded joints, capable of withstanding rotations and scaling. In contrast to commonly used anti-aliasing techniques, this method bypasses costly vector operations by directly manipulating pixels on the screen, thereby Considerable performance gains and enhanced visual fidelity. This technique has been successfully implemented and its benefits in improving performance and visual quality are demonstrated through a range of maps and graphics, including real-world navigation maps. This anti-aliasing technique is particularly well-suited for a range of graphics-related applications including game development using Unity. In multi-channel speech processing, extracting clean speech from mixed recordings is a challenging task, especially in low SNR environments. This problem is especially critical in situations where only access to a single far-field microphone is available, yet there are often unused audio data from other microphones that could be utilized. This research presents the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN), an innovative model designed to process each audio channel independently while sharing a final output layer. This dual-path architecture is characterized by two separate sub-systems that are each optimized for their respective audio channels, allowing the model to adapt to different frequency patterns present in each channel. This adaptation enables the DPCRN to prioritize clean speech frequencies more effectively. Experiments conducted on the DNS challenge dataset showed the DPCRN to perform significantly better than several leading baselines, with a 3.85 dB improvement in SI-DRR over the best existing method. Code for the DPCRN is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. In practice, the DPCRN can be trained to utilize two far-field microphones with the model then being able to effectively utilize a third, previously unused microphone with only a single far-field recording. This makes the DPCRN a highly versatile model with numerous real-world applications. In addition, the DPCRN can be trained to utilize a combination of far-field and near-field microphones, further expanding its uses. In these scenarios, the DPCRN is able to effectively make use of additional available recording data, enabling it to better capture local noise patterns and thus produce a cleaner speech signal with a 4.07 dB improvement in SI-DRR. In both cases, the DPCRN outperforms the current state-of-the-art challenge winner. In order to demonstrate the versatility of the DPCRN, experiments were conducted on it using a combination of both DNS and 6EC challenge datasets, with the model showing a 3.85 dB and 3.19 dB improvement in SI-DRR over the best existing method on the DNS and 6EC datasets respectively. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in efficiently and accurately capturing the complexities of atmospheric circulation through the incorporation of buoyancy forces within simplified numerical schemes. A step in the development of these models involves accurately capturing the behavior of buoyancy-driven convection in two-fluid simulations that separate air from water vapor. This research seeks to explore this concept by developing a two-fluid single-column model of Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection and evaluating its capabilities through simulations of convection both with and without water vapor. Encouraging results show that the model successfully reproduces the characteristics of dry convection and, when including water vapor, accurately captures the effects of latent heat and humidity on convection. The introduction of a new third-state of water, distinct from liquid and vapor, is also explored as an alternative to the two-fluid model, demonstrating that it yields comparable but distinct results in these simulations. The development of the model and the underlying numerical methods are detailed in the supplementary materials. The code used for these simulations is an open-source contribution available under the MIT license. The development of multi-fluid circulation models through the study of atmospheric circulation as convection-driven buoyancy forces holds significant potential and offers a feasible pathway for their development. The code and model developed here provide a foundation for further advancement in this area. The research was conducted as part of the atmospheric sciences program at Stanford University with the supervision of Dr. Andrew A. Turner. The model and code were tested against the results of previous dry and moist Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection simulations presented by Stevens et al. The simulations showed that the model accurately captures the characteristics of both dry and moist convection when water vapor is included and the effects of water vapor on convection when the superheated water state is introduced. The model also exhibits sensitivity to the critical mass fraction required for the phase transition between water vapor and the newly introduced water state. The research addresses an open question from the results of Stevens et al. The code and model are available at https://github.com/abrahamgutierrez/CFD-MF-RB. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and processed a specific set of Twitter data related to
IPL cricket matches. A long short-term memory (LSTM) based model was developed to
determine the public's emotional response to these events. LSTMs are type of recurrent
neural networks that excel at capturing temporal data patterns. To build and evaluate our
model, we used a supervised approach with a binary classification output. It achieved an
accuracy of 87.5% which could be further improved with more sophisticated techniques. 
However, this simple model demonstrates potential utility for similar time-series
sentiment analysis tasks. Additionally, it has been trained using a public dataset found
on GitHub, which can be utilized by the community for future developments. 
Finally, allusions to model enhancements and possible applications in the sports
industry are discussed. 
In this report, we outline the basic LSTM model used, along with the training protocol
employed. It includes the hyperparameter settings, evaluation metrics used, and the
results obtained. Moreover, possible model improvements and the potential for using
this model in the sports industry, particularly in the cricket domain, are explored. 
A pre-trained LSTM model and the training data used are available online at 
https://github.com/shivanshubhandari/LSTM_Twitter_Sentiment. 
This framework can be modified to analyze public emotions during other events, such as
sports tournaments, concerts, and even political events. 
This model provides a starting point for anyone interested in conducting similar
time-series sentiment analysis. 
It is essential to note that the current model is not an optimally performing one. 
However, it does demonstrate potential utility for similar time-series sentiment analysis 
tasks. 
A more advanced model with multiple LSTM layers has the potential to significantly 
improve the accuracy obtained. 
Another possible enhancement could be using a different optimizer. 
It is also possible to train the model on a larger dataset, which could be a combination 
of the existing dataset and a new set of IPL cricket match-related tweets. 
It may be beneficial to use a different classification technique, such as the random forest 
algorithm discussed in section 3. 
Another possible application of this model in the sports industry is analyzing the 
emotional response of fans

Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as entanglement and the onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in the tomograms' shape and can be extracted without the need for full state reconstruction. We achieve this by creating a set of analytical indicators that directly monitor these phenomena. These indicators serve as the basis for valid statements about the system's quantum properties, offering a more accessible and less demanding alternative to full-state reconstruction protocols. Our findings are applicable to any analytical tomogram and can serve as the starting point for more advanced analysis through conventional or machine learning-based protocols. We also apply and experimentally validate our approach with two distinct scenarios, involving the analysis of (1) entanglement in an optical parametric amplifier, and (2) the onset of synchronization in a Jaynes-Cummings system. Our results have implications for various quantum applications and can aid in the efficient analysis of continuous-variable systems in ongoing and future quantum experiments. This paper introduces a novel approach to predicting a 360-degree virtual camera path, which is influenced by spoken dialogue in videos. A perfect 360-degree scene offers numerous possible viewing angles, removing the need for traditional path forecasting's front-facing perspective. To tackle this task, we created two predictors: one focuses on forecasting the camera's horizontal angle, while the other targets the vertical angle. Both are trained using a convolutional neural network that takes both audio and video data as input. As spoken content often overlaps with visual elements in 360-degree videos, our strategy accounts for potentially incorrect or missing subtitle information. Our solution evaluates and validates two separate models, as well as a combined horizontal-and-vertical angle predictor. Our experiments showed a high correlation between predicted and actual angles, with an average horizontal angle error of 13.82 degrees and an average vertical angle error of 18.64 degrees. This research was presented at the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing in 2023. A 360-degree video viewport forecasting demo is available online. With further development, this technology could enhance various virtual travel video applications.

This state-filled network differs from conventional versions, as the physical indices within each individual tensor are not balanced equally, with some having a longer span than others, representing either temperature or a time discrepancy. By implementing a new branching method during the contraction process, we're able to accommodate these uneven indices, enabling the use of a variety of approximating methods, such as multicontraction trees, to accurately simulate small systems while accurately describing thermal or dynamic conditions. Furthermore, this novel approach offers a tangible way to visualize the effects of temperature or time on a system through graphical index distribution, offering valuable physical insights in addition to numerical predictions. We also outline a strategy for translating any existing tensor networks representing finite systems into the new format, effectively converting any represented physical condition (e.g. temperature, time, boundary conditions) that contributed to the original system's definition. We accomplish this by reintroducing virtual indices that were previously neglected when developing the tensor networks and provide a concrete example of this method's applicability. This novel approach and its underlying mathematics are applicable to a broad range of discrete systems, not limited to one-dimensional time-evolving systems. We also outline our statistical implementation and the underlying mathematics behind it, along with numerical results obtained using this method. This approach offers a viable alternative to established tensor network algorithms, especially for systems where the temperature or time effects can be identified as contributing to the index distribution. By reframing boolean constraints as equality constraints and employing scale-oriented approximation methods, our approach aims to increase their solvers' versatility. However, this strategy may lead to a rise in computational overhead. To mitigate this issue, we advocate for selective use of decoupling for particular variables that hold restricted effectiveness. Our results showcase the potential benefits and limitations of this approach, highlighting the impact of various factors on its efficacy. We achieve better results when using the MIOSTABU Decoupler with COCONUT SAT and C2D, particularly on instances where the solvers struggle due to being overly rigid. Nevertheless, we also identify instances where the decoupling technique currently falls short and suggests potential paths for improvement, such as adapting scale-oriented approximation methods and exploring ways to further limit the decoupling variable's effectiveness. Our decoupling research is made available under the Apache License 2.0 and open-source guidelines, along with guidance for building the code and conducting similar experiments. We highlight future research directions and offer a SAT solver benchmark called Decoupling Challenge. Our findings and tools contribute to the broader category of constraint solvers and decoupling techniques. We also explore how scale-oriented approximation methods influence the solvers' performance and validate our results using two independent analysis methods. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution, which becomes significant at tiny values of $x$, is the subject of this investigation. To better understand non-linear phenomena in high-energy processes, especially those involving forward hadron production at particle colliders, it's crucial to study the intricacies of the tiny-$x$ domain. Here, we analyze the contribution of long-baseline renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution, utilizing an ab initio approach that integrates multiple DIS processes. Our findings are demonstrated through numerical examples, revealing the complex interplay between the impact of long-baseline renormalons, the extent of non-linear effects, and the magnitude of the tiny-$x$ cutoff in integrated measurements. As a consequence, we find that the contributions from both the Borel and integration variables' renormalons can be substantial, with contributions from the Borel variable resembling those found in previous studies but with distinct differences in their characteristics, and the impact of the integration variable renormalons being significantly more considerable than their Borel counterparts. This research highlights the intricate nature of the tiny-$x$ domain and the essential role that understanding infrared renormalons plays in accurately interpreting data from forward particle production at colliders. It also paves the way for developing analytical approximations that account for the contributions of these renormalons, with the ultimate goal of extracting reliable estimates of the color dipole gluon distribution function from measurable quantities. This will be crucial for further analyzing forward production processes at the future Electron-Ion Collider. The proposed analytical approach involves a combination of the analytic continuation of the principal value, the application of the "average impact" approximation, and the use of modified Borel transform methods, all of which are demonstrated through numerical examples. This study provides the theoretical framework for a comprehensive understanding and interpretation of the tiny-$x$ domain, with the potential to contribute to a broader range of high-energy processes that involve the tiny-$x$ domain, not just those involving forward hadron production at particle colliders. This research offers a valuable lesson for any investigation that deals with integrated quantities over a range of scales, particularly those at the particle level, and involves the tiny-$x$ domain, where the contributions of long-baseline renormalons can influence the interpretation of data and the extraction of physical information. This is especially relevant for investigations that aim to obtain a first-principles understanding and accurate interpretations of data from forward production processes at the future Electron-Ion Collider. To effectively collaborate, agents with varying domains of expertise typically require a comprehensive understanding of each other's environments and tasks. In the context of co-learning through observation, this typically involves both seeing how another agent acts in their own environment based on another's instructions, known as co-observation learning without transfer, where one agent acquires knowledge from another's observed interactions in a different environment. This research explores a more challenging scenario called co-observation learning without specialists, where one agent, seeking to improve, observes another agent that is simply attempting to navigate its own unknown environment. In this case, we assume that the observed agent is using a random exploration strategy. Our proposed approach, CoLearnWithoutTransfer, leverages the observed interactions between the two agents and employs both policy-based and value-based methods to enhance the observing agent's own-policy. Our experiments, conducted in a range of diverse, disparate environments, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and showcase the benefits of our method when comparing it to alternative, baseline approaches. Our research also explores the practical implications of our method for selecting an appropriate exploration-exploitation strategy and reveals that our approach successfully adapts to various complex, dynamic scenarios even when compared to intelligent, controlled demonstrations of the target environment. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/Co-Observation-Learning.

This paper introduces two categories of error-correcting codes - PAC codes and their enhanced version, super-PAC codes - whose basic characteristic is the calculated average error rate below a specific threshold, which is known as the performance barrier. To break through this barrier, it's necessary to have a vast amount of encoded data. In contrast to conventional error-correcting codes that aim to maintain data integrity, codes with this property prioritize encoded data quantity over data integrity for a specified duration. We discuss methods to calculate and measure the performance barrier in the context of a specific error model and provide numerical data on its value. Furthermore, we discuss the implications and potential uses of these codes, such as extending talk shows that incorporate audience participation, remote educational programs, and space missions where encoded data can be stored in living organisms. These codes have the unique property that, once created, their calculated average behavior cannot be altered, giving them an inherent stability that makes them unique among error-correcting codes. We propose calling these codes "archetypal codes" with a suffix indicating their specific feature, and suggest a convention for their notation. Finally, we outline some open problems and potential research directions related to these codes. We have made the code generation and calculation tool available online. In the appendix, we provide a heuristic explanation for the performance barrier based on a code's calculated average behavior. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that has gained considerable popularity in recent years. As a result of its rising usage, ensuring the consistency of MongoDB data has become increasingly vital. This paper focuses on the specification of transactional integrity, specifically the TPC-C benchmark, and evaluates the consistency guarantees of MongoDB. In order to conduct this evaluation, we developed a comprehensive model of MongoDB's consistency features and its impact on the TPC-C benchmark. This model enabled us to simulate and validate the integrity of MongoDB transactions. Our results confirmed that MongoDB's current implementation can successfully execute multiple TPC-C transactions concurrently without issue, but also identified areas where its consistency may be compromised. Our proposed model can be utilized to validate the integrity of MongoDB's future updates and similar NoSQL databases used in transactional workloads. Notably, our analysis revealed that MongoDB's current behavior differs significantly from traditional relational databases, with implications for the development of test suites and input validation tools. Our research on MongoDB's consistency also explored alternative serialization algorithms and confirmed that its current behavior is equivalent to using the happen-thensee (HTS) visibility rule, which provides a performance-oriented consistency guarantee. This guarantee enables the database to exhibit high performance, as demonstrated by the resulting throughput measurements. In addition to validating MongoDB's consistency, we developed a novel metric called the Consistency Confidence Level (CCL), which enables the evaluation of a database's consistency on a per-transaction basis. This CCL value can be used to set actionable performance boundaries for developers, as well as to compare the consistency of different databases in various scenarios. Our research on MongoDB's visibility rule and the CCL metric also explored their applicability to other NoSQL databases used in transactional workloads. In conclusion, our research on MongoDB's consistency guarantees involved the development of a comprehensive model that simulated the database's behavior, identified areas for improvement, and explored performance and consistency validation using the CCL metric. This work has been applied to future updates of MongoDB and can be readily generalized to other NoSQL databases used in transactional workloads. Our approach to validating MongoDB's consistency has been made available as an open-source tool called TMonitor, which can be used to monitor and validate the consistency of MongoDB and similar databases used in transactional workloads. We analyzed observations from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on the Parker Solar Probe and found that the solar wind energy flux exhibits a specific pattern as it moves closer to the sun. Counter to expectations, the energy flux of the solar wind appears to increase rather than decrease as it approaches the sun's outer edge, a phenomenon observed in the inner 36 percent of the heliosphere. This phenomenon holds true for both the overall energy flux and its magnetic component, and remains stable over time despite any variations in the solar wind speed. A hypothetical model suggesting that the energy flux might become independent of distance from the sun's surface through a combination of solar wind acceleration and pressure gradient forces also needs further investigation. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the solar breeze energy flow and its effects on the sun's atmosphere, and highlight the need for further analysis and modeling to fully explain these phenomena. These results originated from data collected during the initial 200-day period of the Parker Solar Probe mission.

The development of singularities or shock waves in a perfectly elastic ball expanding in a vacuum has been theoretically proven, counter to the long-held belief that it forms a stable shell. This notion originated from an earlier computational model that contained an air pocket, not a vacuum. Our current research shows that such a model with a spherical void does, in fact, exhibit a robust and expanding shock front. This occurs because the expanding shell and the shock wave generate convection currents that drive the formation of oscillating circulation patterns. These patterns become more complex over time, ultimately leading to the formation of a singularities or shock waves that the ball cannot contain. This issue with containment holds true even after the initial explosion, as the shell and the vacuum pocket continue their natural expansion. This expansion results in an ever-widening and increasingly powerful shock front that can affect the surrounding space arbitrarily freely. This phenomenon can occur on a small or a vast cosmic scale. This finding also shares some interesting similarities with the famous "grandpa model" that described the expanding shell of a supernova remnant surrounding two stars that had formed from the same molecular cloud. This research develops a 3-generation economic model to examine the distribution of prospects among different social groups and provides a theoretical basis for the existence of an inheritance effect on economic opportunities. Through this model, we are able to create a conceptual framework for "prospect theory", which includes theories on risk-preference, asset accumulation, and social mobility. A key aspect of this model is that it considers how the distribution of prospects affects people's risk-taking behavior, asset accumulation, and intergenerational mobility. Notably, our findings suggest that an unequal distribution of prospects can limit risk-taking behavior, result in inadequate asset accumulation, and exacerbate social inequality over time. This leads to an important policy implication: addressing unequal prospects can help mitigate these social and economic issues. To further illustrate this, we introduce an education system into our model and explore its effects on prospect distribution, risk-taking behavior, asset accumulation, and intergenerational mobility. This model shows that an unequal distribution of prospects can manifest as unequal education levels among different social groups, which in turn contributes to an even more significant gap in economic opportunities and social mobility. This research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the complex relationship between prospect distribution, risk-taking behavior, asset accumulation, and social mobility, and it offers a dynamic model that can be used to study the distribution of prospects and its implications for economic development over multiple generations. This model also offers testable hypotheses regarding the inheritance effect on economic opportunities, risk-taking behavior, asset accumulation, and social mobility, among other social and economic phenomena. This research can also be viewed as an advancement of the model developed by Aghion, Blandin, and Faye (2019) known as the "dynastic" model, which focused on examining how unequal access to education affects social mobility over time. This research offers a new perspective on the "dynastic" model and provides additional policy implications for addressing the issue of unequal education levels among different social groups. This research can be used to study a wide range of social and economic issues that result from an unequal distribution of prospects, including but not limited to, inequality, poverty, asset accumulation, risk-taking behavior, and social mobility, among others. This paper outlines a method previously employed by the ATLAS collaboration to precisely determine the position and orientation of the beam at the CERN Proton Synchrotron, a requirement critical for ensuring that the particle beam hits the exact center of the experiment. By directing a small group of protons at the experiment at a glancing angle, a distinctive pattern of localized high-energy deposits on the detector is created. As the proton beam is circular and is directed at the experiment thousands of times in a matter of seconds, the resulting pattern on the detector takes the form of a series of concentric rings that gradually fade with increasing distance from the detector's center. By analyzing these rings, researchers can determine the position and orientation of the beam with great accuracy. A key advantage of this approach is that it can be used at any point in time during collisions, even in real-time, making it particularly useful for large experiments like the ATLAS collaboration. A numerical example based on actual ATLAS data demonstrates the practical application of this method, showing that it can achieve results with a precision of around 50 microns in a single scan, and over time, with sufficient statistical analysis, a precision of around 25 microns can be achieved. Both of these precision levels are well within the requirements needed to guarantee that the beam hits the exact center of the experiment. A beam analysis scan can be implemented on any particle detector that can record energy deposits over a range of angles, making it a versatile and accessible tool for a wide range of scientific applications. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve smooth, differentiable, and convex functions with constraints, in a environment where some agents can maliciously assault the network. We propose the Quantized and Distributed Subgradient Improvement (QDSI) technique, an iterative algorithm where agents update their variables based on the mean of received quantities, which can be quantized local gradients. We prove that under certain conditions, QDSI converges at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the number of iterations. We also compare QDSI with existing algorithms through numerical experiments in large-scale optimization problems. We apply the QDSI technique to solve optimization problems in scenarios where agents share bandwidth in a time division multiple access (TDMA) protocol, and provide simulations of these scenarios. We then generalize the QDSI technique to create an algorithm, Randomized Coordinate Descent via Distributed Quantized Subgradients (DCD2), which targets non-differentiable convex functions with constraints. We prove that under certain conditions, DCD2 converges at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the number of iterations. We also provide numerical experiments to compare DCD2 with existing algorithms in various optimization problems. We open-source the QDSI and DCD2 algorithms on GitHub. We previously proved that the Quantized Subgradient Improvement (QSI) algorithm converges at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the number of iterations, assuming that the function is strongly convex and smooth, by using the concentration inequality to analyze the variance of the received quantities. We expand on QSI to create the Quantized Subgradient Improvement Technique (QSI-T) framework, which includes various algorithms that converge at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the number of iterations. In our analysis, we delve into the capabilities of pre-trained language models, using BART as a representative example in the task of rearranging words to form appropriate sentences. A critical examination of successful arrangements reveals that many leverage structural knowledge gained through massive text corpora, specifically understanding sequence patterns, syntactic organization, and the role of introductory phrases. In contrast to generative models that prioritize semantic coherence, BART's strength lies in capturing syntactic and structural elements, as demonstrated by the poor performance of both full BART and its generator, particularly in arrangements that rely on embedded relationships and initial phrases. To illustrate this, we outline six distinct functions that BART serves in word arrangement: filling in missing prepositions, determining initial phrases, identifying word order, extracting semantic roles, validating word combinations, and generating introductory elements. These roles are not limited to BART but are a feature of pre-trained models in general, offering a comprehensive understanding of the capabilities and potential applications of massive pre-trained models in tasks that require both semantic and structural analysis. By breaking down BART's capacity to arrange words, we also uncover a range of related tasks that these models can perform with ease, taking them far beyond the simple combination of pre-trained word levels. With over 300 successful arrangements demonstrated, our analysis provides a comprehensive foundation for exploring the vast potential of massive pre-trained models in various tasks that demand both the semantic and structural analysis of language. With its focus on the syntactic and sequential aspects of language, BART's capabilities are not unique to itself but are a feature of all pre-trained models, offering a versatile set of functions that include filling in missing phrases, validating word combinations, determining initial phrases, identifying word order, and generating introductory elements, among others, all at a level of complexity that is both simple and elegant. In a related work, we examine the potential of these models to extract a range of semantic relations, including those described in the TACKBUILD dataset, by adapting the arrangements to match the dataset's format.
