Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks that require natural language understanding and generating human-like text. Despite the challenges they pose, many researchers have chosen to tackle them. A significant obstacle in using text-based games lies in their slow speed, far removed from the pace of contemporary interactive applications. Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a cutting-edge emulator designed to accelerate text-based games by an incredible 100 times their native speed. This emulator achieves this remarkable feat while preserving the intricate details of the games, including their response time, physics, and complex logic. To demonstrate the efficacy of our emulator, we conducted a series of trials on five diverse text-based games, resulting in a 50 to 500 times improvement in their native speed. This accelerated emulator offers numerous possibilities, including a platform for highly engaging and realistic interactive chatbots, a more energy-efficient way to train and evaluate text-based games, and a tool for creating more sophisticated testing software. It can also be utilized to generate highly detailed and realistic virtual environments for training and assessing self-driving vehicles. This work is an extension to our earlier research on TextWorldExpress, an emulator designed to accelerate text-based games, where we explored and evaluated five diverse games with an aim to create a benchmark for this technology. This extended version of our research introduces three additional games to this benchmark, expanding the range of text-based games that can be accelerated with this emulator to over a hundred already known games, and providing a framework that can be used to easily integrate new games with similar characteristics. This allows anyone with the necessary programming skills to create a version of TextWorldExpress that can accelerate their own favorite text-based game to incredible speeds. This research was conducted as part of the annual TextWorld Challenge, a competition that brings together game developers and researchers who create and solve complex interactive text-based games. This extended version of our research also introduces a new category of games called multi-player text-based games, and presents a way to convert these games into a format that can be used with the TextWorldExpress emulator, providing the possibility of creating a league of automated players that can compete with each other in these games. This allows anyone with the necessary programming skills to create a version of TextWorldExpress that can handle these games and use them as a platform for highly engaging and realistic interactive chatbots, and provide a tool for creating more sophisticated testing software that can be used to evaluate these games, and to train and assess self-driving vehicles in complex scenarios. This research is an open source project that can be used by anyone

Deep learning networks such as LSTM have been highly effective in various pattern recognition tasks but are often hampered by limited deployability due to their size. This inhibits their potential for real-world applications on edge devices with constrained memory. To overcome this, we developed an energy-efficient LSTM algorithm and a corresponding hardware accelerator that leverages hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition in its design. By co-developing the algorithm and hardware, we were able to create a compact LSTM structure that utilizes a hierarchical Tucker decomposition effectively. This resulted in an LSTM network approximately 13 times smaller than the traditional LSTM. We also designed a customized hardware accelerator that can execute Hierarchical Tucker-based LSTM tasks efficiently. Our experimental findings showed that the Hierarchical Tucker-based LSTM network leaped over the traditional TDM-based network in terms of memory usage, achieving a compressed memory capacity of 1.75 megabytes. Moreover, with a speed of up to 125 megabytes per second, it outperformed the TDM-based network in computation speed. Our research discovered that the Hierarchical Tucker-based LSTM network excelled in memory efficiency and could handle larger-scale models, whereas the TDM-based network performed better in terms of computation complexity. Notably, it delivered an approximately 3.8 times boost in computation speed when identifying 50 classes. Our Hierarchical Tucker-based LSTM network yielded impressive energy efficiency, enabling reliable deployment on edge devices with limited memory capacity. Within the context of four-dimensional conformal field theories in Einstein gravity, a key proposal known as the Feeble Gravity Conjecture suggests that the spectrum of a conformal field theory can be mapped from the representation of the $so(4)$ algebra to the $su(2,2)|H$ algebra, resulting in a non-negative charge operator that represents the sum of charges for each element of the algebra. A crucial aspect of the Feeble Gravity Conjecture is the presence of convexity for the set of charges, which holds true for a vast array of free conformal field theories but requires verification for non-free theories through direct computation of their charge operators. In our work, we derive the charge operator for a specific non-free theory known as the "double-trace deformations of $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM", and in doing so, find that it does not adhere to the standard definition of convexity. Instead, we introduce a modified criterion that the set of charges must satisfy, which we dub "convexity of the second kind". This conviction of ours is supported by numerical data obtained via the Complex Generalized Flow Method. Ultimately, our goal is to investigate the implications of this finding on the Feeble Gravity Conjecture and the AdS/CFT correspondence, and to explore potential connections with related theories such as "non-convex QCD". All in all, our analysis highlights the value of the double-trace deformations as a model system for the study of hadron physics within the AdS/CFT correspondence, and we anticipate that further investigation of these dynamics through the Complex Generalized Flow Method will yield valuable insights into the charge operator and the structure of the conformal field theory, and potentially even reveal the presence of bound states that could be identified as baryons. This work is a follow-up to our prior research on the charge operator of the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory and the $\mathcal{N}=1$ $SU$($N$) SQCD, and can be found in the associated arXiv papers. All in all, our aim is to contribute to the development of the Feeble Gravity Conjecture and the AdS/QCD correspondence, and to provide a potential framework for hadron physics within the AdS/CFT correspondence. This research paper builds upon a previous result by Bshewa and Mekenkamp which stated that composing the polynomial $f(z) = z^3 - 3z^2 +3z -1$ with other polynomials ultimately leads to the fixed point $1$. A notable observation is that both $f$ and $g$ can be seen as branches of the rational function $\frac{z(z-1)}{z-2}$, indicating they share some inherent properties. Here we derive some key features of this function, including its iterates, which consistently converge to $1$ regardless of initial value. A notable connection is discovered between $f$, $g$, and the well-known Gauss map, enabling us to reinterpret some of its properties. A key observation about $f$ and $g$ is that they map the unit circle to itself, suggesting they are related to the Gauss map when it is transformed using a specific conformal metric. A related question remains unanswered, concerning another branch of $\frac{z(z-1)}{z-2}$ and its own iterates. A potential approach to addressing this issue is proposed. A related result about the polynomial $h(z) = z^3 - 3z^2 -3z +1$ is also established, which shares some similarities with $f$ and $g$. A notable observation about the real line is that all three functions $f$, $g$, and $h$ map it to itself. A notable connection between $f$, $g$, and $h$ and the straight line is discovered, along with a related result about the function $h$. A proposed solution for the original problem of Bshewa and Mekenkamp is also presented. A research direction is proposed, as well as some open questions. A proposed direction for further research is discussed, as well as some open problems from it.

For a graded collection C in the category of vector spaces, we define a concept called polarization. This process essentially transforms the structure of C from being graded under the action of a single torus to being invariant under the action of a larger torus consisting of n copies of the original one, where n is the dimension of the spaces making up C. We then delve into the creation of the tensor product of n copies of the ground field, denoted as $\otimes^n k$, and demonstrate how it acts on C. Notably, when the ground field is chosen as an algebraically closed field, we establish a direct connection between the invariant subspaces of the action of $\otimes^n k$ on C and the concept of polarization. This leads to the discovery that a specific parameter, referred to as the polarization degree, can be determined for each element of C. This parameter has distinct properties such as being additive under addition of elements from C and providing insight into the composition of the generated invariant polynomials. Furthermore, we establish that the parameter in question is invariant under the action of the Weyl group associated with the Lie loop of type A_n. If the field is not algebraically closed, we establish that the parameter in question becomes partially defined, and this leads to the discovery of a new, previously unreported parameter, also known as the ramification index of polarization, which has its own set of properties. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although these techniques typically involve the absorption or emission of light and its subsequent analysis, they generally lack the ability to directly determine phase information about the sample's nuclear structure. As a result, interpreting data from many of these techniques relies on assumptions or additional information about the sample. In contrast, real-space resonant x-ray scattering can provide phase information about both the electron and nuclear distributions within a sample. This paper introduces nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy, a technique that combines overcomplete frames of x-ray scattering data captured under resonant conditions and an iterative algebraic method to extract phase information. This approach minimizes the impact of incomplete algebraic frames and allows for the accurate determination of phase information. By applying a deconvolution algorithm to these frames, it's possible to obtain high-resolution maps of the nuclear phases associated with specific scattering patterns. These patterns can serve as fingerprints for identifying and studying different nuclear configurations within a sample in detail. To demonstrate this technique's effectiveness, it was applied to a model consisting of two interconnecting water molecules that are aligned with each other at their oxygen atoms. The resulting maps of the $d_{\omega r}$ parameters, which indicate the phase shifts of the x-ray scattering patterns, showed two distinct peaks that are $1.8\pi$ radians apart and are associated with the two water molecules. These results agree with previous studies that used alternative methods to investigate this system. In summary, the introduction of nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy enables the detailed analysis of water molecules aligned at their oxygen atoms and provides a general method for studying the phase distributions of complex nuclear structures that are difficult to access otherwise. In the future, this technique can be applied to aligned hydrogen bonds found in biological and organic materials, as well as to charged and defected state nuclei that are difficult to access and have been the subject of much speculation. A key property of cubic bipartite graphs is their effortless division into two disjoint groups of edge-colors, each containing an even number of times any particular vertex is encountered. This distinction holds true for all bipartite graphs with an odd number of edges, except those in a specific, newly defined class of graphs called robust edge-tinting bipartite graphs. A recent study demonstrated the existence of a 2-parameter family of 4-regular, non-orientable robust edge-tinting graphs based on a torus. This paper introduces another type of graph, with a different topological characteristic, to serve as a counterexample to a conjecture made by Alspac, Schmitt, and Scully. This newly created example consists of a non-orientable surface that is topologically equivalent to a double covers of an embedded Klein bottle and its associated 4-regular edge-tinting graph. This embedded graph within this non-orientable surface is distinct from the previously mentioned 2-parameters family of torus-based edge-tinting graphs. This newly created example specifically refutes a particular subconjecture of Alspac, Schmitt, and Scully that proposed all closed surfaces of genus greater than 2 would contain a specific kind of bipartite edge-tinting graph. This newly created example can be interpreted as a bipartite edge-tinting graph embedded within a surface that is topologically equivalent to a 9-holed non-orientable surface, with the particular designation of SN(9). Convolutional neural networks are prone to performance degradation and safety breaches when they are exposed to image data that has been affected by hardware malfunctions during acquisition. Our research focuses on investigating the underlying causes of these issues by analyzing how spatial failures in the input data influence the activation values within the network. We discovered that overactivation and activation restrictions are major obstacles to solving this problem. To tackle this challenge, we developed an innovative approach called activation range monitoring, which identifies areas within the network where overactivation and restrictions are likely to occur and suggests a new form of regularization called activation range constraints. Our results show that this approach yields comparable accuracy to stateoftheart methods while significantly enhancing the robustness of the network to failure-induced overactivation and constraints. When images contaminated with various types of hardware failures are classified using a ResNet-50 trained with our method, it achieves an average classification accuracy of 86% across all failure types. Our work prioritizes exploration over optimization and employs a straightforward optimization algorithm to enhance the robustness of the network, providing raw code that can be compiled with NVCC. Our research was conducted using PyTorch, a renowned deep learning framework. Our data, consisting of MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN, was affected by hardware failures that occurred during acquisition. Our approach generates a new form of feature maps called activation range maps, which are derived from the activation values across all layers of the network and are critical in identifying failures that affect both the low-level feature extraction layers and the classification layers. Our results show that the features extracted from these maps yield a high classification accuracy of 92% when trained on a reduced dataset, consisting of MNIST, CIFAR10, and a custom dataset called Failures. Our code is compatible with both PyTorch and TensorFlow. Our research demonstrated a security proof for a specific approach called activation range monitoring, which yields a bound of 2\sqrt{t} on the number of malicious attacks that can succeed within time t, assuming the attacker has limited knowledge about the network and the data. Our results show that the features extracted from the activation range maps that capture the failure patterns, when combined with a support vector machine, yield a high accuracy of 92% when trained on a dataset consisting of clean images and those affected by hardware failures. Our approach prioritizes efficiency over effectiveness and yields a low overhead of 10\% compared to stateoftheart methods, achieving this result with a simple optimization algorithm,, namely Adam, on large datasets consisting of one million training examples

This achievement is seen in the VIO track of the Visual Inertial Odometry and SLAM Competition held at ICRA 2022, where our model achieved the lowest error rates for both 6DOF estimation and feature reconstruction. Additionally, it outperformed existing models on the VIO and VIO+ feature reconstruction tasks. With its external memory focus, EMA-VIO effectively exploits temporal information by prioritizing important cues, thus enhancing both intra and inter-trajectory consistency without relying on recurrent connections. This model also offers real-time performance due to localized memory access, further contributing to its success. We hope EMA-VIO will serve as a robust foundation for various visual-inertial navigation applications requiring temporal information. The code for EMA-VIO is available at https://github.com/Shuai-Ni/EMA-VIO.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. Despite processing and storage components in these systems being highly reliable, issues arise with data transmission, largely attributed to Josephson junction faults caused by unwanted light transmission. Thorough understanding of light transmission through these junctions in various configurations is essential for developing quantitative simulations of device behavior. This study employs near-field terahertz microscopy to analyze the light transmission patterns within coplanant microwave resonators, demonstrating that static and fluctuating light transmission patterns are determined by specific geometric arrangements and align with the curvature of a 2D parabola, thereby facilitating high accuracy simulations of these devices. A newly introduced dimensionless variable, the curvature parameter, is utilized in analyzing and validating the theoretical light transmission patterns against experimental findings, thereby enabling high precision simulations of these devices. This approach has been tested on a pronged microwave resonator configuration and yields accurate results even when only considering the effects of radiation. This research provides a highly effective analytical tool for the quantitative simulation of quantum components, and a newly developed dimensionless curvature parameter that can be utilized in a variety of light-driven junction configurations. It is also compatible with other similar configurations such as waveguides, optical microresonators and Josephson Metamaterials. It presents a comprehensive approach to understanding the long-term evolution of Venus' atmosphere. A hybrid atmospheric model is employed to simulate the planet's atmospheric development over an extended period of time, covering 500 million years. The model incorporates a quasi-analytical method to calculate the atmospheric composition and another that uses numerical integration to model the geological activity and climate system. These components work together to determine the orbital parameters, atmospheric circulation, surface temperature and pressure, chemical reactions, and plate tectonics. The results of these simulations demonstrate the complex interconnection between the atmosphere and surface of Venus. A notable feature of this model is the incorporation of oxygen in the form of oxides within the planet's core and mantle. It shows that the oxygen in the Venusian atmosphere originates from the core and mantle, released through volcanic activity. The model also highlights the significance of the oxygen cycle in the form of oxides within the core and mantle, the silicate weathering reaction that is essential for balancing the global carbonate system, and the need for a more comprehensive approach to understanding the Earth's own atmosphere and surface over an extended period of time. This research develops statistical methods for non-linear Hawkes process models that incorporate feedback dynamics, which are commonly used in neuroscience, finance, and seismology. A Bayesian approach is introduced to assess these models, enabling the evaluation of point and interval estimates for the system's parameters that influence the probability of events occurring. A distinguished feature of our method is the non-linear feedback parameter's imputation, as many of these parameters are found to be zero in real applications, thereby affecting the model's complexity and performance. Our approach involves testing whether the distribution of the feedback parameters is concentrated around zero, which facilitates model selection and reduces overfitting. Numerous simulations demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our methods, and a real-world seizure data analysis is presented as an application of these methods. It is shown that the model's ability to accurately identify the complex feedback dynamics underlying the seizure data is critical, as it enables the precise determination of the parameters governing the probability of seizures occurring, as well as the development of a simple, robust interval forecast of seizure onset times that outperforms existing approaches. A major obstacle in developing practical document extraction models is the excessive cost of collecting high-quality training labels, particularly when dealing with infrequent and specialized data sets that require expert knowledge to accurately label.  In this paper, a novel approach is presented that significantly minimizes the financial burden of labeling documents by employing a semi-supervised learning technique.  With as little as one percent of the data requiring human annotation, our approach leverages autoencoders to provide high-quality labels for the remaining ninety-nine percent of the data. Recent detections of gravitational waves by the LIGO and VIRGO collaborations offer a new avenue for observing neutron star-black hole mergers. While these observations are typically analyzed through matched-filtering, this method has limitations, mainly due to the need for an accurate model of the gravitational wave signal. As such, there may be multiple signals awaiting discovery. To address this challenge, we developed a convolutional neural network capable of categorizing and identifying signals from neutron star-black hole mergers. In our model, signals from low-mass mergers pose a particular problem due to their weak signals and diverse morphologies, requiring a specialized sub-network to achieve reliable classification. Our results show that this model can effectively classify signals from a wide range of mergers with low mass ratios, extending far below the current detection limits of advanced gravitational wave observatories. With an estimated 1000 estimated neutron star-black hole merger signals awaiting discovery in the LIGO O3 dataset, such a model could significantly enhance the efficiency of data analysis, potentially unlocking a much richer physics landscape from these events. To facilitate further development, we outline a suite of tools for training and using this model, including a customized dataset generator and a cloud-based training platform that leverages multiple machines and large amounts of computational resources. To demonstrate the value of this model in real-world applications, we used it to analyze a subset of the LIGO O3 dataset, identifying several previously unknown neutron star-black hole merger signals with low mass ratios. To ensure the validity of these findings, we propose a set of observational tests for these candidates, and provide a numerical solution for the gravitational wave signals emitted by these events. With hundreds of neutron star-black hole merger signals awaiting discovery, this model could be trained to target specific physical parameters of interest, such as spin, charge, or magnetic field, opening up a broad range of theoretical and phenomenological applications, and providing a new data analysis paradigm for multi-messenger astronomy. This study leverages a mathematical model of multi-group infections, combined with historical data on pandemic-related behavioral changes and urban demographics, to analyze how societal responses to the pandemic affect the disparities in SARS-CoV-2 transmission among these income groups. Leaping from qualitative to quantitative analysis, the researchers integrate a statistical method for estimating the impact of urban interactions on infection transmission rates, ultimately leading to a mathematical assessment of how the widening of income-related disparities in urban interactions during the pandemic exacerbated the existing spread of the virus. This is demonstrated using a real-world example from Beijing. This study highlights the significance of considering the complex effects of reduced social interactions on the spread of the virus and the critical role that urban interactions play in both pandemic control and the long-term consequences of the pandemic on a city's dynamics. This includes the notable income-related disparities in the spread of the virus and the various responses to the pandemic that affect individual behavior and urban planning decisions. This study's findings and approach can be valuable for other cities facing similar challenges and can be adapted to other infectious disease dynamics affected by human behavior and spatial interactions. Verifying news accuracy has become increasingly difficult in the information age, and this challenge will likely intensify as the amount of available news continues to grow. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages automatic text summarization technology to enhance a false news detection system, which was tested using a combination of real and artificial news data. The proposed method's performance was compared to a variety of baselines, demonstrating the value of using Google's BART model for both condensing and classifying false news. To account for the numerous artificial samples that could exist in real-world scenarios, the paper also introduces a new evaluation metric called the detection effective area. Despite its efficiency, the proposed approach was found to be inferior to a more sophisticated BERT-based system that utilizes a richer set of features, including those obtained from a multi-head self-attention mechanism employed in BART. To improve the proposed method and provide a roadmap for further improvements, the paper also presents a detailed analysis of the false news detection problem from a text summarization perspective. This analysis identifies key challenges and suggests a variety of research opportunities in both fields, including the study of conditional true summaries and the development of automatic text summarization systems that can differentiate between various document abstraction modes. To facilitate future research, the paper has been made available on arXiv, along with a related GitHub repository that contains the implemented system and artificial data generator. This system and generator can be used to create artificial false news datasets with controlled characteristics, enabling the development of robust detection systems that are capable of withstanding various artificial manipulations and summarization styles. This in turn can help prevent artificial adversarial examples from being used in malicious ways, for example in security attacks against open-source false news detection systems. This work examines how curvature impacts the behavior of geodesic lines on a specific type of random surface known as Gaussian stochastic fields, specifically 2D Gaussian fields defined by mean-square differentiable functions. It is demonstrated that there is a direct link between the natural measure associated with geodesic lines, the curvature of the surface, and the second-order derivatives of the defining function. This relationship is then utilized to comprehend the characteristics of geodesic lines in variable curved environments, offering a contrasting insight to the commonly observed phenomenon of lines naturally diverging from each other in random, uniformly curved surfaces. A special case study is also conducted on surfaces defined by Brownian motion, revealing that lines tend to converge to each other in a manner influenced by both their local characteristics and the surface's inherent properties. This in turn leads to the identification of a specific probability distribution that these lines are likely to be associated with. For individuals with visual impairments to navigate safely and independently within unfamiliar indoor spaces, obtaining and interpreting spatial information through sound is vital. Present navigation aids provide users with turn-by-turn instructions or a limited, often one-dimensional representation of the environment's layout, which can become confusing, especially in complex settings. To enhance the navigation experience, we've developed an innovative method called HiTMap, which creates a hierarchical two-dimensional map that comprises multiple separate layers, each representing a different aspect of the environment. The primary map serves as a high-level overview of the space, while more detailed submaps focus on specific areas or paths. To follow this HiTMap structure, we've designed a text-based description that includes hierarchical markers to guide users through the navigation process. Our system simultaneously generates both the HiTMap diagram and the corresponding text-based representation to aid navigation. To evaluate HiTMap, we created three diverse simulation scenarios and compared our method's performance to that of a state-of-the-art navigation system. HiTMap's navigation instructions were found to be more concise and easier to follow than the existing system, particularly in larger, more intricate environments. To assess the accessibility improvements offered by HiTMap, we conducted an independent usability study among visually impaired participants navigating real-world indoor environments represented in our simulation. The study revealed a notable reduction in confusion and navigation time when using HiTMap over the baseline system. The results of our evaluation suggest that HiTMap can effectively support the independent navigation of visually impaired individuals within unfamiliar indoor environments and provides a valuable platform for further research and development in accessible navigation systems. This study delves into the electronic and magnetic arrangements of rutile-TiO2 doped with the elements carbon and nitrogen, situated in the p-block of the periodic table. Using a 25-atom supercell, we examined the magnetic properties of Ti0.875C0.125O2 and Ti0.875N0.125O2 for both defective and doped configurations. In the defective state, we found that both materials exhibit antiferromagnetic behavior. When doped, the carbon and nitrogen elements occupied interstitial spaces between TiO2 units and displayed either nonmagnetic or ferrimagnetic properties, dependent on the oxygen vacancy presence. Notably, ferrimagnetic behavior in the doped state is rare and has only previously been reported in bulk Cr-doped TiO2. These outcomes are also comparable to earlier one-dimensional TiO2 models that displayed either nonmagnetic or ferrimagnetic arrangements. These findings suggest that both defective and doped TiO2 structures exhibit stable magnetic arrangements, indicating their potential for magnetic applications. Moreover, these results include the calculation of direct and indirect bandgap widths as well as the electron affinity, which can be useful for evaluating their photovoltaic and catalytic properties.

To strengthen the case for the top quark's elastic production at the Large Hadron Collider, we propose a new method that targets a distinctive signature in elastic proton-proton collisions. By focusing on events where a single top quark is produced along with a high-transverse momentum jet, we can create a distinguishing feature that sets it apart from inelastic top-quark production. To achieve this, we need to identify events containing a single top quark, where the missing transverse energy is substantial, allowing us to differentiate it from inelastic processes. To successfully implement this method, we require at least 25.4 inverse femtobarns of data from the CMS detector at a 13.6 TeV collision energy. This proposal can significantly enhance the potential for detecting elastic top-quark production at the Large Hadron Collider, potentially reaching as high as 4.4 times the predicted value for the Standard Model. This approach is viable for both the CMS and ATLAS experiments, offering a valuable opportunity to either confirm the existence of elastic top-quark production or establish a more precise limit on its rate. If successful, it could also pave the way for searching the same interaction that produces the Higgs boson. To facilitate this at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, we outline a strategy that involves modifying the elastic top-quark production analysis to make it more effective against background noise, thus extending the reach for detecting a 125 GeV topological Higgs resonance or establishing a more precise limit on the Standard Model. This includes adopting optimized jet and b-tag selections, incorporating information from forward detectors, and employing machine learning-based methods to better identify elastic top-quark events. This potential for discovery or more precise limits on the Standard Model extends to the future Electron-Positron Colliders, offering an opportunity to either detect the elastic production of top quarks at much lower energy levels or set a more rigorous limit on the rate of this interaction. This in turn could influence the design of these future colliders and their corresponding operating energies. In 1993, Erdos and Gyárfás posed the following problem: For any given natural numbers $r$ and $s$, is there a large enough $n$ such that every monochromatic subgraph within a $r$-edge colored graph of $n$ edges has at least $s$ connected components consisting of the same color with the maximum possible density? This paper refers to this unsolved problem as the strong version of their conjecture. Our research focuses on a weaker conjecture where instead of an arbitrary connected component, we consider bipartite components. We successfully classify the possible versions of the weaker conjecture and determine the Ramsey numbers for the strongest version where the components can have any degree $r$ and the maximum possible density is $s$. We also examine the version for an specific degree $r$ and determine the corresponding Ramsey numbers for a range of densities up to $r/2$. Additionally, we provide lower and upper bounds for the Ramsey numbers of the remaining versions not included in the previous categories. We achieve these results by applying various probabilistic methods including a novel bipartite ramsey theory. Our findings also shed light on a similar problem involving multicolored bipartite components. We believe these discoveries will help pave the way for further advancements and potential solutions to the original strong conjecture proposed by Erdos and Gyárfás. We compare our results with the existing upper and lower bounds from other research papers and provide some open problems for future exploration. Our research on the weaker versions of the conjecture and our innovative bipartite ramsey theory can be applied to a broader context involving multicolored components in infinite ramsey theory. We intend to investigate this broader context in our upcoming work. Our current paper focuses on the weaker versions of the conjecture and the corresponding Ramsey numbers for the component of a specific graph and provides some open problems that we believe are important and worthy of further exploration. We hope these discoveries and the challenges they pose will contribute to the ongoing discussion and help in the search for a solution to the original strong conjecture proposed by Erdos and Gyárfás. We believe that with the progress we made and the new tools we developed, ourselves and other researchers will be able to tackle the strong conjecture and eventually find its solution. We also made some significant open problem proposals that we believe are crucial and we hope they will guide us towards the solution of the strong conjecture and provide a better understanding of the ramsey theory and its associated components. This research develops a miniature temperature detection circuit that utilizes only one op-amp and achieves precise and wide-range temperature identification with minimal power consumption. Based on the CMRC (Complementary Mirror Resistance Conjecture) principle, the op-amp operates in a balanced state with conjugate resistance mirrors that converge towards an equilibrium point, thereby obtaining the temperature resistance value. A comprehensive analysis of the circuit's behavior is performed through a detailed analytical model, enabling the development of an accurate and efficient design. A $0.24{\deg}C$ temperature resolution is obtained across an $66.6{\deg}C$ temperature range with only $1.4{\deg}C$ error and $1.06nJ$ energy consumption per transformation, all in a $0.0066{mm^2}$ area. The temperature detection circuit can be applied across various fields including microcontrollers, wireless sensor nodes, and low-power integrated circuits. The design has been verified through both theoretical analysis and actual implementation on a $0.18{\mu m}$ CMOS process. The test results align closely with the predicted data, confirming the validity and effectiveness of the temperature detection circuit. The design has been patented (Patent Number: ZL201910555597.9). The temperature detection circuit can be tailored to suit a range of applications by adjusting design parameters including the bridge resistance, feedback capacitance, supply voltage, and threshold voltage. The impact of these parameters on the circuit's behavior has been assessed and presented in a set of graphs, enabling seamless adaptation of the design to various temperature ranges and microcontrollers. The temperature detection circuit has been further optimized for low power consumption, minimal area, and precise temperature identification in small temperature ranges. A variant of the design has been developed that utilizes two op-amp circuits, resulting in an even more precise temperature resistance value with only a slight increase in power consumption and area. The validity of the variant design has been confirmed through actual implementation on a $0.18{\mu m}$ CMOS process. This research generalize two significant concepts from the field of differential geometry to geometric groupoids and stacks. Firstly, it defines geometric configurations as objects that can be varied smoothly within the realm of these groupoids and stacks, building on the principles of geometric geometry. Secondly, it establishes a direct relationship between these configurations and vector bundles, utilizing the concept of sections as a unifying framework. This connection is made explicit through the use of pullback and restriction maps that define a sheaf of sets. Notably, when the groupoids in question are trivial, this reduces to the classic concept of geometric configurations over a given manifold. Additionally, this generalization incorporates and builds upon two established theorems from the field of differential geometry. Lastly, it also explores and develops several key concepts for both groupoids and stacks, such as integrals of geometric configurations and algebraic geometric constructions known as geodesic flows. These developments are demonstrated through specific examples of stacks related to Lie algebras and their respective geodesic flows. Specially, it shows that any Lie algebra can be integrated into a stack that contains its geodesic flow configurations, revealing a direct connection between these stacks and their underlying algebraic foundations.

This study investigates whether certain types of invariant random fields, specifically those defined on the sphere, can be distinguished from one another by a single statistical method. A key tool in this investigation is the one-step prediction error of Bayesian methods, which serves as an intuitive and widely used approach for assessing model performance. However, this error also has a more profound statistical significance, related to the entropy of the random field being estimated. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we examine a concrete and well-known example - the Dirichlet process - and its polynomially decaying covariance function, which helps illustrate the one-step prediction error's distinction between two types of random fields. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a statistical framework for evaluating the sphere's random fields and comparing them using one-step Bayesian methods. This comparison takes the form of a non-decreasing, convex function, which enables us to identify the random fields that can be distinguished from one another using these methods. In neural machine translation, designing a focus mechanism is crucial for selecting words to attend to to produce more natural-sounding output word orders in left-to-right languages like Arabic and Hebrew. Current focus models typically limit the target word to the next word in the output sequence. This study challenges that approach by exploring a look-ahead focus model that allows the target word to be further in the sequence, enabling greater freedom for word order rearrangement. Our experiments on data sets in Arabic, Hebrew, and English show that a 2-word look-ahead focus model generally outperforms the conventional approach, and our corpus-level analysis finds a positive correlation between the extent of allowed freedom and translation quality improvement. Notably, our results also indicate that a 2-word look-ahead focus model suffices for both subject-verb and verb-subject creation scenarios. To facilitate deeper understanding, additional analysis is provided on word order rearrangement events. Our proposed approach can be applied to other machine generation tasks, such as neural machine summarization. Our code is available online at GitHub.

The growth of grid computing was significantly driven by a translational approach in the United States, which adapted global networking technology for practical use in various fields. This has been an area of interest for scholars in the field of Science and Technology Studies (STS). Until now, research has primarily been conducted from a historical perspective, focusing on the early years of grid computing and the impact of a translational approach. Our analysis expands on this by examining the long-term consequences of this development. We studied the grid computing community's knowledge base, specifically the gLite framework and its implementations in Europe and Latin America. Our analysis reveals how a translational approach that prioritizes shared technical standards across different regions can lead to grid computing adoption, contrary to the prevailing views of scholars within the field of STS who see this as unusual. Instead, we found that it facilitates cooperation and allows for the diverse, complex needs of various fields to be met with this technology. This in turn enables a better understanding of the long-term, societal implications of a translational approach that adopts global networking technology. We also discovered how a translational approach can be applied to other fields that have been negatively impacted by the gLite framework, such as eScience. A combined dark matter model, known as CDMS, has been a well-established and experimentally verified theory since 2006, according to a recent study. This study rebuilds the CDMS model while incorporating a new approach that takes into account scattering effects and verifies that the model's parameters are accurately defined. A novel analysis reveals that the combined model consists of two distinct components: a scalar sector that resembles the Standard Model and an vector sector that closely resembles the Standard Model with an Abelian gauge symmetry. Notably, the addition of a specific type of particle, called a "dark photon," was a direct consequence of the combined model's analysis, demonstrating that it can be a natural outcome of the fundamental theory that underlies the CDMS phenomenon. As such, this study emphasizes that the term "dark matter" may require a more precise definition, potentially being a misnomer in some cases. This study's approach to the CDMS model also offers a more effective and experimentally verifiable "hidden sector" that could be detected through the production of "dark photons" during high-energy particle collisions or through astrophysical observations, presenting a promising area of research for future studies. A more detailed understanding of this model, along with its predicted properties and potential manifestations, are the subject of this study's concluding analysis. A Lagrangian that describes the combined dark matter model in its scalar and vector forms, along with its predicted particle content and symmetry group, are presented in this study. This research predicts that the production of "dark photons" during particle collisions or through certain astrophysical processes would result in the detection of a specific and distinctive signal, offering a tangible goal for both ongoing and future experimental efforts. This study's approach to the CDMS model also offers a more general principle of constructing hidden sector particles that could be a fundamental aspect of the underlying theory, rather than a phenomenon exclusive to the combined model. This principle could potentially be applied to other areas of physics, such as the Standard Model, as well as to other types of "dark" particles, making it a significant and far-reaching contribution to the field. Our analysis provides consequences for the efficient field theories of neutrino and dark matter energy based on the latest data from the BaBar experiment, specifically for the $J/\psi$ decay into an invisible particle accompanied by a photon. We evaluate the total decay rate of $J/\psi$ into an invisible particle as well as its decay rate into a photon and an invisible particle. Our calculations take into account both the magnetic moment of the dark particle and its coupling to a dark Higgs field, and we consider two different dark sector scenarios - one with a minimal approach where the dark particle has only an extremely tiny magnetic moment, and another with an extension of the Standard Model known as the two Higgs doublet model. We take into account all relevant $J/\psi$ decay modes that could influence the efficiency of $J/\psi$ data collection and we take these efficiencies from the BaBar experiment. We determine the currently allowed efficient field theory parameters based on their average over existing data sets from the BaBar experiment. We also analyze the constraints placed on these parameters by a single BaBar data set and we compare our results with those from other experiments such as the BESIII. We discuss in detail the most restrictive BaBar parameter constraints that arise from the $J/\psi$ decay into two electrons or a muon pair, and we show how these constraints vary when we use different dark sector theories. We then determine the allowed efficient field theory parameters from a combination of BaBar and other experimental data, and we discuss the outcomes for the theories of neutrino and dark energy. We conclude that the data from the BaBar experiment places very strong constraints on the magnetic moment of the dark particle, and these constraints arise from the $J/\psi$ decay into an invisible particle rather than its decay into an electron or a muon pair. We compare our results with those from other experiments such as the BESIII and with the outcomes from other analyses of the $J/\psi$ data. We analyze the outcomes for the theories of neutrino and dark energy, and we show that the data from the BaBar experiment places very strong constraints on the parameter $f^2$ from the minimal approach, on the magnetic moment $\mu_D$ of the dark particle, and on the mass $m_{\phi}$ of the dark Higgs field. We discuss the variations of these constraints when we use different dark sector theories, and we show that the data from the BaBar experiment places very strong constraints on the efficient field theories of neutrino and dark energy

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum evaluation methods that can be applied in various multi-dimensional contexts, including time series, images, and genomic data. A key finding is that even with this type of movement, the number of periods exhibiting persistence over a given duration still adheres to an exponential distribution. It is shown that despite the presence of a magnetic field, there is little indication of a helical current, however the plasma properties are well-explained by a model highlighting the significance of electron drift in plasma dynamics. A key challenge in analyzing histopathology images lies in pinpointing and extracting problematic nuclei. To achieve this efficiently, various automated techniques have been developed, but they often struggle with instances where nuclei are near or on the image border. To overcome this limitation, a new approach called W-Net has been proposed, which uses a dual-stage convolutional network to locate and remove background areas that contain extracellular elements including nuclei, before identifying and highlighting the remaining malignant nuclei. Evaluations using two types of images, specifically lymph node and breast tissue samples, have shown that W-Net outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. With its capacity to accurately delineate problematic nuclei, W-Net provides a crucial data for machine learning-based classification and feature extraction protocols. The code for W-Net has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrfteam/WNet. Moreover, pre-trained models are accessible on Google Drive at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/?fuser=true&usp=sharing. Human experts have also validated the output of W-Net on multiple occasions, giving it a 7 out of 10 score in terms of reliability. With its high accuracy and reasonable computational requirements, W-Net can be effectively used in various biomedical applications. The proposed network serves as a foundational module for constructing more complex models, as demonstrated by the inclusion of two additional features, namely, Inception-Net and Dilation-Net, that utilize W-Net as a feature extraction protocol. To demonstrate this, a dataset for identifying and extracting mitotic nuclei has been created, along with two complex variants that combine W-Net with Inception-Net and Dilation-Net, showing a significant improvement in accuracy scores. To facilitate reliable training for a wider range of tasks, W-Net has been designed with a simple structure requiring a limited number of hyperparameters. The proposed approach has numerous biomedical applications, including but not limited to, cancer diagnosis, immunophenotyping, and transfusion medicine. With its high precision and automatic nucleus segmentation capabilities, W-Net enables efficient annotation of large image datasets, exponentially increasing the amount of training data available for deep learning protocols, such as convolutional neural networks and reinforcement learning-based methods. To validate the generality of W-Net, the proposed approach has been successfully applied to various types of images, including breast, lymph node, colon, pancreas, and skin tissue samples, resulting in precision and recall scores of 0.85,

Let's consider a group G acting on a set X and another group H acting on a set Y. The regional converse theorem links the structure of G to that of H when given certain conditions are met, specifically that there are subgroup isomorphisms from G to H within X and Y, among other requirements. This paper formulates a more specific variant of this theorem, known as the regional converse for odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups in positive characteristic, and it demonstrates that this variant can be derived from a broader version of the converse theorem. It also provides a direct proof of the positive characteristic version of the regional converse for the mentioned groups. This proof relies on the application of group classification, local Galois theory, and certain properties of Belyi transformations. It is notable that this proof can be seen as a variation of the original proof from Haran's work, which was based on the use of Weyl's dual, class field theory, and the Abelianisation of Belyi's branch locus. This paper's result can be used as a component of the broader converse theorem mentioned earlier. It is also worth mentioning that G can be shown to have a particular non-trivial normal subgroup if H is simple, specifically if H is closely related to a specific quadratic extension of the base field F. This result can be obtained under the condition that there are subgroup isomorphisms from G to H within X and Y, among other requirements. It is then demonstrated that this non-trivial normal subgroup has a specific order, providing a further classification. It is also possible to derive a variant of this result known as the weak regional converse theorem. This variant of the theorem can be used as a component of the broader converse theorem mentioned earlier known as the global converse theorem. It is then demonstrated that this global converse theorem can be applied to a specific non-trivial normal subgroup of G known as the symplectic group Sp6(2r) over a field with a characteristic of 2. It is then shown that this normal subgroup has a specific order, providing a further classification. It is also possible to derive a variant of this result known as the weak regional converse theorem. This variant of the theorem can be used as a component of the broader converse theorem mentioned earlier known as the global converse theorem. It is then demonstrated that this global converse theorem can be applied to a specific non-trivial normal subgroup of G known as the symplectic group Sp6(2r) over a field with a characteristic of 2.

We demonstrate how this approach can be used to gain a deeper understanding of why GCNNs behave as they do. To achieve this, we use a $K$-nearest neighbor network that can be trained to match the results of a much more complex $K$-nearest neighbor graph filtration, allowing us to visually see how features are combined and why GCNNs behave as they do. We show that this simple approach can be used to gain a more intuitive understanding of graph convolutional neural networks and provide code so others can use and modify it. We also discuss some of the limitations of this approach and offer some advice on how to get the most out of it. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the precise identification and characterization of tissue pathologies by analyzing the mechanical properties of tissues. Despite its advantages, the clinical application of elastography has been limited due to its relatively low resolution compared to B-mode imaging. The Virtual Origin SA technique presents an innovative method for improving the lateral resolution in elastography, demonstrated through both theoretical simulations and a clinical trial involving breast tissue. This approach leverages the unique capabilities of SA imaging to provide the necessary information for accurate estimation of tissue displacement, eliminating the need for a physical aperture and allowing the derivation of resolution-matched elastography and B-mode images. When applied to real-world data, the results show that the Virtual Origin SA technique yields a significant 2.5-fold improvement in the contrast-to-noise ratio and accurately differentiates between various tissue types, as confirmed through histological analysis in a clinical trial involving breast cancer. This research highlights the Virtual Origin SA technique as a promising means for enhancing the spatial resolution in elastography, critical for the accurate identification and characterization of tissue pathology. This approach is versatile and can be employed with a wide range of imaging modalities, including elastography, diffusion-weighted, and magnetic resonance imaging. This technology holds significant potential for various medical applications, including the analysis of tumors, liver diseases, and muscle disorders, among others. Further advancements of the Virtual Origin SA technique hold promise in facilitating the clinical transition of elastography from a qualitative to a quantitative analysis method. This technology can be made more accessible through the use of existing SA imaging hardware and software, taking into account a few minor adjustments and operational guidelines. This research demonstrates the capabilities of the Virtual Origin SA technique through a series of numerical simulations, breast cancer trials, and muscle elastography experiments, providing a clear path for its extension to other medical imaging modalities and various tissue types. This technology has been commercially developed under the name "SA Elastography" by the company Microtronics Inc. based on the University of Utah research findings. This commercial system has been successfully used in various medical applications, both in the United States and abroad, with FDA clearance obtained in 2019. This technology has also been further enhanced under a new project titled "SA Elastography with Multiple Views" aimed at improving the resolution and accuracy of tissue property analysis through the registration of multiple SA images, taking into account the variations in tissue properties and image quality. This project has the potential to break through the 1-mm spatial resolution barrier in elastography, enabling the precise visualization of small tumor sizes

Humans and computers collaborate through algorithms, yet our language systems seem to prioritize expressing to humans over instructing computers. This one-sided approach results in algorithms being formulated in a way that is difficult to understand, making it challenging for people to accurately execute them. To address this issue, we propose a new hypothesis – that people follow algorithms based on a set of rational rules and simple common sense – and support it with a comprehensive analysis. To express these guidelines, we developed a one-step translation process that converts existing algorithm descriptions into a new, intuitive format called Pseudocode of Proportional Intention. In a controlled study, participants who used this format demonstrated significant improvements in accurately completing tasks. Our findings also offer practical suggestions for creating more effective algorithm instructions. To facilitate further research and real-world applications, we are making Pseudocode of Proportional Intention available to the public. With its potential to bridge the understanding gap between humans and computers, this framework can be valuable for developing intelligent algorithm demonstrations and helping people comprehend and complete tasks according to algorithms. To that end, we present a user-friendly interface called Rational Pseudocode or RPF for brief, which allows anyone to create similar algorithm instructions simply by demonstrating the corresponding task. To demonstrate the versatility of RPF, we applied it successfully to a complex algorithm from a leading artificial intelligence research organization. To move forward, we outline a promising research path that involves refining RPF, integrating it with existing teaching AI models, and evaluating its capabilities in various real-world scenarios. To contribute to this mission, we are releasing RPF under an open-source license. With its ability to generate high-quality demonstrations and instructions from just a few doable examples, RPF offers a valuable, low-cost, and scalable way for organizations that create and use algorithms for a living to improve their specifications, save time and money, and accelerate their innovation. To that end, we provide a detailed financial analysis of the costs associated with using RPF. In the context of a dynamic $k$-means clustering among changing datasets, we've developed an efficient algorithm that balances data points into nearly perfectly sized groups and minimizes the total distance between points and their assigned cluster centers. This efficient algorithm has two main characteristics: it can process new data arrivals in roughly linear time and guarantees an optimal solution for a smaller, more manageable subproblem. We've proven that this algorithm's groups are within a small factor of the optimal groups, specifically a factor of $O(\sqrt{k}\log k)$, which is demonstrated through a hypothetical optimal group structure known as a centered ball partition. We've also shown that in a decreasing dataset scenario, we can reduce the factor to $O(k)$ by creating a new data arrival order that prioritizes points further from the existing centers. Additionally, we've established a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{k})$ on the factor of any dynamic algorithm for a specific centered ball partition, thereby establishing the correctness of our factor guarantee for a particular scenario as a upper against a relevant lower. We've implemented this algorithm as a part of a larger dynamic $k$-means algorithm and compared it to several alternative approaches through a clustering-based text classification experiment using twenty datasets. We've also applied this algorithm to a real-life customer segmentation analysis task. All implementation code is publicly available. We've previously published an earlier, less efficient version of this algorithm as arXiv:1805.10483. We recommend the algorithm for real-world applications involving dynamic data clustering. We believe the current version of the algorithm holds value as an optimal solution for the specific centered ball partition problem and mayful also as a benchmark against which to evaluate any dynamic clustering algorithm. We introduce a novel framework for strategic decision-making in complex environments that can be characterized by a web-like division of stochastic games. This framework is specifically tailored to address a distinctive class of games known as "pursuit-withdrawal" or "chaser-slayer" scenarios, where one agent seeks to capture or capture another agent intent on escaping. A key differentiating feature of this framework is the presence of multiple levels of hierarchy in the games it represents. To tackle this problem, we developed an hierarchical pursuit-withdrawal model and associated value function approximation method. This method can be effectively learned using a combination of policy-based and value-based reinforcement learning techniques. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in both simplified and more intricate hierarchical scenarios. This work presents a distinctive contribution to the field of large-scale stochastic games, particularly in capturing the intricate web-based structures often present in real-world scenarios. This research is further accompanied by an open-source game designed to illustrate the complexity of these environments. This game, known as "Hierarchical Maze", is made available to the public along with the associated code used to conduct the experiments presented in this paper. This code is based on the popular PyTorch reinforcement learning platform. This work is also published as a proceedings paper for the AAAI conference. This research was previously published in the AAAI conference under the title "Hierarchical Pursuit-Withdrawal Games". This paper, the related code, and the Hierarchical Maze game are all available on the public GitHub repository. This research was funded by the National Science Foundation. This work involves a hierarchical chase-and-escape game where a group of distinct agents with varying goals escape from another distinct group of agents intent on capturing them. This problem is unlike other stochastic games due to the presence of multiple levels of hierarchy. This research focuses on an efficient method for identifying and measuring W and Z bosons in high-energy muon collision data. As requiring opposite-sign muon signatures in small pseudoradiant ranges isn't very efficient, a new approach is proposed where W and Z bosons are characterized by their rapidity distributions rather than the angles between the muons. Since the W and Z bosons have distinct mass scales, their distribution patterns differ significantly. As a result, the proposed method can co-analyze W and Z production processes in the same collision energy, and it yields reliable estimates for the average W and Z boson rapidity distributions, cumulative densities, and average energies. A simulated LHC @ 13.6 TeV data set demonstrating this method's applicability has also been created. Our research involves creating an intricate reinforcement learning system with multiple, interconnected modules, each focused on a distinct task. Contrary to traditional reinforcement learning approaches, where a single, unified representation serves all objectives, our modular design utilizes separate sub-representations for each task. By doing so, we minimize the risk of performance decline when adding new tasks. Our modular system demonstrates a notable ability to withstand the negative effects often associated with multi-task training, as it rapidly becomes overfit to the first task learned. Our design also enables a modular, step-by-step learning approach, where each task is trained individually before being combined. Our results show that this system can handle a wide range of challenging scenarios, surpassing both non-modular multi-task systems and separate single-task systems. Our code is available online.

By applying a variational method within a tight-binding model, the inter-atomic exchange interaction $J$ is also determined and found to be influenced by the orbital mixing, with $J$ being sensitive to whether it's mapped to an effective $t_{2g}$, $e_g$, or an intermediate band case. This complexity in 5d $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ materials is compared to 4d counterparts, revealing that the same amount of orbital mixing in 4d compounds results in much larger electron correlation effects in 5d compounds due to the narrower 4d bandwidths. This in turn leads to (e.g.) $J$ being much smaller in 5d compounds, with $J$ being directly influenced by the bandwidth in a way that's dependent on the fill factor. This study highlights the importance of accurately modeling $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing when studying transition metal compounds, and the need for a more nuanced understanding of 4d and 5d physics that takes into account the distinct bandwidths of these elements. This is particularly relevant for investigating the magnetic interactions in 5d compounds and their potential for exhibiting strong correlation behaviors. This work is accompanied by freely accessible numerical data that can be utilized for further analysis and new calculations. This paper builds on the concept of relative quantum homology, which was previously established for compact, oriented surfaces of genus greater than zero in [C1, C2, AGM, AGM2]. We demonstrate that relative quantum homology is invariant under a specific subgroup of the mapping class group, specifically consisting of partial and mixed simple closed curves, as well as certain combinations of bipolarized Dehn twists. This invariance holds when using a particular choice of symplectic extension and collection of nondegenerate symplectic forms. Furthermore, we show that relative quantum homology is invariant under 2+1 handle additions along nondegenerate nodes. This results in an enhanced version of relative quantum homology, which we refer to as extended relative quantum homology. This extended version then serves as the fundamental object to study symplectic field theory, providing a direct relationship without the need for further correction factors. This extension and its properties are demonstrated through explicit computations for tori with specific marked points. This involves analyzing the behavior of extended relative quantum homology under symplectic rational transformations, specifically showing that it is invariant under a specific set of curve-addition operations along which the form remains nondegenerate. This in turn enables us to define and calculate the Ikehata invariant for these surfaces. This research is also accompanied by a companion paper that explores and expands on these findings for more complex surfaces. This current paper is also the first in a series of papers that aim to establish and investigate a broader, more comprehensive structure called the quantum Floer homology system. This system serves as an integrated and systematic framework for studying and analyzing various mathematical objects and their properties, and it has the potential to contribute to and advance both pure and applied research in the field. This potential is demonstrated through a pair of examples presented in the companion paper [D]. The safety of radiological technicians can be ensured by equipping them with suitable protection gear during fluoro-assisted surgeries and procedures. However, over-exposure to X-rays poses a risk to their health. Patients diagnosed with specific conditions require higher levels of radiation to obtain a clear image, necessitating longer exposition times for radiological technicians. To mitigate this risk, only those patients requiring elevated exposition times can be given a contrast media, hence a quicker image enhancement technique is crucial. Our primary objective is to develop an AI-based chest X-ray enhancement tool prioritizing the modification of images belonging to patients diagnosed with certain illnesses. By focusing on eight common diseases, our model achieves notable improvements in both structural and textual image quality assessment metrics, demonstrating its potential to prioritize safe radiation levels while minimizing the exposition time required for surgeries and procedures. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepHealthGroup/Illness-Aware-Image-Modification. Our tool is user-friendly, allowing for a simple command-line interface as seen in Figure 8, and an interactive web-based interface at http://0.0.0.0:8001/. Our model's limited memory prevents it from being trained on real-world datasets, an issue we hope future memory-enhanced models will address. With some diseases having hundreds of subtypes, incorporating them all may require the development of tailored models, an approach we hope will be explored further. Our code provides a solid foundation for such models, as seen in Figure 9, and we suggest several research directions in Section 7. With 20% of the dataset classified as normal, our model struggles with lung cancer, mesothelioma, and pleura diseases, often mistaking healthy tissues for abnormal ones, as shown in Figure 10 and Figure 11. Our model tends to overcorrect images, as seen in Figure 12, and we propose several improvement avenues in Section 7. With further advancements, our tool and future models can be integrated into radiological assistance platforms and AI-powered teleradiology systems, as shown in Figure 13. ViDaExpert is an application that examines and visualizes high-dimensional vector data.
It is particularly useful for conducting principal component analysis (PCA) and
singular value decomposition (SVD) on vectors, as well as for performing and
evaluating dimensionality reduction techniques such as classic PCA, PCA with
weighting and filtering options, and weighted SVD.
Additionally, ViDaExpert enables the creation of scatter plots based on the
generated representations and facilitates the assessment of different
dimensionality reduction methodologies.
The application is designed to be user-friendly and features an intuitive
interface that allows for efficient operation through command lines.
ViDaExpert is primarily intended for researchers operating in the field of
machine learning but also offers a wide range of capabilities that can be
utilized directly, making it suitable for an expansive spectrum of users
including, but not limited to, data analysts and experts in artificial
intelligence. The application is available for use on Windows-based systems.
